name: Singed Squire
text: Upon an upturned helmet sits a squire with a shield across his knees and no eyebrows upon his face. The shield is scorched black in front, and so is the greater part of the squire. "Do not chase the bull," he says, before you can ask him anything. "If ever you meet a shaggy bull with the mane of a horse and horns that curl right back upon themselves, you will think that such horns are useless and that you may safely chase it. I beg of you, do not."

options.label: Name the beast that did this to him

pass.outcome: "A bonnacon," you say, and he looks upon you as one sufferer upon another. "You have read your Pliny, and so you know that its horns curl too far back to be of any use. Therefore it runs, and as it runs it sprays the ground behind it with dung that burns like fire, over three iugera, which is near two acres. My master is at his bath." He shares his burn salve with you, against the day when you meet the next one.
pass.chronicle: Named the squire's beast a bonnacon. It burns what follows. Got his salve.

fail.outcome: "A fire-bull?" says he, with a sigh. "It is a bonnacon, and Pliny had word of it from the shepherds of Paeonia. Its horns curl too far back to be of use, and so it runs, spraying burning dung over near two acres behind it. My master went to his bath yesterday, and he has not yet come out of it."
fail.chronicle: A singed squire told me of a bull called a bonnacon. New to me.

road.hint: Never give chase to a bull that defends itself from the hinder end.

options.label: Give him something to eat and hear the rest
options.outcome: He eats like a man who has long lived upon nothing but his pride. "In some seasons it has its lair a floor or two below us," he says, "and cold will slow it. Get close before it can turn about, or else keep a wall between you and its hindquarters. And take this with you, for my master says that he never wishes to see a bottle again."
options.chronicle: Fed the singed squire. Never chase the shaggy bull. Cold slows it.

road.hint: A squire who has eaten may tell the rest of his tale.

options.label: Leave him to his scorch marks
options.outcome: "Remember that it comes from the back!" he calls after you as you go upon your way.

name: Gikk
text: A small goblin crouches trembling in the corner with a fresh bruise above one eye, and in his claws he holds up a trinket. "No hurt! No hurt! Gikk not with the band now. Band make Gikk carry fire-pots, Gikk drop one, Gikk run." He casts a fearful look over his shoulder. "Gikk give shiny for not-stabbing. Gikk know where band sleeps."

options.label: Accept the trinket and let him go
options.outcome: Gikk thrusts the trinket into your hands and scrambles away into a crack in the wall that you had not marked until now. It is wonderfully well made, and you suspect that it belonged until lately to another of his band.

options.label: Feed him, and ask him to show you the floor
options.outcome: Gikk eats with both hands, and afterward with one claw he draws the whole floor in the dust, showing you where the band sleeps, where the fire-pots are kept and where the way goes down. "Gikk's grandmother was kobold," he says proudly. "Mine-goblin. Old miners curse her for a blue ore that give no silver and fill the furnace with poison smoke. They name it after her: kobold. You say cobalt."
options.chronicle: Fed Gikk, a runaway goblin. He drew me the whole floor in the dust.

road.hint: A runaway can show you where his old band sleeps.

options.label: Shoo him away
options.outcome: Gikk yelps and flees with his shiny, and for a little while you hear his small feet pattering away into the dark, and after them a sound that may be sobbing.

name: Very Small Rat King
text: Three rats whose tails are knotted together look down upon you from a little cairn of pebbles, and the middle one wears a bottle cap upon its head for a crown. It squeaks at you with evident authority and the other two squeak as if in agreement, so that they seem to be negotiating some matter of state.

options.label: Offer them some food
options.outcome: The Rat King receives your offering with royal dignity and takes brief counsel with its court. Then one of the rats brings out a small pile of coins from somewhere within the cairn and nudges it toward you, by which you understand that you have honoured a treaty of trade.

options.label: Bow to the Rat King
options.outcome: All three rats sit up very straight, and the crowned one touches its bottle cap with one tiny paw, as a sovereign salutes a faithful subject. A curious lightness comes into your legs, for the court of the Rat King has blessed your passage.
options.chronicle: Bowed to the Rat King, three rats knotted by their tails. He accepted.

road.hint: Even a very small king may be pleased by a bow.

options.label: Try to untangle their tails

pass.outcome: With the point of your knife you work the knot slowly loose, while the crowned rat bites your thumb as a matter of principle. A true rat king is a sore affliction to the rats, whose tails are so glued with dirt and grease that none of them can run, and most are found starved. The greatest ever found was thirty-two black rats knotted in a miller's chimney, and it is kept in a museum at Altenburg. These three scatter in freedom, and the crowned one leaves to you all the treasury of its cairn.
pass.chronicle: Cut the Rat King's tails free. The crowned one left me its treasury.

fail.outcome: The knot is tighter than it looks, for dirt and grease and old blood have set in it like glue, and when the rats squeal you leave off before you do them harm. A true rat king seldom comes apart, and most are found starved and knotted still. These three gaze at you as though they knew it.
fail.chronicle: Tried to untangle the Rat King's tails. The old knot would not give.

road.hint: A king whose tails are knotted cannot run until someone sets it free.

options.label: Leave the rats to their politics
options.outcome: The Rat King follows you with the cool gaze of a monarch who has watched many adventurers go by and looks to see many more, and behind you the squeaking of the court returns to its business.

name: Wat Rowe
text: An old man sits upon a step with a lamp-pole across his knees and a flask of oil in his lap, resting for the third time to get his breath. Six lamps burn on the stair above him, one to each landing, but below him the Long Stair goes on down through floor after floor in darkness. "I have lit six," he says. "The seventh stands at the very bottom, a few floors down yet, and my knees have given over speaking to me." He holds up the flask. "Would you do it for me? It lies on your way, as it lies on everybody's way, and that is the whole reason for lighting it."

options.label: Take his oil and swear to light the seventh lamp
options.outcome: He gives the flask into your hands as an heirloom is given, for such it is. "Do not let it go out," he says. "Nobody remembers who lit a lamp, but everybody remembers falling."

oath.what: Light the seventh lamp at the foot of the Long Stair.

thread.hint: The seventh lamp waits cold at the foot of the Long Stair.

options.chronicle: Have old Wat's oil. Promised to light the seventh lamp at the stair's foot.

road.hint: A lamp may spare many a fall, though it be forgotten who lit it.

options.label: Carry him down a flight to wake his knees
options.outcome: He weighs nothing and complains the whole of the way. You carry him one flight down to the next lamp-post and up again, and by the top his knees have consented to speak with him once more. "Now the worst of it is done," he says, "and I shall take the rest slowly, a floor at a time."
options.chronicle: Carried old Wat a flight to wake his knees. He'll walk the rest himself.

road.hint: An old lamplighter may wish to be carried rather than replaced.

options.label: Wish him well and go on
options.outcome: "Well, perhaps my knees will speak to me tomorrow," he says, and he bends over his pole to get his breath for the fourth time.

name: Young Scribe
text: A young man in a scholar's robes stands blinking in the dark, anxiously clutching a leather satchel and a lantern that has gone out. "I am making a record of the beasts of the dungeon for the Cartographers' Guild," he explains. "My light failed, and I have seen nothing yet that was worth the writing. Could you describe to me what you have met? I am able to pay for each entry."

options.label: Describe the creatures you've fought, truly

pass.outcome: You tell him what each beast truly did rather than what it seemed to do, and his pen races to follow you. "Extraordinary, for you truly saw them! Most adventurers say no more than 'it was big'." He counts out your coins. "Did you know that all the old bestiaries copy one little book? It is the Physiologus, written in Greek at Alexandria, and it gives first a beast and then its lesson. I mean to write the first that tells only what the beast does."
pass.chronicle: Described my foes truly for a young scribe's bestiary. He paid well.

fail.outcome: You do your best and he writes it all down, but you can see by his face that half of it has turned already into a bestiary, with beast and story and moral. "Most adventurers say only 'it was big'," he sighs, and he pays you for a single entry.
fail.chronicle: Described monsters loosely to a young scribe for his guild.

road.hint: A scribe will value most what you truly saw.

options.label: Share food for his journey
options.outcome: He takes the food with great relief and searches gratefully in his satchel. "Have this in return, for I copied it in the library and possess the original already. It is true scholarship of the dungeon, and nothing like the popular stuff."

options.label: Buy a fair copy of his guild notes
options.outcome: From the back of his satchel he sells you a fair copy, blushing at the price, though it is an honest one. "Those are the Guild's rates," he says. "I asked whether I might give it away, and it is not allowed."

options.label: Point him toward the exit
options.outcome: He is torn between relief and a scholar's disappointment. "Perhaps... yes, perhaps that would be wisest," he says. He writes one last note, sets a small asterisk beside it and shuffles away toward the surface, holding his satchel close.

name: Old Traveler

tells: one eye is bright; the other is hidden

text: By a dry well an old man in a grey cloak and a broad-brimmed hat sits upon a rock, leaning on a spear as upon a staff. One of his eyes is bright, and the other is hidden beneath the brim. On the beam above him two ravens sit, looking first at you and then at him, as though they kept a record of all they saw. "It is a long road down," he says, in a voice like distant thunder. "Have you anything for an old wanderer's supper?" When he shifts upon the rock, you notice that his boots make no sound at all.

options.label: Share food with him
options.outcome: He eats slowly and speaks of wells, which of them are deep and which are worth the price of drinking from them. When next you look up from your own bread, the ravens are gone and the old man with them.
options.chronicle: Fed a one-eyed old man with two ravens. He talked of wells.

road.hint: An old man who talks of wells may know what a drink from one can cost.

options.label: Ask what he paid for his drink at the well

pass.outcome: His laughter is like thunder a great way off. "I paid an eye, and it was cheap at the price. Mimir would like you well," he says, and he lays his thumb upon your brow.
pass.chronicle: Asked the man in the broad hat of his well. I think I know who he is.

fail.outcome: "Water is water," he says, and before you can ask him more he is gone from the rock.

road.hint: You must mark what an old wanderer lacks before you know what to ask him.

options.label: "You aren't a wanderer at all, are you, Grandfather?"
options.outcome: He tips back the hat, and the other eye is not there. "Men have called me Wanderer, and Grey-Cloak, and Hanged One, for I have more names than teeth." With that he rises, and he is taller than the corridor should allow. "Mimir's Well lies below you, if you would learn what wisdom costs. And beware of the giant who loves riddles."
options.chronicle: Called the old wanderer by his true name. He didn't deny it. Ravens followed.

road.hint: A god in a borrowed hat may be better pleased to be known than to be fed.

options.label: "I need my supplies."
options.outcome: "Of course," he says. "A man's supplies will keep him alive until the day when they cannot." Over his head the two ravens mutter to one another.

name: Wandering Herbalist
text: Along the wall moves a small, wiry woman with a lantern, peering at the fungus through a jeweler's glass, and she spares you scarcely a glance. "I am making my catalogue. Do not touch the blue ones, for they will numb your tongue for a week. Do you want supplies, or will you only hover there?"

options.label: Trade food for one of her potions
options.outcome: She accepts your ration with the brisk nod of her trade and presses a little stoppered vial into your hand. "It is this morning's brew. I put more trust in the apothecaria than in the labels, so drink it with care."
options.chronicle: Traded food with a herbalist. Beware the blue mushrooms.

road.hint: Leave the blue mushrooms well alone.

options.label: Buy a restorative potion
options.outcome: She brings out a small clay bottle and watches you drink as closely as any physician, and at once a true warmth runs through you. "It is bloodmoss and ginger from the deep caves," says she. "It serves for most kinds of creature, and you are welcome to it."

options.label: Ask which of her mushrooms she would eat

pass.outcome: You point to the pale one with a skirt about its stem and a cup at its foot, and say that you would not eat that. She lowers her glass. "It is the death cap, and of all who die of mushrooms more than nine in ten die of that one. For half a day there is nothing, then sickness, and then a day of seeming better while the liver fails. Yes, you will do." So saying, she gives you a bottle from her own belt.
pass.chronicle: Knew the death cap. The herbalist gave me a potion from her own belt.

fail.outcome: You choose the blue one, and she is too late to stay your hand. "I told you not to touch the blue ones," she says, while your tongue grows thick and foolish. Then, being just, she adds, "The pale one beside it, with the skirt and the cup, is a death cap. That one will not numb you, for it waits a day before it does its work."
fail.chronicle: Tasted a blue mushroom. Numb tongue. The herbalist showed me a worse one.

road.hint: The pale mushroom with a skirt and a cup may wait a day to do harm.

options.label: Leave her to her research
options.outcome: She has forgotten you already and bent to her glass again, muttering notes to herself, and the light of her lantern dwindles behind you as you walk on.

name: Brix
text: From behind a stalagmite springs a goblin in a waistcoat with far too many pockets, and he flings his arms wide. "HELLO CUSTOMER! Brix has very good items! Definitely not cursed! Most of them! Best prices in dungeon, guaranteed by Brix personally!"

options.label: Buy the special item at the price you agreed
options.outcome: Brix hands it over as though he were being robbed in broad daylight, and he counts your coins twice before he speaks. "Customer is hard. Brix respects."
options.chronicle: Haggled Brix the goblin down to a fair price. He respected it.

options.label: Buy his "special item"
options.outcome: From a pocket much too small to have held it Brix draws a little thing wrapped in what seems to be an old sock. "Is good! Brix promises! Mostly!" he cries, and he has vanished before you can ask him anything further.
options.chronicle: Bought from Brix the goblin. He swore most of his stock wasn't cursed.

road.hint: Some of a goblin's wares may well be cursed.

options.label: Buy a wand from him
options.outcome: "Ooh, fancy customer wants fancy item!" cries Brix, and he digs through one pocket after another until he finds a wand that is a little scorched at one end. "Barely used! Only misfired twice!"

options.label: Haggle with him

pass.outcome: You tell him that the best price in the dungeon is the one on which two people agree, and that his "guaranteed" counts for nothing until you have both nodded. He mutters for a while, and then he names a true price. "Brix only shouts the big number," he confesses. "Big number is for customers who don't know."

fail.outcome: You argue, and Brix argues back the faster, having more pockets to draw upon, and the price does not move. "Brix price is Brix price!" Only afterward do you think of the answer, that a price is no more than what buyer and seller agree to, and that you were never bound to agree.

road.hint: The first price that a goblin shouts is seldom his true one.

options.label: "No thank you, Brix."
options.outcome: Brix is wounded to the heart. "No customer? But Brix had such good deals today..." With a small and tragic sigh he withdraws behind the stalagmite, and you feel a little guilty as you go.

name: Barnaby Thrupp, Lost Merchant
text: A portly man has blocked the corridor with an overturned handcart and is muttering furiously as he strives to pile up his rolled maps again. "Thirty years in the trade, and still I cannot read these wretched things! I bought this one from a monk, and the corridors go nowhere that it says they go. You there, perhaps we could help one another?"

options.label: Buy a potion from him
options.outcome: He rummages in the cart with an eagerness that rouses your suspicion and draws out a bottle from somewhere near the bottom. "It is the best stock in the dungeon, or very probably so. Good fortune to you, friend!"
options.chronicle: Bought supplies from Barnaby Thrupp, who can't read his own maps.

road.hint: A merchant who cannot read his maps will sell his wares none the less.

options.label: Buy a scroll from him
options.outcome: He claps a rolled scroll into your hand with all the confidence of a man who has no notion what it does. "It is guaranteed authentic, or it mostly is. Probably."

options.label: Read his map for him

pass.outcome: You turn the sheet a quarter round and every corridor falls into its place, for the monk drew it in the old manner of the great mappae mundi, with east at the top toward the rising sun, which is the Orient. For thirty years Barnaby has held his maps with north uppermost. He kisses the sheet and gives you a copy of it, with a bottle besides for your trouble.
pass.chronicle: Read Barnaby Thrupp's old map for him. It had east at the top.

fail.outcome: You turn it every way, and so does he, but the corridors will not agree. Three turnings later it comes to you that the monk drew it in the old manner, with east at the top like the mappae mundi, and by then Barnaby is out of hearing.
fail.chronicle: Failed at Barnaby Thrupp's map. Saw too late it had east at the top.

road.hint: An old map need not have north at the top.

options.label: Leave him to his maps
options.outcome: He waves you on without lifting his eyes, for already he is disputing with the map under his breath, and for some way there follows you the sound of a man being worsted in debate by a piece of parchment.

name: Baucis and Philemon

tells: a grey-bearded giant of a man
two small pinions in his hatband

text: In an alcove an old man and an old woman have made their home, with one stool, one pot and one very suspicious goose. Two travellers crowd the table already, a grey-bearded giant of a man and a younger with two small pinions in his hatband. "More guests!" says the woman in delight. They have but half an onion and a heel of bread among them all, and these they set before you. The pitcher of thin wine has been poured out a dozen times, and yet you see that it is full to the brim still.

options.label: Eat what they offer; refusing would shame them
options.outcome: It is the best half onion that you have ever eaten. They watch each bite with delight, and afterward they go hungry to bed, as they have long been used to do.
options.chronicle: Ate the whole supper of Baucis and Philemon, at their urging.

road.hint: You may honour a poor household by eating gladly what is offered.

options.label: Put your own food on the table and share it out
options.outcome: So five sup at a table laid for one. The old man tells how they first met while the old woman corrects him, and the grey-bearded guest laughs so heartily that the wall creaks.
options.chronicle: Shared my rations with Baucis, Philemon and their two strange guests.

road.hint: More than bread may be shared at a poor couple's table.

options.label: Look at the pitcher, then at the grey-bearded guest

pass.outcome: You watch the pitcher fill itself as the old woman pours, and when you lift your eyes you find the grey-bearded guest looking back at you, and his eyes have the colour of a summer storm. He lays a finger upon his lips and turns to the old couple. "You have been kind to strangers," he says, "and you may ask what you will." They look at one another, and Philemon answers, "Let neither of us have to bury the other." Then the young guest with the wings upon his hat winks at you.
pass.chronicle: The old couple's pitcher never empties. They asked to die on the same day.

fail.outcome: You see a very good pitcher and two large strangers, and you have some suspicion that the younger of them has stolen your spoon.

road.hint: A pitcher that never empties may show you who is sitting at the table.

options.label: Offer to catch the goose for their pot
options.outcome: In the old tale that goose outran two gods, and it outruns you as well. The old couple applaud the attempt while the goose settles on its stool again, much satisfied, and the grey-bearded guest is wiping tears of laughter from his eyes.
options.chronicle: Chased the old couple's goose round their alcove. Could not catch it.

road.hint: A goose may be under the protection of the guests.

name: Wynn the Pilgrim
text: A young woman in a traveller's robes sits against the wall with her boot off and her ankle swollen to the size of an apple, while her torch sputters beside her. She holds a wooden rosary that is plainly another's, for its beads have been worn smooth by some other thumb. "It is my mother's," she says. "She always meant to carry it to the Shrine of the Deep, and she never got round to it." She tries to rise and cannot. "Would you walk with me as far as the next stair?"

on_arrive.outcome: At the stair she touches the rosary to your forehead. "Mum bought it at Walsingham," she says. "A lady there dreamed of Nazareth and built a copy of the Holy House, so that English folk could go to Nazareth without crossing the sea, until King Henry pulled it down. Mum would have liked you, for she was always fond of people who walked slowly."
on_arrive.chronicle: Saw Wynn to the stair. She blessed me with her mother's rosary.

on_fail.chronicle: Lost Wynn short of the stair. Couldn't find her mother's rosary here.

options.label: Walk her to the next stair
options.outcome: She weighs nothing as she leans upon your arm, and she talks the whole of the way.

road.hint: There is strength in walking slowly beside one who is lame.

options.label: Give her food for the walk
options.outcome: She eats and gives you thanks, and then she limps on alone, very slowly.

options.label: Strap her ankle so she can walk on her own

pass.outcome: You bind it in a figure of eight beneath the arch and about the ankle, firm but not tight, and see that her toes stay pink. With rest and cold, a firm wrap, and the foot raised whenever she sits, she will manage well enough. She stands to make trial of it and sets out for the stair at her own pace, and at the corner she turns to bless you with her mother's rosary.
pass.chronicle: Strapped Wynn's ankle. She walked to the stair alone and blessed me.

fail.outcome: To be safe you wrap it tightly, and within a minute her toes are white and cold and you must cut the wrapping off again. Too tight is worse than none, for a wrap should be firm and never tight. She is sitting there still, and still she asks your help.

road.hint: Bind a hurt ankle firmly, but not too tight.

options.label: Wish her well and move on
options.outcome: "God will provide," she says, and after a moment, "I suppose." She sounds less certain of it than she would wish to be.

name: Osric the Mapmaker
text: A lean, exact man paces the corridor with a measuring cord, murmuring distances to himself and marking them upon a chart stretched over the board that he carries. On seeing you he taps the map. "You have been deeper than I today, and I can pay for what you know of distances, junctions and any features worth the noting. What do you say?"

options.label: Share what you've seen, and check his triangles

pass.outcome: Your junctions close his triangles, and he whoops for joy. "Measure one line truly, and after that only angles. So Snellius mapped Holland, from steeple to steeple, and so the Great Survey of India found the tallest mountain on earth from a hundred miles away." He pays you, and he lets you take a copy of his chart.
pass.chronicle: Helped Osric the mapmaker close his triangles. Copied his chart.

fail.outcome: Your junctions will not close, and he frowns upon the chart. "A map that does not close is no more than a story. Measure one line truly and then the angles, and the triangles will tell you when you have lied." Yet he pays you something for your trouble.
fail.chronicle: Told Osric the mapmaker what I saw. His triangles wouldn't close.

road.hint: A map grows truer when two share what each has seen.

options.label: Buy a copy of his current map (50g)
options.outcome: He brings out a fair copy, drawn and noted with a sure hand, and as you study it you find his sense of space all but uncanny, for the whole plan settles into your mind like something long known to you.

options.label: Decline and continue on
options.outcome: "Another time, perhaps," he says with a shrug, and returns to his measuring. As you round the corner you hear him murmuring new distances, wholly rapt already in the architecture of the place.

name: Saint Martin
text: When next you rest at the foot of the stair, you dream of a man in half a cloak who stands amid a great company of angels, and it is your half that he wears. He turns it about so that they may see the cut edge. "Look," he says to them, "for this is how I was clothed today."

options.label: Wake
options.outcome: You wake with your armour whole again, and it is warm, as though another had but lately been wearing it.
options.chronicle: Dreamed of a man in the half cloak I gave. Woke with my armour whole.

road.hint: Half a cloak given away may be worn by one whom you did not expect.

name: Tilly Hollins
text: A child of perhaps eight years sits in the middle of the corridor with a lantern, eating an apple in great contentment, and she looks up at you without any fear at all. "Hello, are you lost? I know all the paths on this level. My dad's a miner, and I'm not supposed to be here, only he doesn't know it yet."

text_variants.text: A child of perhaps eight years sits in the middle of the corridor with a lantern, eating an apple in great contentment, and she looks up at you without any fear at all. "Hello, are you lost? I know all the paths on this level. My dad's a miner, and I'm not supposed to be here, only he doesn't know it yet. Have you seen my brother Davy anywhere?"

options.label: Share food and ask about the layout
options.outcome: You trade her a ration for ten minutes of the most thorough instruction in any dungeon that you have ever received, given with much waving of her hands. She tells you of three shortcuts, two trapped passages and a very large rat whom she has named Gerald, and when she has done you feel wonderfully sure of your bearings.
options.chronicle: Tilly, a miner's girl, showed me the paths here. She named a rat Gerald.

road.hint: A child who knows every path will know who else has walked them.

outcome_variants.outcome: You trade her a ration for ten minutes of the most thorough instruction in any dungeon that you have ever received, given with much waving of her hands. She tells you of three shortcuts, two trapped passages and a very large rat whom she has named Gerald, and when she has done you feel wonderfully sure of your bearings.
outcome_variants.chronicle: Tilly, a miner's girl, showed me the paths here. Asked after her brother.

options.label: Ask why her dad's crew keeps a canary

pass.outcome: "Because it stops singing first," you say, "before a man can know that the air has gone bad." She beams at you. "It's carbon monoxide, and you can't smell it. Mr Hollins says a canary feels it long before a man does, and when it falls off the perch you run." She is so pleased that she draws every path upon the floor for you with the end of her apple core.
pass.chronicle: Told Tilly why miners keep canaries. She drew me all the paths here.

fail.outcome: "For company?" you guess, and she looks upon you with pity. "It's for the bad air. That's carbon monoxide, and it has no smell at all. The canary feels it long before a man does, and when it falls off the perch you run, as everyone knows."
fail.chronicle: Tilly, a miner's girl, had to tell me the canary warns of bad air.

road.hint: The bird falls silent before the men know of the danger.

options.label: Just share food, she should eat
options.outcome: She takes it solemnly, wraps it in her apron and pats it. "It's for later. My dad says never eat the dungeon mushrooms unless Mrs. Herbst has looked at them first." She seems very wise for eight years old, and you hope that she will find her way home.

options.label: Tell her to go home
options.outcome: "I will in a minute," she says, and does not stir. You walk on, troubled by a feeling that she has been here longer than you and understands this place the better, and that she will leave it exactly when she herself decides to go.

name: Hob Tanner
text: A mill wheel turns in an underground race, the air is white with flour, and the miller Hob Tanner, a big man with a bigger thumb, is weighing a widow's sack. The scale says less than the sack does; anyone watching closely can see the thumb. He sees that you have seen it, and he winks. "Gleaners don't check," he says, "so I'll tell you what, friend. You shall have three loaves for the price of one, and you never saw a thing." The widow, Gyda Fenn, is counting out her coppers and does not look up. "It's always light in the autumn," she says, to no one at all. "The damp gets into the grain."

options.label: Take the cheap bread and say nothing
options.outcome: He wraps the loaves in a cloth that is white with flour from everyone else's grain, and the widow carries her short measure home.
options.chronicle: Bought cheap bread from the thumb-on-scale miller. A widow pays for it.

road.hint: Cheap bread may be paid for out of another's short measure.

options.label: Tell the widow about his thumb
options.outcome: Gyda looks long at the scale and at the thumb, and last of all at Hob. Then she calls the other gleaners to her, every one of them, and they stand about the scale with folded arms while he weighs each sack afresh, and his sons walk you very firmly to the door.
options.chronicle: Told the gleaners of the miller's thumb. They watch him. His sons threw me out.

road.hint: A thumb upon the scale is easily seen by any who will look.

options.label: Make up the widow's short measure from your own purse
options.warning: The scale says less than the sack does; anyone watching closely can see the thumb.
options.outcome: She thanks you, much puzzled, while Hob grins and weighs the next widow's sack with the same thumb, and it is plain that you cannot pay for all of them.
options.chronicle: Paid one widow's short measure myself. The miller still cheats the rest.

road.hint: If you pay for a cheat's victims, the cheat may go on cheating.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Hob winks at you again as you go by, and the widow goes on counting out her coppers.

name: Tibbet, Apprentice Alchemist
text: A youth with singed eyebrows and ink upon his fingers sits beside a little burner on which three potions are bubbling at once. "Oh, thank goodness, a real person! I have need of someone to try them in the field, and they should be safe, probably. My master always said that the second batch is the dangerous one, and this is the third, so statistically..."

options.label: Test his potions properly before you drink

pass.outcome: Instead of sniffing at the flasks you waft the fumes of each toward your nose, and when you hold a lighted splint over the one that is fizzing, it pops. "Hydrogen," you tell him. "It is lighter than air and it burns, so do not drink the one that pops." Tibbet writes this down with enormous respect and gives you the good one.
pass.chronicle: Tested a young alchemist's potions by splint. Drank the one without a pop.

fail.outcome: You drink the purple one, which tastes of burnt copper and high hopes, and for a space your shape is not quite your own. When this has passed, you find Tibbet holding a lighted splint over the fizzing flask, and it pops. "Hydrogen," he says. "I should have made that test first, and so should you."
fail.chronicle: Tested a young alchemist's potion on myself. No lasting harm.

road.hint: Test every potion, for the second batch is the dangerous one.

options.label: Buy a tested potion
options.outcome: "I am fairly confident of this one," he says, handing you a blue vial. "There is only about a fifteen percent chance of anything unusual, which is very good indeed for a batch of this size!"

options.label: "Best of luck with your research."
options.outcome: He is disappointed, but he bears it like a philosopher. "Fair enough. There are few who have the true spirit of scientific inquiry," he says, and at that very moment one of his potions turns a brilliant purple. He gazes at it in wonder. "That... is new."

name: The Seventh Lamp
text: At the foot of a long stair stands an iron post with an empty lamp-cup at its head, and on the steps above it the six lamps that Wat lit are burning still. The seventh cup is cold, and beneath it these words are scratched in the iron: FOR THEM AS COME DOWN AFTER. The stair below is very dark and so is all this floor, for your own light is guttering, and Wat's flask holds the only good oil that you have.

options.label: Fill the cup with Wat's oil and light it
options.outcome: The wick takes at once, as though it had long been waiting, and the light goes down the stair much farther than a lamp of that size should reach. Somewhere far above you, very faintly, a bell rings a single time.
options.chronicle: Lit the seventh lamp on the Long Stair, as I promised old Wat.

road.hint: A lamp lit for strangers will guide your own feet as well.

options.label: "I lost Wat's oil."
options.outcome: You say it aloud to the cold cup, since there is no one else to hear it. The stair below remains in darkness, and somewhere above you an old man is listening still for the sound of a bell.
options.chronicle: Lost Wat's oil before the seventh lamp. Its cup stays cold.

road.hint: Oil promised to a lamp is still owed, even when the flask is lost.

options.label: Keep the oil for your own light
options.outcome: For floors afterward your own light burns brighter and warmer, but the seventh cup stays cold behind you, and the stair below it is left in darkness for whoever comes next.
options.chronicle: Burned Wat's oil for my own light. The seventh lamp stays dark.

road.hint: Oil that was given for the lamp of all travellers sits ill in a private one.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: You walk on, and behind you the seventh cup stands cold upon its post.

text_variants.text: At the foot of a long stair stands an iron post with an empty lamp-cup at its head, and on the steps above it the six lamps that Wat lit are burning still. The seventh cup is cold, and beneath it these words are scratched in the iron: FOR THEM AS COME DOWN AFTER. The stair below is very dark and so is all this floor, for your own light is guttering, and Wat's flask is no longer in your pack.

name: Luminous Mushrooms
text: Three enormous mushrooms glow with a soft violet light in a side alcove, and their caps swell and fade in a slow measure. As you draw near you become aware, though you could not say how, that they are curious about you and mean you no harm, but only watch you closely. One of them leans a very little way in your direction.

options.label: Taste a small piece of one

pass.outcome: You know what you are looking upon, for these are cousins of foxfire. True fungi can glow, and honey fungus in rotting wood the brightest, by the same art as the firefly, in which a luciferin burns slowly with oxygen and gives out light instead of heat. Aristotle saw it and called it cold light. You take the smallest piece from the edge, and it leaves your mind as clean as a window after rain.
pass.chronicle: Tasted a little glowing mushroom, with care. It cleared my head.

fail.outcome: You take a great bite from the middle, and for a long while your sight is filled with slow purple figures of geometry. When they have cleared you remember that glowing fungus is real enough, the cold light of rotting wood, and that a thing may be real and yet not fit to eat.
fail.chronicle: Bit a glowing mushroom and saw shapes. Glowing is not the same as safe.

road.hint: A rotting log may glow by the firefly's art.

options.label: Sit in their light for a while
options.outcome: You rest in the gentle pulse of their glow. A great calm is upon you, to be near living things that have no fear of the dungeon and do nothing but live, grow and shine, and your hurts are eased a little.
options.chronicle: Rested in the light of three curious mushrooms. Felt better for it.

road.hint: Some things that watch you in the dark are only curious.

options.label: Leave them in peace
options.outcome: The mushrooms watch you go with whatever sense they have for watching, and for some while afterward the violet glow lingers at the edge of your sight, a small and patient light amid the darkness.

name: Crying Girl
text: In the mouth of a side passage sits a small girl, sobbing as though her heart would break. "My da's hurt, he's just in there, please, please come." You see that her hands are clean. Her tears have left no tracks in the soot on her cheeks. In the dust behind her the prints of big boots lead away into the dark, and none of them return.

options.label: Go with her to help her da
options.warning: Her tears have left no tracks in the soot on her cheeks.
options.outcome: You have gone three steps into the dark when a club finds the back of your head. When you can see again your purse is the lighter and two men are coming back for the rest, and somewhere behind them a man laughs and says, "Good girl, Wren."
options.chronicle: Followed a crying girl to help her father. A trap: men with clubs.

road.hint: Tears that leave no tracks in soot may never have been shed.

options.label: Look harder before you go in

pass.outcome: There are no tracks in the soot, her hands are clean, and the boots have gone in and have not come out. So you go round by the other passage and come up behind three men who crouch in the dark with clubs, awaiting the girl's next customer, and they are not ready for you. Afterward Wren sits upon a rock and stares at you. "They took me off a caravan," she says. "They said they'd sell me if I didn't cry good." When you point her to the stair she sets out for it, but she turns back for the wreckers' purse before she goes away at last.
pass.chronicle: Saw through a crying girl's trap, got behind the men, sent Wren home.

fail.outcome: You look, but see only a crying child, so you go in, and there men with clubs are waiting to rob you.
fail.chronicle: Looked hard at a crying girl and missed the trap. Lost my purse.

road.hint: Before you follow weeping into the dark, look well at the dust upon the floor.

options.label: Throw her a coin and walk on
options.outcome: She catches it without looking, as hands can do only when they have had much practice.
options.chronicle: Threw a coin to a crying girl and walked on. She has done this before.

road.hint: Hands that need not look to catch a coin are practised hands.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: The crying ceases as soon as you are past, and after a little space it begins again behind you for whoever next comes by.

name: Drowned Girl
text: At the edge of a black water a girl of about nine sits upon a stone step, wet through and holding out an empty hand, and a little way off an old ferryman leans upon his oar. "No coin, no crossing," he says. "Those are the rules." "My stepfather kept my coin," says the girl. "He said that the dead have no need of money." She has been sitting here, the ferryman tells you, since the reign of a king whom nobody now remembers.

options.label: Pay her fare
options.outcome: Charon bites the coin and nods, and holds out his hand to help her aboard. She pauses on the ferry to wave to you, and waves still until the dark takes the boat.
options.chronicle: Paid Charon a drowned girl's fare. Her stepfather had kept her coin.

road.hint: A small coin given for a stranger's crossing may long be remembered.

options.label: Argue the rule with Charon

pass.outcome: You show him that the rule requires a coin and does not say whose coin it must be, and that he has been paid already in her waiting. He grumbles, but he takes half a fare from you and lets her come aboard.
pass.chronicle: Argued Charon's rule. He took a drowned girl across for half fare.

fail.outcome: "Those are the rules," says Charon, and he will not be moved.

road.hint: Even a ferryman's old rule may yield a little to one who will reason with him.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: She does not lower her hand, but holds it out again to the next who passes by.

name: Corran Vey, Treasure-Hunter
text: Out of the shadows a man comes stumbling toward you with a rough map clutched to his breast. His gear is costly but much battered, and he has the look of one who has been too long underground. "My name is Corran Vey. I have found something, a cache two junctions east, but there is something guarding it, with eight legs and a web across the door. At this hour I have more need of what you carry than you have yourself."

options.label: Sell him a potion (take 50g)
options.outcome: You hand him a potion, and he pays you in coin with trembling hands, already on the move. "You have saved my life, and I shall remember it," he cries. With that he rounds the corner at speed, and you are never to learn whether he was right about the cache.

options.label: Give him food from your pack
options.outcome: His face crumples with relief. "Take this, for I cannot use it. My hands shake so that I cannot read it as I should." He presses a scroll upon you and is away down the corridor without another word.
options.chronicle: Sold food to Corran Vey, a desperate treasure-hunter, at a fair price.

road.hint: A starving man may pay for bread with what he cannot use himself.

options.label: Tell him how to get past the spider

pass.outcome: You tell him what you know, that a web spider sees little and hunts by feel along its threads. So you pluck a strand on the far side of the door while he slips in by the wall, and the spider runs to your plucking. He is out again before it can turn, bearing the cache in a sack, and he counts half of it into your hands. "I would have walked straight through the web," he says.
pass.chronicle: Plucked the spider's web so Corran Vey got by. He split the cache.

fail.outcome: At your word he goes in swiftly, and he comes out more swiftly still, with web in his hair and nothing else to show for it. Later you remember that a web spider sees little and hunts by feel, and that a pluck on the far side of the door would have called it away.
fail.chronicle: Told Corran Vey to rush the spider's door. He came back with only web.

road.hint: A web spider feels for its prey along the threads.

options.label: Wish him luck and move on
options.outcome: For a moment he gazes at you, and then he nods with a quiet dignity. "So be it, and that is fair enough, for it is every man for himself down here." He straightens his coat and walks away east toward whatever may be waiting for him.

name: Hamund, the Singing Bones
text: In the corner of a chamber a tidy pile of bones is humming, and of that there can be no mistake. When you draw near a dry voice rises out of the heap. "I know that tread, and it is another seeker's. Hamund the Bold, they called me, though I would sooner they had called me Hamund the Careful. I have lain here a hundred years and have seen many of your kind come and go. Ask your question, for I am going nowhere."

options.label: Ask about dangers ahead
options.outcome: The bones clatter softly as they consider their price, and you leave the gold upon the floor. "Mm. That is fair." A dry whisper fills your mind with the echoes of passages and shadows, and for a little while you are aware of things that lie just beyond your sight.
options.chronicle: Asked the singing bones of Hamund about the road ahead.

road.hint: The dead have had long years in which to learn the roads about them.

options.label: Ask how he died
options.outcome: "It was overconfidence," the bones answer at once. "I had an enchanted sword and a plan, and when I met a basilisk I looked it in the eye to show that I was not afraid." They are silent a little, and then the voice goes on. "For a time I was a statue, until the statue fell over."
options.chronicle: Hamund the Bold's bones say he died looking a basilisk in the eye.

options.label: Ask him what would have saved him

pass.outcome: "You know the old books," he says, well pleased. "Pliny swears that a weasel fed on rue will slay a basilisk, and the bestiaries say that it dies of its own reflection. I had neither the one nor the other. Take my buckle, which is of polished brass, and watch the beast in that and never in its eye." At his words you feel a little more stubborn, and a little less like stone.
pass.chronicle: Have Hamund's buckle to watch a basilisk in. Never meet its eye.

fail.outcome: "Was it courage?" you guess, and the bones laugh, which is a terrible noise to hear. "I had courage. A weasel would have served me better, or else a mirror, for the old books say that a basilisk dies of its own reflection. Never meet its eye."
fail.chronicle: Hamund the Bold's bones warn me: never meet a basilisk's eye.

road.hint: Some beasts are best watched in a mirror.

options.label: Walk away from the talking bones
options.outcome: "That is rude," the bones remark as you depart. Behind you the humming begins again, a slow melody without a source, and it follows you down the corridor for longer than it should.

name: Moneylender's Purse
text: In the dust you find a fat purse with FISK stitched upon it, and within it gold and eleven folded debt markers that bear the marks of miners. A wheezing man in a good coat comes searching back along the corridor. "My purse! I am Ottokar Fisk. I lent to those families when no bank on Gullet Row would." A widow follows him at a distance. "At a fifth a month," she says, "and my husband signed it drunk." Fisk does not turn his head. "He signed it sober," he answers, "and he asked me twice."

options.label: Give Fisk his purse, markers and all
options.outcome: He counts it before your face with little courtesy and gives you no word of thanks at all, while the widow watches the markers go back into his coat.
options.chronicle: Gave Fisk the moneylender his purse, debts and all. A widow watched.

road.hint: A lost purse belongs to its owner, though you may have no love for him.

options.label: Keep the gold. Give the widow her husband's marker
options.outcome: The widow Agna takes the marker, folds it very small and puts it away inside her dress. "Thank you," she says, and she means it truly. Farther up the corridor Fisk is searching still, wheezing as he goes, and he does not look back.

delayed.text: Upon a stair-post you find a notice in Fisk's square hand: NO MORE LOANS ON GULLET ROW. THIEVES ABOUT.

options.chronicle: Kept Fisk's gold, freed a widow of debt. No more lending on Gullet Row.

road.hint: When you give from another's purse, someone must still bear the cost.

options.label: Burn the markers and give him back the gold
options.warning: I lent to those families when no bank on Gullet Row would.
options.outcome: The markers go up in a pretty little flame while Agna weeps. Fisk takes back his gold with shaking hands, and he says in a very low voice, "Then I shall lend to nobody."

delayed.text: A miner's lad stops you on the stair. 'Fisk gave up lending after his markers burned, and nobody else will lend to us, so Mam couldn't buy her seed.' He has no notion at all that it was you who burned them.

options.chronicle: Burned Fisk's markers, returned his gold. He'll lend to nobody now.

road.hint: When a lender's books are burned he may be unwilling to lend again.

options.label: Leave the purse where it fell
options.outcome: You walk on, and behind you, while Fisk's back is turned, the widow is the first to come to the purse.
options.chronicle: Left a moneylender's purse lying in the road for whoever comes first.

road.hint: What you leave lying on the road is left to whoever passes next.

name: Moaning Woman
text: A woman lies slumped against the wall, moaning in pain. Her long dark hair hangs over her face, her body shudders with every ragged breath, and one hand clutches at her stomach. She does not look up as you draw near. The moaning has a rhythm to it, like somebody counting.

options.label: Kneel down and try to help her
options.warning: The moaning has a rhythm to it, like somebody counting.
options.outcome: You reach out to part the hair from her face, and her head jerks upward. The face beneath is grey and rotting, and the eyes are pure white. "I'LL SWALLOW YOUR SOUL!" she shrieks, and she has raked you across the chest before you can stir, for she was dead all the while.
options.chronicle: Knelt to help a moaning woman. She was a Deadite, and scratched me.

road.hint: Beware of moaning that keeps time like somebody counting.

options.label: "It's a trick. Axe out, or whatever you've got."

pass.outcome: You draw your weapon and come at her from the side. The "woman" springs up faster than any living thing, her grey flesh splitting in a horrible grin, but you are ready, and one clean stroke makes an end of it. As you wipe your weapon clean you say only, "Groovy."
pass.chronicle: Smelled a moaning Deadite's trick. Weapon out before she turned.

fail.outcome: You are nearly ready, but not wholly so, and she rakes you once as she comes down upon you.
fail.chronicle: Saw the Deadite coming but was too slow. She got a claw in.

road.hint: Good, bad: the one who wins is the one holding the axe first.

options.label: Say the words, to be sure. "Klaatu, Barada, N... Necktie."
options.outcome: You certainly said all of the words, for the most part. The floor cracks in two places and two more of them climb out to join her, and it may be that you said one of the words wrong.
options.chronicle: Botched the old words with 'necktie'. Two more Deadites climbed out.

road.hint: Such old words must be said exactly, or else left unsaid.

options.label: Walk away and leave her be
options.outcome: You give the moaning figure a wide berth. As you round the corner the moaning stops, and when you look back there is no woman there at all.
options.chronicle: Walked past a moaning woman. The moaning stopped behind me.

name: Freezing Beggar
text: A wind colder than any should be beneath the earth comes up the stair out of nowhere, and at a stone gate a beggar sits huddled against it, all but naked and blue with cold. All who come through the gate step round him with their eyes turned away. You have a cloak about you, and you carry something with an edge to it.

options.label: Cut your cloak in half with whatever blade you carry, and give him half
options.outcome: The blade passes cleanly through the cloth. He draws your half about his shoulders and lifts his eyes to you once, and there comes upon you a strange feeling that he knows your name.
options.chronicle: Gave half my cloak to a beggar at a cold gate. He seemed to know me.

road.hint: Half of your cloak might be enough to shield a man from the cold.

options.label: Give him food
options.outcome: He eats and shivers still, for it is the cold that is killing him and not hunger.
options.chronicle: Gave a freezing beggar food. It did nothing for the cold.

road.hint: A man who freezes has need of cloth as well as bread.

options.label: Step round him like everyone else

name: Bronze Automaton
text: Propped against a pillar sits a figure of bronze no larger than a boy, with one arm missing and the clockwork silent in its breast. A single vein of bronze runs down it from neck to ankle and is closed at the heel with a bronze nail, and the nail is working loose. Its eyes of glass flicker. "The craftsman made me," it says, in a voice like the keys of a music box. "The one who built these walls. Little brother... of the great guard of Crete. My nail... I cannot reach my nail. Can you carry something? In my place?"

options.label: Accept its remaining charge (take damage)
options.outcome: It holds out the hand that remains to it, and something leaps between you like a spark, sharp and cold. "Guardian's... charge... transferred. You will hold it better than I do now." The glass eyes grow dim and the figure is still, and all about you is wrapped a faint humming of protection.
options.chronicle: Took a broken bronze guardian's last charge. Its task is unfinished.

road.hint: A failing guardian may still have its charge to give to another.

options.label: Seat the nail in its heel

pass.outcome: You know the tale of Talos, the bronze giant who walked three times a day about Crete casting boulders at ships. He had one vein of ichor from neck to ankle, stopped with a nail, and when by the spell of Medea he grazed that ankle on a rock, his life ran out of him. You press the nail home and fold the bronze over it, and the little automaton sits up straight. "Grateful," it says. A hidden drawer clicks open in its base, and you remember it was said of Daedalus that he made statues so lively that they ran away unless they were tied down.
pass.chronicle: Pressed home a bronze automaton's heel nail, Talos's weak spot. It paid me.

fail.outcome: You work the nail the wrong way, and it slides out in your fingers. Golden ichor runs down over the bronze heel as it ran out of Talos when Medea had dizzied him and he grazed his ankle on a rock, and the little automaton watches it flow. "Ah," it says. "The heel. Always the heel." Then, as you watch, the light goes out of its glass eyes.
fail.chronicle: Pulled a bronze automaton's heel nail in error. It died as Talos did.

road.hint: A giant of bronze with one vein has but one place of weakness.

options.label: Leave it to rest
options.outcome: "Understood," it says. "I will... wait." Its eyes sink to a faint flicker, and as you go you wonder how long it has waited already, and how much longer it must.

name: Old Nan and the Cat
text: A woman's figure, as thin as mist, sits cross-legged on the dungeon floor with her head in her hands, weeping softly. She looks up as you approach, and her eyes are empty of all colour and her clothes are of a fashion many years gone. "Oh, another adventurer. Have you... have you seen my cat? His name is Cobbler, and he was orange."

options.label: Sit with her for a while
options.outcome: For a time you sit with her in friendly silence, and by degrees her weeping is stilled. "He'll be down there somewhere," she says. "He was always one to go exploring. If you see a big orange tom who looks as if he owns the place, tell him Nan's waiting." Something in her quiet grief has steadied your own mind.
options.chronicle: Sat with Old Nan's ghost. Must send her cat Cobbler home if I see him.

road.hint: A ghost who searches for her cat may linger until he is found.

thread.hint: Somewhere below, a ginger ghost-cat called Cobbler has wandered off from Old Nan.
thread.closed_line: Cobbler is home with Old Nan.

schedule.lost_line: Never did find Old Nan's cat, Cobbler.

options.label: Tell her you haven't seen a cat
options.outcome: "He was very good at catching rats," she says softly, "and he kept me company when the dungeon was quiet." She fades a little as she looks past you. "It is very quiet now."

options.label: Walk away quietly
options.outcome: You slip past without a word and do not look back, though behind you the soft weeping begins again, until the dark has swallowed it.

name: Cobbler
text: A big orange cat sits upon a step washing one paw, and you can see the step through him. He is a tom, ginger to the tip of his tail, with a torn ear and the air of one who owns the place. At the sight of you he leaves off washing and looks at you as though you smelt of someone that he knows.

options.label: Tell him Nan is waiting for him

pass.outcome: You crouch and speak low and do not stare, for to a cat a hard stare is a threat and a slow blink is friendship. Slowly you blink, and after a long moment he blinks in answer. Then he is away up the stair with his tail held high, a big ginger tom like most ginger cats, for four in five of them are toms, since the orange rides on the X. Somewhere far above you an old woman leaves off her crying.
pass.chronicle: Won Cobbler's trust with a slow blink and sent him home to Old Nan.

fail.outcome: You reach straight for him with staring eyes, and he is gone as only a cat can go. A hard stare is a threat to a cat, and a slow blink would have been friendship. You can but hope that he finds his own way back to her, as cats most often do.
fail.chronicle: Reached for Cobbler and he vanished. Could not send him to Old Nan.

road.hint: A slow blink will say more to a cat than any word.

options.label: Leave him to his paw
options.outcome: He returns to the washing of his paw, and he will go when it pleases him, as is the way of cats.

name: Frozen Viper
text: In a cold side cave lies a snake as long as a man, stiff with the cold, and the frost has dulled the zigzag upon its back. It lifts its head a single inch. "Warm me," it whispers. "Let me lie inside your shirt, only until I can move. I am not that kind of snake." Its pupils are slits, and its head is the shape of a spade.

options.label: Warm it inside your shirt
options.warning: Its pupils are slits, and its head is the shape of a spade.
options.outcome: It soon grows warm against you, and then, very nearly as if it begged your pardon, it bites you. "It is my nature," it says.
options.chronicle: Warmed a frozen viper in my shirt. It bit me. Its nature, it said.

road.hint: A snake may swear that it is harmless and bite you none the less.

options.label: Set it on the warm rock by your light, at arm's length

pass.outcome: You lift it with a stick, lay it on the warm stone and step back well beyond its reach. When it has thawed and uncoiled it regards you with something like respect. "That was wise, for I would have bitten you. It is my nature." And it tells you where a dead trapper left his purse.
pass.chronicle: Thawed a viper at arm's length. It told me of a dead man's purse.

fail.outcome: You misjudge the stick, and the snake bites you before you can step away.
fail.chronicle: Tried to thaw a viper from a safe distance. Stood too close.

road.hint: Help a viper, if you must, from a stick's length away.

options.label: Leave it to the cold
options.outcome: "That is sensible," it hisses. "In your place I would not warm me either."

name: Father of Three
text: Outside a shut door a man in a coat that once was fine sits counting the same four coins over and over, and he has not seen you. From behind the door comes the whispering of three girls, who are disputing which of them shall go into service with the goblin tallyman so that the other two may eat. Above the door there is a gap about as wide as a purse, and you judge that one full purse would settle the whole of the debt.

options.label: Drop a purse through the gap and slip away
options.outcome: The purse lands with a clink that ends the dispute at once, and by the time the door opens you are round the corner, so that none can thank you, since none knows who you are. In just this manner Bishop Nicholas of Myra gave on three separate nights, and only on the third did the father catch him at it.
options.chronicle: Left a purse in secret for a poor father and his family.

road.hint: A gift left in secret lays no debt upon those who receive it.

options.label: Put the gold in his hand and let him thank you
options.outcome: He weeps and calls out his daughters to curtsey, and he presses upon you the ring of his dead wife and will not hear you refuse it. It is a good ring, and all the while the girls keep their eyes upon the floor.
options.chronicle: Paid a poor father's debt to his face. His daughters looked at the floor.

road.hint: A gift made before a man's children may put them to shame.

options.label: Walk on; your own purse is thin enough
options.outcome: The whispering goes on behind the door, and as you pass, the man begins again at the first of his four coins and counts them over.
options.chronicle: Walked past a poor father counting four coins outside his door.

road.hint: Counting four coins again will never pay a father's debt.

name: Ornate Mirror
text: A mirror as tall as a man stands in the corridor where no mirror has cause to be, and its silver frame is carved with serpents that devour their own tails. Your reflection gazes back at you half a second too late, and then it smiles, though you yourself have not smiled. "Touch the glass," it says in your own voice. "I have something that you lost."

options.label: Touch the mirror
options.outcome: The glass is cold as ice and yields like water. Something is pressed into your palm, and when you snatch back your hand your reflection wears a look of content. A small thing lies in your hand, and you have no memory of ever having lost it.
options.chronicle: Touched a mirror that smiled first. Wearing what it gave me, warily.

road.hint: If a reflection smiles before you do, it wants something of you.

options.label: Offer it some mana
options.outcome: Your reflection inclines its head and reaches through the glass to lay a rolled scroll on the floor at your feet. "It is a fair trade," it says, "and you may come again when you have more."

options.label: Name the trick of the glass

pass.outcome: It is the trick of Narcissus, as you know from your Ovid, who tells of the boy that saw his own face in a forest pool and loved it, and stayed gazing until he wasted away and a flower grew where he had lain. So you look upon the frame and leave the face alone. A reflection that no one watches has nothing to hold you by, and sullenly it lets go of what it was holding.
pass.chronicle: Watched the frame of Narcissus's mirror, not my face. Got what it held.

fail.outcome: You look into your own eyes to learn what it desires, and some while is lost to you there. When you come to yourself your neck aches and the reflection is smiling, and too late you know it for the trick of Narcissus, the boy who loved his own face in a pool and never turned his eyes away.
fail.chronicle: Stared too long into a smiling mirror, as Narcissus did.

road.hint: A pool once held a boy captive by his own fair face.

options.label: Walk past without looking at it
options.outcome: "That was wise," your reflection says to your back. You walk on, and you could have sworn that a second pair of footsteps came after you, though it is very likely that there was none.

name: Stone Fox
text: A fox sits motionless in the corridor and watches you. Its fur has the colour of granite, and its eyes are of amber glass. When you halt it rises and paces once about you without a sound, and then it sits again with its back to you, plainly expecting that you will follow.

options.label: Follow the fox
options.outcome: It leads you by a road that you would never have chosen, winding and doubling back upon itself, until it sits before a crack in the wall. In the little chamber beyond lies something left by an adventurer before you, and when you turn about the fox is gone.
options.chronicle: Followed a stone fox where it led.

road.hint: A fox that wishes to be followed may have something to show you.

options.label: Offer it something to eat
options.outcome: It sniffs once at the offering and touches it with its nose, and for a long moment its amber eyes are lifted to yours. Then it breathes upon you, cold and clean, and when it has vanished you find that you yourself have become very hard to see.

options.label: Call the fox by its name

pass.outcome: "Teumessian," you say, and at once it stands still. This was the fox that no hunter could catch, which was loosed upon Thebes, and men hunted it with Laelaps, the hound that caught whatever it pursued. That the riddle might have an end, Zeus turned both to stone as they ran, and some say that he set them in the sky as the Great Dog and the Little. Now that it is named it walks straight, without any doubling back, to a crack in the wall where a hound of stone stands frozen in mid-leap, and at the hound's feet lies something that an earlier seeker left.
pass.chronicle: Named the stone fox Teumessian. It led me to the hound that never caught it.

fail.outcome: "Here, boy," you call, and it runs as it has always run. Nothing ever catches the fox of Teumessos, for even Laelaps, the hound that caught all things, could not do it, and Zeus had to turn both of them to stone to end the chase.
fail.chronicle: Called to a stone fox without its name. It ran. Nothing catches it.

road.hint: The fox that none could catch was hunted once by a hound that never failed.

options.label: Let it sit and walk around it
options.outcome: It watches you pass and does not move, but when you look back from the next turning it is facing another way already, as though it had never been waiting for you at all.

name: Limping Lion
text: A lion lies across the passage, licking one forepaw and growling at it, for the paw is swollen to twice its size about a black thorn as long as your finger. He looks upon you as an ailing man looks upon a barber-surgeon.

options.label: Take the paw in both hands and draw the thorn
options.outcome: He roars, and a claw has opened your forearm before he has made up his mind not to eat you. Then the thorn is out and he is washing the paw with great dignity, as though the whole affair had been his own design. As for the thorn, you keep it, for it seems to you the kind of thing that a person ought to keep.
options.chronicle: Drew a thorn from a lion's paw. He spared me. Kept the thorn.

road.hint: A lion may long remember who drew the thorn from his paw.

options.label: Toss him some food and edge round
options.outcome: He eats it without getting up, and his yellow eyes follow you as you edge past him, but the paw is left as it was.

options.label: Back away slowly
options.outcome: He permits it, and the growling that follows you down the passage is meant for the paw and not for you.

name: Ysolde
text: Behind a fallen portcullis stands a woman whose hands are raw from striving to lift it, and she has a stoppered vial tucked into her dress. "Is there anyone? My girl Elara, she's seven, I left her with my pendant and told her seven sleeps." When she sees you she thrusts her face against the bars. "Have you seen a little girl?"

options.label: Tell her Elara has the pendant and went home
options.outcome: Ysolde leans her forehead on the bars, laughing and crying at once. Then she sets her strength to the gate and you set yours, and together you raise it a hand's breadth, and then a foot. She slides beneath with the medicine. "It's Benno's fever. If I run," she says, and without staying to finish she is off at a run.
options.chronicle: Told Ysolde that Elara went home with the pendant. Raised her gate.

road.hint: News of her child may be worth more to a mother than any gold.

options.label: Tell her you took the pendant from her girl, and give it back
options.outcome: You confess it before she can read it in your face: that Elara saw the pendant at your belt and asked for it back, and that you kept it, because you wished for every advantage in this place. Ysolde grows very still behind the bars. Then she puts her hand through them, and into it you give the pendant. Still you lift the gate together, and she slides beneath. "She's seven," she says, and of that matter she says no more, but makes for the stair at a run with the pendant held in her hand.
options.chronicle: Owned to Ysolde I took Elara's pendant. Returned it, raised her gate. Not forgiven.

road.hint: What you kept from the child may still be given into her mother's hand.

options.label: Help her lift the gate
options.outcome: Together you raise it a foot, and she slides beneath. "Where is she?" she asks, and you tell her where you left Elara, but of the pendant you tell her nothing. For a long while she looks at your empty hands, and then she goes upon her way.
options.chronicle: Raised Ysolde's gate, said where Elara is. Said nothing of the pendant.

road.hint: A mother may read in your empty hands what you kept from her child.

options.label: Help her lift the gate, with the pendant out of sight
options.outcome: You tuck the pendant inside your collar before you lay hold of the bars, and together you raise the gate a foot so that she can slide beneath. "Where is she?" she asks, and you tell her where you left Elara. She thanks you twice and runs for the stair, and for as long as she is in sight the pendant lies cold against your chest.
options.chronicle: Raised Ysolde's gate with Elara's pendant hidden in my collar.

road.hint: A pendant hidden from a mother will lie cold against your chest.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: As you walk on, you hear behind you the portcullis grinding once more against her hands.
options.chronicle: Left a woman trying to lift a portcullis with her bare hands.

road.hint: An iron gate will not yield to one pair of hands.

name: Davy Hollins
text: Under a fallen roof beam lies a boy of about sixteen, pinned from the hips downward, and he is very calm, as people are who have resolved not to be afraid. "I'm Davy, the shoring boy. I told Gorran the north prop was rotten." He comes near to laughing. "Old Gorran says never lift a beam off a man, for it kills him. He says wait for the crew." Below the beam his legs have turned an evil waxen colour, and the crew is a long way off.

options.label: Lift the beam off him now
options.outcome: The beam comes up with a groaning of wood and you drag him clear. The colour begins to return to his legs, and with it comes the pain, and with the pain the shock, so that very swiftly he is growing grey and cold.

road.hint: An old foreman's rule about beams may not save the man who lies under one.

options.label: Do as the old foreman says, and wait for the crew
options.outcome: You sit beside him and wait, but the crew is a long way off, and by the time their lamps come round the corner he has died, pinned still and still waiting to be lifted.
options.chronicle: Left Davy Hollins pinned till the crew came. He died. Should have lifted it.

road.hint: To wait for help is not always the careful course.

options.label: Go for the crew yourself
options.outcome: You run until you find the crew and you lead them back as swiftly as you went, but Davy is asleep beneath the beam and he does not wake again.

options.label: Give him a healing potion
options.outcome: He drinks it in great gulps, and the grey goes out of his lips. "Biscuit," he says, which proves to be the name of his dog. He will limp for a year, but he will live.
options.chronicle: Freed Davy Hollins and gave him a potion. He'll limp, and live.

options.label: Keep him flat and warm, stop the bleeding, and wait with him

pass.outcome: You lay him flat and cover him with what your pack can spare, raising nothing, and you press upon the cut where the beam bit him and talk to him so that he will stay with you. When the crew comes he is cold and frightened, but he is alive.
pass.chronicle: Freed Davy Hollins, kept him flat and warm for his crew. He lives.

fail.outcome: You do all that you can think of, and some of it is wrong, and the shock is swifter than you are, so that he dies in the midst of talking about his dog.
fail.chronicle: Freed Davy Hollins but lost him to shock. Must learn more of healing.

road.hint: Once a man is freed from a beam he must still be tended.

name: The Voice in the Wall
text: The stonework here is older and rougher, and cut with a mason's marks that are unlike all the rest. When you look closer a voice speaks out of the very stone, slow and deep. "Seeker, I cut these stones for the craftsman Daedalus, in the service of King Minos, and when the work was done the king walled up the men who knew the plan. I know the way through, and I know what waits at the centre."

options.label: Ask how a man finds his way out

pass.outcome: "Thread," you say, and the stone hums with pleasure. "Ariadne, the king's daughter, gave the Athenian a clew, which is a ball of thread, and he tied it at the door. Your word 'clue' is that same thread. And when he met the starry one, Asterion, at the centre, he did not hack at him, for on every painted jar the Athenian drives his blade in." Then the stone shows you the whole of this floor, turning by turning.
pass.chronicle: A voice in the wall showed the turnings. Theseus had thread, and thrust his blade.

fail.outcome: "Luck," you say, and the stone sighs. "It was thread, Ariadne's clew, a ball of it tied at the door, and your word 'clue' is that thread. Remember it when you meet the starry one at the centre."
fail.chronicle: A mason's voice in the wall says a clue was once a ball of thread.

road.hint: An old stone may remember how a man got free of the maze.

options.label: Listen to the mason's story
options.outcome: The telling is long, for stone is slow of speech. You hear how Daedalus built the Labyrinth so cunningly that he could scarcely find his own way out, how Minos shut him in a tower with his son Icarus to keep the secret, and how they flew out on wings of feathers and wax, but the boy flew too near the sun, so that the wax ran and he fell into the sea that bears his name still. You ache from standing motionless so long, yet when it is ended a warmth comes through the rock like a blessing, and the voice rumbles, "GO WELL."
options.chronicle: Heard out the mason's voice on Icarus, who flew too near the sun.

options.label: Back away from the wall
options.outcome: "That is wise," the wall says without reproach, and its marks are plain stone once more. When you look back from the next turning, they are no longer where they were.

name: The Voice of the Last Priestess
text: Behind a fallen column a faint voice speaks out of the marble, and it is a woman's voice, patient and dry. "Seeker, I tended the lamp in the goddess's house until none was left to see it lit. The temple of the grey-eyed one has a gorgon at its heart now. Shall I tell you how a gorgon dies?"

options.label: Ask her how Perseus did it

pass.outcome: "I think that you know it already," she says, and so you do. Perseus never once looked upon Medusa, but watched her in Athena's polished shield, and he took her head with the harpe, a curved sword lent to him by Hermes, which is a blade for cutting rather than thrusting. Afterward the goddess set the head upon her aegis. "Watch her in a mirror," the priestess says, "and cut, and do not thrust." Then the air about you takes on a faint polish, like bronze.
pass.chronicle: Athena's priestess says watch Medusa in a polished shield. Use a curved blade.

fail.outcome: "Never look upon her," the priestess says. "Perseus watched her in a polished shield and cut off her head with a curved sword, the harpe. You must cut, and do not thrust." Then her voice grows thin within the marble and is gone.
fail.chronicle: A priestess's voice in the marble warns me: never look at the gorgon.

road.hint: He who slew the gorgon never looked upon her face.

options.label: Leave her to her lamp
options.outcome: "The lamp is out," she says, "but I tend it none the less."

name: The Voice under the Cinders
text: Beneath a crust of cinders a voice grinds out of the rock, old and bitter. "Seeker, I am Hreidmar. The gods once paid me a ransom of gold for my son Otr, whom Loki killed, and for that gold my son Fafnir killed me, and he lay down upon it and became a worm. Would you know how my son can die?"

options.label: Ask how Fafnir can be killed

pass.outcome: "It cannot be done from above, for his scales will turn every edge." Then he tells you how a youth named Sigurd dug a pit in the track by which Fafnir crawled down to drink, and lay in it until the soft belly passed over him, and drove his sword straight upward. "My other son Regin taught him that," the voice grinds, "meaning to have the gold for himself. Strike from below, and strike with the point."
pass.chronicle: Hreidmar says his son Fafnir was stabbed from a pit, up into the soft belly.

fail.outcome: "From below," says the voice impatiently. "Sigurd lay in a pit on the worm's path to the water and stabbed upward into the belly, and whoever bears a sword should know as much as that."
fail.chronicle: A bitter voice under the cinders says Fafnir was killed from below.

road.hint: A dragon's belly is softer by far than its back.

options.label: Leave the old dwarf to his grievance
options.outcome: "Gold," the voice says to no one at all, and the cinders settle over it once more.

name: The Voice under the Ice
text: A face as great as a door is frozen into the ice of the wall, and it is a giant's face with its eyes shut. As you draw near the eyes open, and the voice is like the moving of a glacier. "Small one, I watched the gods bind the wolf. I was there upon the island when all of them laughed, save the brave one, who did not. Ask me what you will."

options.label: Ask what bound the wolf

pass.outcome: "Gleipnir," says the giant, and he tells of a ribbon soft as silk that the dwarves made from six things: the sound of a cat's footfall, a woman's beard, the roots of a mountain, the sinews of a bear, the breath of a fish and the spittle of a bird, which is why none of these is left in the world. Fenrir would suffer them to tie it only if a god would lay a hand in his mouth, and this Tyr did. When the ribbon held, the gods all laughed save Tyr, for he had lost his hand. "Remember the one who paid," says the ice, and the cold about you loosens its grip.
pass.chronicle: A giant in the ice told me what made Gleipnir. Tyr gave a hand to bind the wolf.

fail.outcome: "It was a ribbon," the giant says, "soft as silk and made of things that are not, a cat's footfall and a mountain's roots, and there had to be a god's hand in the wolf's mouth to win his consent. The hand was Tyr's." With that the great eyes close again within the ice.
fail.chronicle: A giant in the ice says a ribbon bound the wolf. It cost Tyr his hand.

road.hint: The wolf was bound by things that are not found in the world.

options.label: Let the giant sleep
