options.outcome: The eyes close, and from a great way within the ice you hear a long creaking.

name: Diogenes
text: In a great clay jar in the middle of the corridor sits a filthy old man, and he holds up a lighted lantern, although there are torches every ten paces. He shines it in your face. "I am looking for an honest man," he says, "and it has been a slow century. Are you one?"

options.label: "I am."
options.outcome: He holds the lantern long to your face and then lowers it. "No," he says, and his eyes go past you down the corridor, for he is searching still.
options.chronicle: Told Diogenes I was honest. He didn't believe me.

road.hint: It is easier to call oneself an honest man than to be found one.

options.label: "I am."
options.outcome: "Honest, and soft," he says. "You paid a thief's debt, did you not? I can always tell." And for all that, he does not put out his lantern.

road.hint: It is easier to call oneself an honest man than to be found one.

options.label: "I am."
options.outcome: He looks upon you for a long while, and then he blows out the lantern. "Then I may leave off looking," he says, and sits back well content. But a moment afterward he lights it again. "No, I shall examine you once more tomorrow."
options.chronicle: Told Diogenes I was honest. He believed it, but will check tomorrow.

road.hint: It is easier to call oneself an honest man than to be found one.

options.label: "Not always."
options.outcome: He laughs until he coughs. "You come closer than most," he says, and he shares a heel of bread with you, which is the greater part of all that he has.
options.chronicle: Admitted to Diogenes I'm not always honest. He shared his bread.

options.label: "Is there anything I can do for you?"
options.outcome: "Yes," he answers from the depths of his jar. "Stand out of my light."
options.chronicle: Offered Diogenes help. He told me to get out of his light.

road.hint: There is great strength in a man who wants nothing from you.

options.label: Ask him why he lives in a jar

pass.outcome: "You know why," he says, well pleased. "A man who needs nothing cannot be bought or bribed or robbed." He tells you that he owned a cup once, until he saw a child drinking from cupped hands, and that he threw it away. Then he shows you how one may live upon less, and you find that your own needs are the fewer.
pass.chronicle: Diogenes taught me to do with less. Who needs nothing can't be bought.

fail.outcome: "For the view," you guess, and he laughs at you. "It is because a man who needs nothing cannot be bought. I had a cup once, until I saw a child drink from his hands, and then I threw the cup away." With that he returns to his search for an honest man.
fail.chronicle: Asked Diogenes about his jar. He threw out his cup on seeing a child do without.

road.hint: A man who needs no more than a jar cannot be bought.

name: Lena
text: A girl of about fourteen, with her mother's satchel and her mother's squint, plants herself squarely in your path. "Mam said it was a stranger with a potion. She said to look for the one who didn't ask anything for it." She holds out the satchel to you. "You don't owe me anything, for I've come here to pay you."

text_variants.text: A girl of about fourteen with her mother's squint bars the corridor, holding a ratting pole as one holds a spear. "Mam described you, down to the boots," she says, and though her voice shakes, the pole is steady. "She got home, and it's no thanks to you. I have come for her satchel."

A girl of about fourteen, with her mother's satchel and her mother's squint, plants herself squarely in your path. "Mam said it was a stranger who knew a tourniquet. She said you swore at her leg till it listened, and didn't ask anything for it." She holds out the satchel to you. "You don't owe me anything, for I've come here to pay you."

escort_lena.name: Lena

on_arrive.outcome: At the foot of the stair Lena gives you the last of her mother's tonic, and she is away up the steps again before you can argue with her.
on_arrive.chronicle: Lena saw me to the stair past every trap, then went home.

on_fail.chronicle: Lost Lena, Marta's girl, on the stairs.

escort_lena.on_fail_trapdoor: The floor gave way under me. Lena was left behind.

options.label: Take her mother's kit
options.outcome: She looks relieved, as one does when an account has been closed. "Mam will be glad of it, for she hates owing."
options.chronicle: Marta's girl paid me her mother's debt in potions. Took them.

road.hint: When a debt is repaid, both sides may cease to think of it.

options.label: "Keep it. Go home."
options.outcome: She argues and you win, though narrowly, and she climbs the stair with the satchel still upon her shoulder and the look of one who means to try again.
options.chronicle: Refused Marta's kit. Sent her girl Lena home with it.

road.hint: To refuse repayment is a gift also, though it has a cost of its own.

options.label: "Walk me down one floor. You know the traps."
options.outcome: She grins with her mother's own grin, and says, "Step where I step."

road.hint: One who learned the traps from her mother is well worth following.

options.label: Tell her it was you, and pay back the bread too
options.outcome: You count the potions into her mother's satchel, and the price of the bread besides. "It was me," you say. "I took them from her when she could not stand, and I am sorry." For a long moment the pole does not move. "Mam said you'd lie or you'd run," Lena says. "She didn't have a word for this." She slings the satchel and goes, but halfway up the stair she stops and turns her head. "I'll tell her you said it."
options.chronicle: Owned to Lena I robbed her mother. Repaid the potions and the bread.

road.hint: To confess a theft costs more than to repay it, and it may win more.

options.label: Give back what you took
options.outcome: She takes them and examines every stopper. "That's the potions," she says, "but Mam counted the bread as well." With that she goes her way, and she does not look back.
options.chronicle: Gave Marta's girl back the potions. Still owe for the bread.

road.hint: What is taken from a mother, her daughter may come to collect.

options.label: Tell her it's all gone
options.outcome: "Then I hope it was worth it," she says, and she spits with great accuracy upon your boots and goes.
options.chronicle: Told Marta's girl the medicine was spent. She spat on my boots.

road.hint: Some debts may stand unpaid for ever after.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: She watches you go by, and for a moment she has exactly the look of her mother.

name: Ostrander
text: At the bottom of a drop a man has sunk to the chest in a sucking pit of black mud. "A rope! For the love of God, a rope!" His coat is a wrecker's coat, as black as tar, and in the mud beside him lies a dark lantern on a pole, such as is hung upon a cliff so that ships will think that a harbour lies there. "I know what I am," he gasps, "but pull me out even so."

options.label: Throw him your rope
options.outcome: You haul him out, and he lies on the brink coughing up mud until he can grin at you with very fine teeth. "You're a saint," he says, "and saints are good for business." Then he takes up his lantern and goes upon his way.
options.chronicle: Pulled Ostrander the wrecker from a pit. He kept his false lantern.

road.hint: A rope thrown without terms will serve whatever the man does afterward.

options.label: Make him swear on the rope never to light a false lamp again, then pull
options.outcome: "Swear it," you say, and he looks at the rope and at you, and at the mud that has come up to his chin. "Never another false light," he says, "on my mother's grave." So you pull, and he leaves the lantern behind him in the pit.
options.chronicle: Saved Ostrander once he swore off false lamps. He left his lantern.

road.hint: A rope with an oath upon it may draw a man out of more than a pit.

options.label: Leave him
options.outcome: "I know what I am," he cries after you as you go, "and that is why I asked you."
options.chronicle: Left Ostrander the wrecker in his own pit.

road.hint: A man who is caught in his own trap has shown you what manner of man he is.

name: Grumwald
text: Your road comes to another chasm and another rope bridge, where Grumwald, who minds his cousin's bridge now, sleeps beside a new box. The sign reads "TOLL A COIN. TROLL ASLEEP. PAY ANYWAY," and beneath that, in newer paint, are the words "YES, YOU."

text_variants.text: Your road comes to another chasm and another rope bridge, where Grumwald, who minds his cousin's bridge now, sleeps beside a new box. The sign reads "TOLL A COIN. TROLL ASLEEP. PAY ANYWAY," and beneath that, in newer paint, are the words "NUMBER NINE CROSSES FREE."

Your road comes to another chasm and another rope bridge, where Grumwald, who minds his cousin's bridge now, sleeps beside a new box that is chained fast to his ankle. The sign reads "TOLL A COIN. TROLL ASLEEP. PAY ANYWAY," and beneath that, in newer paint, are the words "ESPECIALLY YOU."

options.label: Pay the toll
options.outcome: One yellow eye opens on you. "Number Nine has paid me twice," rumbles the troll, "and that has never happened before."
options.chronicle: Paid at Grumwald's second bridge, though his sign let me cross free.

road.hint: A troll long remembers the face of one who pays his toll.

options.label: Pay the toll
options.outcome: One yellow eye opens. "Huh," says the troll, and it seems to you that some long account between the two of you has now been squared, or very nearly so.
options.chronicle: Paid at Grumwald's new bridge. His sign meant me. We're about square now.

road.hint: A troll long remembers the face of one who pays his toll.

options.label: Pay the toll
options.outcome: One yellow eye opens and watches you while you pay your toll and go across.

road.hint: A troll long remembers the face of one who pays his toll.

options.label: Wake him and tell him who emptied his box
options.outcome: You lay your hand upon a knee as broad as a millstone and shake it, until one yellow eye opens and then the other, and the troll sits up to the whole of his great height. "It was I who emptied the box at the first bridge," you say, "and I took both fistfuls." While he watches, you feed a tenth of your purse into the new box, coin by coin, and it is long before he speaks. "Forty years I have had that box," he rumbles at last, "and you are the first that ever came back to say it." Then with his thumb he rubs out the words ESPECIALLY YOU, and settles himself to sleep once more.
options.chronicle: Owned I robbed Grumwald's box, repaid with interest. I'm off his sign.

road.hint: Grumwald might have been woken to hear a confession, and he would remember that also.

options.label: Cross
options.outcome: The bridge holds beneath you as you cross, and behind you the troll snores on without any change.
options.chronicle: Crossed another Grumwald bridge. His new sign seems meant for me.

road.hint: A troll's bridge may remember a little of all who cross it.

name: Elspeth
text: Up the corridor, against the stream of all that moves there, comes a woman bearing a candle in a jar. She is thin as a reed and walks like one who lay sick abed a month ago. "Aldric told me that a stranger was carrying his sin for him," she says, "and the cordial did its work on me." Then she sets the candle down and holds out her arms. "I have come to carry it back."

text_variants.text: A woman with a candle in a jar halts before you. "You are the one who bore Aldric's stone," she says. "The altar broke it, and he felt it go, all the way up in our kitchen. He has a farm to mend, and so he sent me to tell you."

options.label: Let her take the stone
options.outcome: She takes it in both her arms and staggers, but she makes no complaint. "There is an altar two stairs below," she says. "I will carry it there and break it, and then I can go home unburdened." Her candle goes out as she turns away, and she goes on without lighting it again.
options.chronicle: Let Elspeth take Aldric's stone to an altar to break, then go home.

road.hint: A burden taken up for another may honourably be handed back.

options.label: "I gave Aldric my word. I'll finish it."
options.outcome: For a long while she looks at you, and then she lights your way to the next stair with her candle, and from there she climbs homeward alone.
options.chronicle: Refused Elspeth Aldric's stone. The promise is mine to finish.

road.hint: One who gave his word may wish to keep it unaided.

options.label: Thank her for the news
options.outcome: She presses the candle upon you, jar and all, and you see that it burns without any wax, as candles are said to do in some of the old stories.
options.chronicle: Elspeth, Aldric's wife, thanked me. Left a candle that burns without wax.

road.hint: A word with Aldric's wife might have won you a candle to show you your road.

options.label: Keep walking
options.outcome: She stands watching until you are out of sight, and then she goes on her own way.

name: Man Who Is Owed
stance_note: Steel-man: Pike is sincere and selfless, and Basil the Great's sermon is the strongest Christian case for his claim, quoted accurately. The pass answers it (§3.9: a duty on the giver, not a right in the receiver) by showing the harm of the principle to a third party, not by mocking the man.
text: A gaunt man in a patched apron steps into your path with a basket, and behind him a thin girl stands silent, watching your pack. "I am Gerrold Pike," he says. "You carry rations and she has none. Saint Basil said it, and he meant it: the bread you hold back belongs to the hungry. It is not yours to give, for it is hers, and I have come to collect it." There is no asking in his voice, but only the calm of a man who has never in his life kept back a crumb for himself.

options.label: Put a ration in his basket
options.outcome: He hands it whole to the girl, whose name is Nell, and does not taste it himself. Then he turns to an old pilgrim who is coming down the stair behind you with one heel of bread, and gently, as of right, he holds out the basket to her as well, and she gives up her bread to him, believing that she must.
options.chronicle: Paid Gerrold Pike for a hungry girl. He took a pilgrim's last crust.

road.hint: Pike means well, but he will gather his due from the poorest traveller too.

options.label: Give it to the girl yourself
options.outcome: Nell takes it in both hands and eats as though someone might snatch it back, and Pike nods, content if not well pleased. "That is good," he says, "but you would have owed it to her whether you felt like giving or not."
options.chronicle: Fed a hungry girl myself. Pike says I owed the bread either way.

road.hint: The hungry girl might have had the bread from your own hand.

options.label: Answer him: a gift owed is no gift at all

pass.outcome: You tell him openly that it is your duty to feed her, and that you will do it because you choose to do it. But Basil was telling the rich man what he ought to do, and gave no other man a warrant to collect. What is taken by right is a gift no longer, and it makes servants of those who give, beginning with that old pilgrim. For a long time Pike is silent. At last he climbs back up the stair to the pilgrim, and with both hands he gives back her bread. "I have been taking it like a tax," he says, "and Basil never asked me to be a tax."
pass.chronicle: Won Pike over: charity owed is no gift. He gave the pilgrim's bread back.

fail.outcome: Your argument grows tangled, and Pike is so kind about it that you lose the thread altogether. He takes the ration as his due and gives it to Nell, and then he turns with his basket toward the pilgrim.
fail.chronicle: Lost the charity argument with Gerrold Pike. The pilgrim still paid.

road.hint: Pike might have been shown that a duty is no debt for others to collect.

options.label: Refuse him and walk on
options.outcome: Pike nods as one who looked for nothing else, and turns with his basket to the next traveller upon the stair.
options.chronicle: Refused Gerrold Pike a ration for the poor. He asked the next traveller.

road.hint: Had you refused Pike, he would have asked the next traveller.

name: Samson
text: In a hall of the caves a wedding feast is spread. At the head of the table sits a huge man with hair to his waist in seven braids, and thirty sullen young men line the benches. "I am Samson of Zorah," he says, grinning, "and I have a riddle and a wager: thirty fine cloaks says you cannot answer it. Out of the eater came something to eat. Out of the strong came something sweet." By the door the leader of the thirty plucks at your sleeve. "We had it out of the bride," he whispers, "for we told her we would burn her father's house. Pay us, and the answer is yours."

options.label: Answer it yourself, staking a fifth of your purse

pass.outcome: "A lion," you say, "and the honey that the bees made in its carcass." Samson roars and smites the table so that it cracks. "That was honestly come by," he cries, "but these will seek it in another fashion." He looks long upon the thirty, and not one of them can lift his eyes from his plate.
pass.chronicle: Solved Samson's riddle myself: lion and honey. His thirty had best beware.

fail.outcome: You guess amiss, and Samson takes your stake with a shrug, as if half sorry for it. "They had seven days to find it," he says, "and you had but a minute."
fail.chronicle: Guessed wrong at Samson's riddle and lost my stake.

road.hint: The riddle could be answered honestly, without what was wrung from a frightened bride.

options.label: Buy the answer from the thirty
options.outcome: "A lion, and honey," you say, and Samson's face grows very dark. "Somebody has been talking to my bride," he says. He pays you what he owes, and afterward he goes out with the thirty, and from the hall you can hear the sound of his vengeance upon them.
options.chronicle: Bought Samson's answer from men who bullied his bride. He paid, then went for them.

road.hint: The thirty had an answer to sell, but they got it by the bride's tears.

options.label: Tell Samson his bride was threatened, and give up the wager
options.outcome: Samson grows very quiet, and in him that is more terrible than any roaring. He sends four of his own men with clubs to sit outside her father's house, and only when that is done does he go in search of the thirty.
options.chronicle: Told Samson of the threat to his bride. He guarded her, then went hunting.

road.hint: In the old tale no one warned Samson, and his bride's house was burned.

options.label: Decline the wager

name: The Piper
text: A line of children comes dancing down the corridor behind a tall man in a coat of red and yellow who plays upon a pipe, and their eyes are open and empty. After them runs a fat man in a mayor's chain, puffing and crying out to you, "Stop him. I'll pay, I'll pay." The Piper does not slacken his step. "He promised me a thousand guilders for the rats," he says, "and he paid me fifty, and laughed." Last of all a small boy on a crutch is falling behind, weeping as he strives to keep up.

options.label: Pay the Piper his thousand yourself
options.warning: Stop him. I'll pay, I'll pay.
options.outcome: The Piper looks at your gold and then at the mayor, and he pockets it and plays a different tune, so that the children blink and turn about and go home. The mayor wipes his face. "That was generous, very generous," he says. "Hamelin thanks you." But he makes no offer to repay you what you have laid out on his behalf.

delayed.text: Nailed to a stair-post you find a notice that reads "HAMELIN SEEKS A RAT-CATCHER. FAIR TERMS. B. HARDEKOPF, MAYOR."

options.chronicle: Paid the Piper myself. Hamelin's children are home. Mayor won't repay.

road.hint: Had you paid the mayor's debt for him, he might soon have owed another.

options.label: Make the mayor pay what he owes, staking your breath

pass.outcome: You catch the mayor by his chain of office and lift it, so that the Piper can see the seal of the town upon it. A contract made under that seal, you say, binds all Hamelin and not Hardekopf alone, and Hamelin is here before you, dancing. At that the mayor pays in full from the purse at his belt which he swore was empty. The Piper counts the money and nods and plays the children home, and the first to come back is the boy upon the crutch.
pass.chronicle: Held Hamelin's mayor to the Piper's contract. He paid. The children went home.

fail.outcome: The mayor argues that the contract was for rats and never for sorcery, and while you dispute with him the music gets into your feet, and you dance until you fall. When you rise, the corridor is empty but for the mayor, alone now and grey, and the boy on the crutch, who was too slow to follow and is crying in the dust. The mayor takes the child, whose name is Hans, by the hand. "I will get this one home, at least," he says.
fail.chronicle: Lost the argument with Hamelin's mayor. The Piper took all but the lame boy.

road.hint: The mayor's promise bore the seal of Hamelin, and he could have been held to it.

options.label: Carry the lame boy out of the line
options.outcome: You lift the boy on the crutch out of the line, and he fights you, weeping, for he longs to go where the music is. But the others go into the hill and the hill closes behind them, and then he struggles no more, and he tells you that his name is Hans. The mayor, alone now and grey, takes him by the hand. "I will get this one home, at least," he says.
options.chronicle: Got the lame boy from the Piper's line to the mayor. The rest are gone.

road.hint: The lame boy at least might have been lifted out of the dance.

options.label: Stand aside
options.outcome: The music goes by you and the children with it, and last of all the mayor, promising still as he passes out of sight.

name: Sir Aldric
text: Beside a new-made cairn kneels a knight with a black stone still lashed to his back, and near him lies an empty vial of crystal, the same from which you drank. He does not lift his head or speak. A pilgrim's staff leans upon the cairn, though whoever brought the news down from the surface has not stayed with him, and scratched upon the topmost stone you read the one word ELSPETH.

options.label: Kneel beside him a while
options.outcome: He gives no sign that he knows you are there, but after a long time he puts out his hand and straightens a stone that was straight already.
options.chronicle: Found Sir Aldric at his wife's cairn. He will not speak.

road.hint: Sir Aldric might have had company in his grief.

options.label: Offer to take the stone now
options.outcome: Very slowly he shakes his head, and you understand that the stone has become a part of the cairn now, or else that he has.
options.chronicle: Offered to take Sir Aldric's stone, too late. He will keep it.

road.hint: You might still have offered to bear Aldric's stone, though too late to save her.

options.label: Tell him it was you who drank it, and ask to carry the stone
options.outcome: "It was I," you say. "I drank her cordial. You asked me for help, and I took the one thing that could have saved her." For the first time he looks up at you. "Nobody has said it," he answers, "neither the pilgrim nor the priest, and I have waited a long while for somebody to say it out loud." With stiff fingers he works the straps loose and lays the black stone in your arms, and it weighs all that he told you it would. "There's an altar somewhere below," he says. "I'm going home to bury her properly." Then he climbs the stair without his burden, slowly, as a man might who is learning once more to walk.

person_status.last_line: There's an altar somewhere below. I'm going home to bury her properly.

options.chronicle: Owned I drank Aldric's wife's cordial. Have his stone. He went to bury her.

road.hint: Had you owned to drinking the cordial, Aldric might have given up his burden to you.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: As you go by he leans forward to rest his head upon the cairn, and you hear the stone upon his back grinding against his armour.
options.chronicle: Passed Aldric at a cairn. The empty vial was the one I drank.

name: Great Lion
text: For three rooms something heavy has kept pace with you in the dark, and now it steps into the light. It is a lion in his prime with a full mane, scarred across the muzzle and bearing a pale old mark on one forepaw, and he sits down in the middle of the corridor and waits to see what you will do.

options.label: Hold out the thorn

pass.outcome: You hold it low and still upon your open palm with your eyes cast down, as one should offer anything to a great cat that has not yet made up his mind. He smells the thorn, and after it he smells you, and then he lays the whole of his huge head against your breast and pushes, as a cat of the hearth will do.
pass.chronicle: The lion I helped came back grown. Knew the thorn and leaned on me.

fail.outcome: You hold it up too quickly, and he flinches back. Then with great delicacy he takes the thorn from your fingers in his teeth, as a hound takes a morsel of bread, and walks away with it into the dark.
fail.chronicle: The lion came back. Startled him. He took the thorn and left in peace.

road.hint: A lion may know again the thorn that was once drawn from his paw.

options.label: Stand very still
options.outcome: He regards you a long while, and then he pads past you so closely that his flank brushes your leg as he goes.

options.label: Throw him food and back away

name: Ostrander
text: Across a chasm a lamp is glowing, as warm and welcoming as if a path ran to it, but it stands upon the wrong side of the chasm, where no path goes.

text_variants.text: At the lip of a chasm a lamp burns upon an iron pole, and it stands on the right side, where the path is. Beneath it a man in a wrecker's coat sits trimming the wick, and you know him for Ostrander. "Never another false light," he says, before you can ask. "I swore it on your rope, and this lamp has been lit at every watch since that day."

options.label: Sit under his lamp a while
options.outcome: You sit a while beside him, and he tells you all the places where the floor gives way.
options.chronicle: Found Ostrander keeping a true lamp at a chasm, true to his oath.

road.hint: One who keeps a true lamp by a chasm may have good counsel to give.

options.label: Walk toward the light
options.outcome: The path ends one step short of the light. You fall a short and painful way into a cut where two men in wreckers' coats are waiting with clubs, and above you somebody laughs softly and trims the wick.
options.chronicle: Followed a false lamp. It was Ostrander's, whom I pulled from a pit.

road.hint: A lamp may be hung on the wrong side of a gulf to lead travellers into harm.

options.label: Look for whoever is holding it

pass.outcome: You find Ostrander in the shadow beneath the lamp, and he sees that he has been seen. At once he blows out the flame and runs from you into the dark.
pass.chronicle: Caught Ostrander, whom I once saved, at false lamps again. He ran.

fail.outcome: You see nothing there but the light, and yet for no reason that you could name you turn aside and go round by the long way.

road.hint: Before a lamp is followed, it is well to look for the hand that holds it.

options.label: Go round the long way

name: Lawspeaker's Rock
text: Two families face one another across a flat rock beneath a lamp-stone, holding their axes low, and a big man lays a bag of silver on the rock. "I am Hallbjorn," he says. "I killed Kol over a whale stranded on the shore of the under-sea, and I am sorry for it, and there is his price." Kol's brother Steinar will not look at it. "Silver cannot sit at my table in my brother's place." Then every face is turned toward you. "You are a stranger, and strangers have no side," says Hallbjorn, "so speak the law for us."

options.label: Speak the law: the price, the oath, the outlawry

pass.outcome: You speak it as the old lawspeakers did, case by case: the price for a free man killed in hot blood, the oath of peace that is sworn upon the ring, and the outlawry of whoever breaks it. So it was done in Iceland, where the lawspeaker bore the whole law in his memory and recited a third of it every summer from the Law Rock at Thingvellir, in the rift where two plates of the earth draw apart. Steinar hears you to the end, and then he takes up the silver slowly, as if it weighed more than it does, and puts out his hand to Hallbjorn.
pass.chronicle: Spoke the law at a blood feud. They took silver instead of the axe.

fail.outcome: You stumble over the price and the oath, and Steinar hears you falter. "Then there is no law here," he says. At that the axes are lifted, and Hallbjorn dies upon the rock with his silver beside him.
fail.chronicle: Forgot the middle of the law at a blood feud. They used axes.

road.hint: The law, well spoken, may stand between a grudge and an axe.

options.label: Add your own silver to sweeten the price
options.warning: Silver cannot sit at my table in my brother's place.
options.outcome: Steinar looks at your coins lying upon Hallbjorn's. "Now a stranger pays the price of my brother," he says, "and so he is worth less than I thought." With that the axes are lifted, and Hallbjorn dies upon the rock, on top of his silver and of yours.
options.chronicle: Added my silver to a blood price. It cheapened the dead man. They used axes.

road.hint: A grieving brother may hear an insult in the silver of a stranger.

options.label: Tell Steinar to take his revenge
options.outcome: "Blood for blood," you say, and Steinar nods as calmly as if you had done no more than speak to him of the weather.

delayed.text: By the stair stands a new cairn with the names of Hallbjorn's two sons scratched upon it, and beneath them someone has added in a fresh hand, "AND STEINAR."

options.chronicle: Urged Steinar to revenge. A later cairn bore his name among others.

road.hint: To urge revenge upon Steinar would only have raised more cairns.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Behind you the silence upon the rock lengthens as you go, until at last it breaks and you hear the feud begin.
options.chronicle: Left a blood feud at the law rock. Heard it break out behind me.

road.hint: Had you walked on, the rock would have had no lawspeaker.

name: Nestor of Pylos
text: Halfway up a broken pillar sits a very old man in very old bronze, with his spear planted beside it like a ladder. "I am Nestor of Pylos, and I am not stuck," he says. "I am resting where I landed. When the Boar of Calydon came at me I vaulted on this spear into a tree, and a man of my years does not come down from such a thing in a hurry. Sit, then, and I will tell you of the hunt, and I shall leave out none of it."

options.label: Sit down and hear all of it
options.outcome: He tells how Artemis sent the boar because a king forgot her at the harvest, and how half the heroes of Greece came to hunt it. A huntress named Atalanta drew first blood with an arrow, for which the men have never forgiven her, and Meleager made an end of it with a spear. "They say that a beast of that blood roots about below here still," says Nestor. "Blades skid off the bristles, but a point goes in." When at last you rise you are stiff, and strangely ready for whatever may come.
options.chronicle: Heard out all of old Nestor's tale of the Calydonian Boar.

road.hint: Old Nestor's tale of the boar is long, but there is profit in hearing it all.

options.label: Ask him who drew the boar's first blood

pass.outcome: "Atalanta," you say, and his old eyes shine. "With an arrow, behind the ear," says he, "and the men have not forgiven her yet, though it was Meleager who finished it with a spear." He leans down toward you. "Since you listen, hear this: a beast of that blood roots about below here still. Blades skid off the bristles, but a point goes in, so set your spear against the charge and let it run itself onto the point." Then he shows you how you must stand to meet it.
pass.chronicle: Nestor says Atalanta drew the boar's first blood. Blades skid, a point goes in.

fail.outcome: "Meleager?" you guess. "Meleager killed it," says the old man, much disappointed, "but Atalanta drew first blood, with an arrow, and the men never forgave her. Young people never have any patience for the middle of a story."
fail.chronicle: Nestor corrected me: a huntress drew the Calydonian Boar's first blood.

road.hint: It was an arrow, and no spear, that drew the first blood of Calydon's boar.

options.label: Help him down and move on
options.outcome: He comes down by slow stages, complaining bitterly of these modern pillars. "In my day," he says, "we had good trees to land in."

options.label: Leave him on his pillar
options.outcome: "In my day," he calls after you from his pillar, "we had good trees to land in."

name: Tarek the Guard
text: Among broken bales of salt and a dead mule a broad-shouldered man sits on an overturned crate with his head in his hands, and at the sound of your step he looks up too quickly, and with too much hope. "My name is Tarek, and I was guard to a caravan on the salt road," he says. "The ground opened under our camp three nights ago and we came down with it. The others went to look for the way up and have not come back. Please tell me that you know the way out, or that you have food, or both, and I will take them in any order you like."

options.label: Give him food and directions
options.outcome: He eats quickly, and then he stands and squares his shoulders. "You are a decent soul," he says, and gripping your forearm as one soldier does another he speaks over you the blessing of the guardsmen: "Keep your left side covered." At the words a steadiness settles about you like a second coat.
options.chronicle: Gave Tarek, a lost caravan guard, food and directions.

road.hint: A lost man has need of food as well as of a road.

options.label: Help him find which way is up

pass.outcome: You wet a finger and hold it up until you feel a cold draught upon one side, for a cave breathes through its mouths, and where the air moves there is a way to the open sky. You follow the draught with Tarek to a crack that has daylight at the top of it, and he laughs aloud for joy. "The bales that nobody can carry are yours," he says. "On the old caravan roads to Timbuktu salt was traded for gold, and it will still buy a fair amount."
pass.chronicle: Found Tarek's way up by the draught. He left me the salt.

fail.outcome: You lead him the wrong way, downhill toward the water, and he follows because you sound so sure. Only afterward does it come to you that a wet finger held in the draught would have shown the road, for a cave breathes through its mouths, and where the air moves there is a way out.
fail.chronicle: Led a lost guard the wrong way. Should have felt for the draught.

road.hint: The moving air of a cave may show the way out.

options.label: Buy salted provisions from the broken bales
options.outcome: He sells you salt fish and hard bread out of the stores of the caravan at a fair price. "The owners would wish to be paid," he says, "and I shall have need of coin up there, if there is still any world up there to spend it in."

options.label: "Sorry, I'm lost myself."
options.outcome: He gives a short and tired laugh, and it is honestly meant. "Of course you are," he says, and nods toward the dark. "Well, it is company for a few minutes, and that is something."

name: Saint Brendan
text: Upon a low black island in an underground sea, where no tree grows, fourteen monks in wet habits are building a fire to cook their Easter supper, while from the bow of a leather boat an old monk watches them with a look that you cannot read. "I am Brendan," he says, and nods to you courteously. "Will you help the brothers with their fire?" The island is warm beneath your boots, and you feel that it rises slowly and falls again, as if it were breathing.

options.label: Help the brothers build up the fire
options.warning: It rises slowly and falls again, as if it were breathing.
options.outcome: The fire catches beautifully, and then the island shudders from end to end and goes down like a stone. All of you are cast into black water among floating loaves and a cauldron, while Brendan, who is in no way surprised, draws out his monks one after another with a boathook.
options.chronicle: Lit the monks' fire on an island. It was a fish. Saint Brendan fished us out.

road.hint: It is wise to look well at an island before a fire is kindled upon it.

options.label: Look at the island properly

pass.outcome: You mark that the island is warm and breathing and bare of trees, and that at its far end is a hole which mists every few minutes, and you get the brothers back into the boat before the fire is lit. Then Brendan laughs aloud for the first time in seven years. "We will say the Mass upon his back without a fire," he says, "for he has been patient with us." So it is done, and you stay with them to hear it.
pass.chronicle: Saw the island breathe. Brendan's monks said Mass on the whale, no fire.

fail.outcome: To your eyes it is an island like any other. Only afterward, as you stand dripping, do you learn that sailors call it Jasconius, the fish so great that Brendan's monks once lit their Easter fire upon its back.
fail.chronicle: Took an island in the underground sea for land. It was no island.

road.hint: The island of Brendan's monks was warm, and it breathed.

options.label: Share your food with the brothers
options.outcome: The brothers bless the food, and you who gave it, and then they go back to the building of their fire.

options.label: Wish them a happy Easter and go

name: Wren Hallet, Scout
text: Propped against a pillar is a young scout with an ill-wrapped wound in her leg, pale but wakeful. "Do not trouble with the north passage," she says at once, as if she had been waiting for someone whom she might warn. "There is something down there that does not die clean." She winces and shifts her weight from the leg. "I would offer you a trade, but just now I have very little to bargain with."

options.label: Re-dress her leg properly

pass.outcome: You unwind the foul bandage, wash out the grit with clean water, press a pad on the cut until it ceases to seep, and bind it firmly, for a wound wrapped over dirt will fester and a clean one will heal. She stands and tries the leg, and then she draws you a rough map of the north passage. "It does not die clean because steel only slows it," she says. "Use fire, or something blessed, for that is what put the last one down in the end."
pass.chronicle: Bound Wren Hallet's leg. Use fire or blessing in the north passage, not steel.

fail.outcome: You draw the old bandage tighter over the old dirt, and she winces. "That will fester," she says. "You must always wash it first." She will manage, and in spite of all she gives you her warning: "Steel only slows it, so use fire, or something blessed."
fail.chronicle: Bound a scout's leg badly. Wash first. Steel only slows the north passage thing.

road.hint: A wound will fester if it is bound over dirt.

options.label: Give her bandages and splints (60 gold)
options.outcome: She takes the stores with great relief and binds herself with a practised hand, and then she presses into your hand a rough map of the north passage, with the creature's rounds marked in red. "It walks in a circle," she says, "and there is a space of time when the way is open. That is how I got out."

options.label: Sit with her until she can walk
options.outcome: You help her bind the wound as it ought to be bound, and you wait beside her until she has strength enough to stand. She will not rest until she has returned the kindness, and bringing out a little satchel of salves she tends some of your own hurts with a skilful hand. "A scout is taught such things," she tells you.
options.chronicle: Sat with Wren Hallet till she could walk. Beware the north passage.

road.hint: A scout who came back is worth sitting with.

options.label: Wish her luck and move on
options.outcome: "Aye," she says, to no one in particular. As you go you hope that she will find her way out, though by now you have seen enough of this dungeon to know how hard a thing it can be to go on hoping.

name: Bramble the Vendor
text: Where several passages meet, a stout halfling has made a little cookfire in the very midst of the dungeon, and from the pot upon it rises a truly savoury smell. He stirs it cheerfully. "Before you ask, yes, I have a permit, and no, I will not tell you who issued it," he says, "and yes, it smells as good as it looks. Now, will you have some or will you not?"

options.label: Buy a bowl (fills you up)
options.outcome: It is truly excellent, rich and well seasoned and served in a chipped but clean bowl, and as you eat it standing you feel almost like one who lives in a house again. "It is a good recipe," you say, when you are able. "A family secret," says he, with a wink, "and it is mushrooms, for everything down here is mushrooms."
options.chronicle: Bought excellent stew from a halfling with a permit.

road.hint: Bramble sold good stew, whoever gave the permit.

options.label: Buy extra provisions
options.outcome: He wraps a portion in waxed cloth as deftly as any merchant. "It keeps two days, or three if you do not think about it too hard," he says, and he tucks a little packet of herbs beside it. "That is for flavour, since even an emergency deserves some flavour."

options.label: Guess what's in the pot

pass.outcome: "Morels," you say, when you have smelled the pot, and he beams upon you. A true morel has a cap pitted like honeycomb and is hollow all through when it is sliced, while the false are stuffed within as if with cotton, and nobody sensible eats of those. "And never raw," he says, "for raw, even a true one will turn your stomach, but cooked it is the best thing under the earth." Then he gives you a bowl for nothing, and a portion wrapped for the road.
pass.chronicle: Guessed morels, ate the halfling's stew free. True ones are hollow.

fail.outcome: "Beef?" you guess, and he laughs. "Morels," says he. "A true one is hollow all through when you cut it, and that is how you may know it from a false. And always it must be cooked." He goes back to his stirring. "The bowl is still for sale."
fail.chronicle: Guessed wrong at the halfling's stew. Morels, always to be cooked.

road.hint: A true morel may be known by being hollow through.

options.label: "Just enjoying the smell."
options.outcome: "That is free of charge," he says grandly. You linger a little longer than you have need to, and he does not hurry you, and you find that you are very thankful for so small a kindness.

name: Thrar Coalhand, Journeyman
text: A young dwarf with a grinding wheel strapped to his back is sitting on a fallen column, pedalling the wheel and holding a blade to it so that the sparks fly out in a fan. "Thrar Coalhand, journeyman, upon my wander-years," he says, squinting at you through hair that is black with soot. "I cannot make you armour, for that is work for the masters, but I can put an edge on anything, and that weapon of yours has a sorrowful look to it."

options.label: Pay him to sharpen your weapon
options.outcome: Thrar pedals until the wheel howls, and he draws your blade along it in short and careful strokes. When he gives it back, the torchlight runs differently upon it, keener and more hungry. "Now that is a proper tool," he mutters, well content.
options.chronicle: Paid Thrar, a journeyman dwarf, to sharpen my weapon.

road.hint: The dwarf who found fault with your blade could have made it keener.

options.label: Ask him who the best smiths ever were

pass.outcome: "The sons of Ivaldi," you say, "and Brokkr and his brother." He grins through the soot. "Now you talk sense! Ivaldi's sons made Skidbladnir, the ship that has a fair wind as soon as her sail is raised and folds small enough to go in your pocket, and Brokkr's brother made Draupnir, the gold ring that drips eight more like itself every ninth night." Then without asking he takes your blade from you, and he puts an edge on it for nothing.
pass.chronicle: Named the great smiths to Thrar the dwarf. He sharpened my blade for nothing.

fail.outcome: "Wayland?" you guess. "That was an elf," says he, offended on behalf of all his people. "The sons of Ivaldi made a ship that folds into your pocket, and Brokkr's brother made a ring that drips eight more every ninth night. You should go and learn your tales."
fail.chronicle: Named the wrong smiths to Thrar the dwarf and offended him.

road.hint: Thrar knows what dwarves once made a ship to fold into a pocket.

options.label: Have him grind the rust and nicks out of your gear
options.outcome: Thrar clicks his tongue at every pit and freckle of rust and takes them out upon the wheel one by one, with many opinions upon each. "Rust is only metal that has stopped caring," says he, "and the wheel puts it in mind of its duty."
options.chronicle: Had Thrar the dwarf grind the rust out of my gear.

options.label: "Just browsing, thanks."
options.outcome: He shrugs and bends to his wheel again with no more words, and long after he is lost to sight the whine of it follows you down the corridor.

name: Old Veska
text: Bent over a heap of broken weapons, an old woman searches through them as patiently and happily as one who has loved such work all her life. She holds a snapped sword hilt up to the light and admires it with all her heart. "That is fine craftsmanship, even ruined," she says, and then she catches sight of you. "Ah! You have gear that still works, and that interests me greatly."

options.label: Trade gold for her oddments
options.outcome: She gropes in her bag and draws out a trinket that has the look of scrap, yet hums faintly upon exactly the right note. "I found that one near a fallen shrine," she says, "and something lives in it still." It seems to give her great delight to see you so doubtful.
options.chronicle: Traded with Old Veska, who collects broken weapons.

road.hint: Old Veska could read in broken things how well they had been made.

options.label: Let her examine your weapon, and guess its making

pass.outcome: She turns it to the light, and you talk of metal together: how the famous blades of Damascus were forged from wootz, a steel made in crucibles in India, and how the watered pattern upon them was the steel's own grain, folded into the blade. "You know your steel," she says approvingly, and she shows you the sweet spot of your blade, where a hit lands best. "You are the latest chapter in its tale, so try to be a good one."
pass.chronicle: Old Veska showed my blade's sweet spot. Damascus steel was Indian wootz.

fail.outcome: "Hammered from a horseshoe?" you guess, and she sniffs. "Hardly. The best of the old blades were of Damascus, forged from wootz, which is crucible steel from India, and the watered pattern was the steel's own grain." She gives it back to you. "You are the latest chapter in its tale, so try to be a good one."
fail.chronicle: Guessed my weapon's make wrong. Old Veska told of Damascus steel.

road.hint: Old Veska could read in broken things how well they had been made.

options.label: Decline and keep moving
options.outcome: "That is sensible," she says, already turning back to her heap, "and most things that are worth the finding are best found by accident in any case."

name: Apprentice Runescribe
text: A girl not long out of childhood, in an apprentice's robes too large for her, is carefully drawing runes upon the dungeon floor and muttering as she works. She looks up in alarm, having forgotten that monsters also use this passage. "Oh, good, you look human!" she says. "My master says a ward needs the rune of Tyr, and I have the whole futhark here, only I cannot remember which of them is his. Do you know it?"

options.label: Help her find Tyr's rune

pass.outcome: You point to the arrow, the rune of the letter T, which is named Tiwaz. "Of course," she breathes. The futhark takes its name from its first six letters, f-u-th-a-r-k, as the alphabet does from alpha and beta, and the old poem bids a warrior carve victory runes on the hilt of his sword and name Tyr twice. So she inks the arrow twice upon a scroll and gives it to you. "It is yours," she says, "for you found it."
pass.chronicle: Found Tyr's arrow rune. Carve it on a hilt and name Tyr twice.

fail.outcome: You point to the wrong one, and she copies it with perfect trust, and it does nothing at all. Afterward she finds the right one for herself, the arrow Tiwaz, which is Tyr's rune and the one that the old poem says to carve upon a sword hilt. "It is the arrow!" she calls after you, and she is a little smug.
fail.chronicle: Showed an apprentice the wrong rune for Tyr. His is the arrow.

road.hint: The young apprentice had need of one who knew Tyr's rune.

options.label: Buy one of her scrolls
options.outcome: The bargain is fair, though she drives it harder than you would look for in one of her years. The scroll that she brings out was plainly copied from a far higher book than any that ought to be open to her, and you think it wiser not to ask how she came by it.

options.label: "I don't know runes. Good luck."
options.outcome: "Right. Well, I shall puzzle it out," she says, and she turns again to her work as steadfastly as a woman who has been underrated all her life and has long since ceased to mind it.

name: Thökk

tells: the white seams of old stitches
a salmon tail in her pot
laughs like someone who has just knocked over a lamp

text: By a cookfire in the mouth of a cave sits an old giantess in rags, with a salmon tail sticking out of her pot. Outside all things are weeping, so that the water runs down the stones in sheets, and a tired young god with a messenger's staff is waiting at the threshold. "I am Hermod," he says to you. "Ask her yourself, but she will not weep for my brother." The old woman laughs like someone who has just knocked over a lamp, and upon her lips you see the white seams of old stitches. "Thökk will weep dry tears," she says. "Let Hel keep what she has." Then she holds out to you a ring of red gold. "And you will say nothing."

options.label: Take her ring and say nothing
options.outcome: She closes your fingers about the ring, and outside Hermod waits a long while, until at last he turns and goes home alone.
options.chronicle: Took a giantess's ring for silence. She won't weep for Baldr. His brother left alone.

road.hint: The giantess's ring was offered as the price of silence.

options.label: Refuse her ring, look hard at her mouth, and tell Hermod what you see

pass.outcome: "Those are the stitches of Brokk," you say, "the dwarf who sewed up the mouth of Loki." Hermod's face grows very still. The old woman laughs one last time and is not there, and a fly goes out of the cave very swiftly. Baldr must remain in Hel, but now the gods know who kept him there, and Loki shall answer for it with a long binding.
pass.chronicle: Told Hermod the giantess's stitches were Loki's. She fled. Baldr stays dead.

fail.outcome: You know that you have seen such scars somewhere, and you cannot tell where. Hermod thanks you none the less, and he goes home bearing nothing but the knowledge that there is one creature in the world who would not weep.
fail.chronicle: Refused the ring of a giantess who won't weep for Baldr. Can't place her face.

road.hint: The scarred lips of her who would not weep might have betrayed who she was.

options.label: Weep for Baldr yourself
options.outcome: You weep, and it is not hard where all things about you are weeping, but it changes nothing for Baldr. "Dry tears," says Thökk, and is well pleased.
options.chronicle: Wept for Baldr with all the world. It did not help him.

road.hint: Your tears for Baldr could not suffice while one creature still withheld hers.

options.label: Walk on

name: Aristodemus
text: A Spartan in a red cloak that has faded to brown sits polishing a bronze shield which is bright already. "I am Aristodemus, and you will have heard of me," he says. "I was sent home sick from the Hot Gates while the three hundred died. They call me the Trembler now, and no man speaks to me or gives me fire." He tries the spear-point upon his thumb. "There is a horde below, and I mean to die before it so well that they must cease to call me that. Tell me that I am right."

text_variants.text: A Spartan in a red cloak that has faded to brown sits polishing a bronze shield which is bright already. "I am Aristodemus, and you will have heard of me," he says. "I was sent home sick from the Hot Gates while the three hundred died. They call me the Trembler now, and no man speaks to me or gives me fire." He tries the spear-point upon his thumb. "There is a horde below, and I mean to die before it so well that they must cease to call me that. Tell me that I am right." Then he frowns. "A boy of the Legion came through here telling my story over to himself, and I hope that he had the ending wrong."

on_arrive.outcome: At the foot of the stair he halts. "You walk like one who means to go home," he says, "and I had forgotten that it was allowed." Then he turns and climbs back by the way he came, upward to the light.
on_arrive.chronicle: Saw the Trembler safe to the stair. He has gone home himself.

on_fail.chronicle: The Trembler fell beside me facing the foe. None can call him that now.

options.label: "Live. Dying well won't change what they call you."
options.outcome: He stares as though you had struck him, and then by slow degrees the look passes and he begins to think upon what you have said.

delayed.text: Upon the stair you find a vault door of bronze that has been forced and wedged open with a Spartan spear, and the hoarder within will have no more need of his goods.

options.chronicle: Told the Trembler to live. Later found a Spartan spear wedging a vault.

road.hint: The Spartan, if he were told to live, might yet find work for his spear.

options.label: "Go and die well."
options.outcome: He rises, and for the first time his cloak hangs upon his shoulders as a soldier's should.

delayed.text: On the stair you come to a low doorway with a bronze shield wedged across it, face outward and brightly polished, and a spear-point is broken off in its rim. Behind it the children of a caravan lie asleep in a heap of blankets, all unharmed, but of the Spartan who set it there you can find no sign.

options.chronicle: Sent the Trembler to die well. Later found his shield over sleeping children.

road.hint: A Spartan's shield may guard others when he is gone.

options.label: "Walk a floor with me first, and decide on the way."
options.outcome: "I will walk one floor with you," he says, "and no more than the one."

road.hint: With company for a little way, the Spartan might have turned his steps toward home.

options.label: Call him what they call him
options.outcome: "Trembler," you say, and he nods as calmly as if you had told him the hour, and bends once more to the polishing of his shield.
options.chronicle: Called a Spartan the Trembler to his face. He only nodded.

road.hint: The Spartan bore his shameful name already, and to repeat it would add to his load.

name: Doctor Finch
text: In a doorway stands a figure in a long black coat and a beaked mask, with a writing board in his hand. "Ah, a living one," he says, and his voice comes nasal through the mask and as cool as a surgeon's knife. "I have been making a catalogue of the afflictions down here, and you appear to be whole, which is remarkable at such a depth. Have you any symptoms that I should record, such as bleeding, visions or involuntary cursing?"

options.label: Let him examine you, and talk shop

pass.outcome: He prods and pokes, and as he works you talk of his craft. His beak is stuffed with herbs, for his teachers believed that plague rode upon bad air, which is called miasma, and that a sweet smell would keep it off. "That was wrong, of course," he says cheerfully. "A London doctor named Snow mapped the cholera dead in Soho, found that nearly every one had drunk from one pump, and had its handle taken off. It was germs in the water, and no bad air at all." And being pleased with you, he treats you for nothing.
pass.chronicle: Talked shop as Doctor Finch treated me. His herbs stop no plague.

fail.outcome: You tell him that it must be the herbs in his beak that keep him well. "Miasma," he sighs, "which is to say bad air. That is what my teachers believed, and my teachers were wrong, for a doctor named Snow traced the cholera to a single water pump." He writes a note upon his board. "My fee stands, if you wish to be treated."
fail.chronicle: Wrongly praised Doctor Finch's herbs. Plague is germs, not bad air.

road.hint: The beaked doctor would gladly have talked of his craft with a living patient.

options.label: Buy a curative compound
options.outcome: He takes a small vial from a rack of others exactly like it and labels it in a tiny, careful hand. "Take it with water and never with strong drink," he says. "Take it with no other potion unless you understand what you are doing, which very probably you do not." All this he says with no more tenderness than if he were addressing the vial.

options.label: Have the Doctor treat what ails you
options.outcome: "Fascinating, and disgusting, but chiefly fascinating," says the Doctor, as he works through your ills one by one with tongs and tinctures, talking all the while. When he is done you are free of every one, and you suspect that he now has the whole of your sickness in a jar.
options.chronicle: Paid the beaked Doctor to cure me. He kept a sample.

road.hint: A doctor of plagues has a cure for most ills of the deep.

options.label: "I'm fine. Good day, Doctor."
options.outcome: "You are demonstrably not fine," he says, and for all that you have told him he writes a note upon his board, and you find it strangely comforting.

name: Morrow
text: Upon the stair a man in a stolen priest's cassock waits with two friends in locust masks. It is Morrow, and he spreads his hands and smiles. "You set me free," he says, "and so I have brought my friends to thank you."

text_variants.text: Upon the stair a man in a stolen priest's cassock waits with two friends in locust masks. It is Morrow, and he spreads his hands and smiles. "You set me free," he says, "and so I have brought my friends to thank you. The old man told you I would be back, did he not? He always did spoil a surprise."

options.label: Fight
options.outcome: All three come at you upon the stair, and Morrow fights to the last in that stolen cassock, as one who feels no shame in the wearing of it.
options.chronicle: Morrow, the cultist I freed, brought friends. Fought on the stair.

road.hint: A false priest who is set free may wait upon a later stair with his friends.

options.label: Remind him you saved his life
options.outcome: "That you did," says Morrow courteously, "and it is the reason that I am letting you go first."
options.chronicle: Told Morrow he owed me his life. He agreed, and attacked anyway.

road.hint: Little is to be hoped from the gratitude of a liar.

name: Calla Strand
text: A woman with many scars sits with her back to the wall, oiling with great care a short sword that she plainly does not mean to use again tonight, and there are too many new bandages on her arms. "You have that look," she says, without raising her eyes, "the look of one who still believes that this was a good idea."

options.label: Ask her how she beat the gnoll pack

pass.outcome: "So you know your history," she says. Gnolls hunt as hyenas do, circling and pulling down the one who runs, and so you must not run, but stand with your back to a wall, points outward and shields together, as the Scots stood in their schiltrons at Bannockburn, where the English horse could not break them. "A beast will not run onto a hedge of points, and neither will a man," she says, "so stand." And she drills you until your very feet have learned it.
pass.chronicle: Calla Strand drilled me against packs, Scots fashion: back to a wall, points out.

fail.outcome: "Charge them first?" you ask, and she laughs, though it hurts her ribs. "That is how a fight with a pack is lost, for they circle and pull down whoever breaks. You must stand with your back to a wall and your points outward, as the Scots did at Bannockburn in rings of spears."
fail.chronicle: Calla Strand says never charge a pack. Back to a wall, points out.

road.hint: A pack will pull down the one who runs.

options.label: Ask her for a sparring lesson (costs SP)
options.outcome: She lifts an eyebrow, but she nods, and for an hour she drills you in stances of defence and in the governing of your breath when you are hard pressed.
options.chronicle: Sparred with Calla Strand, pit fighter. She found the same rib each time.

road.hint: A weary fighter may still have an hour's lesson for one who asks.

options.label: Buy her spare shield
options.outcome: For a long moment she looks at the shield before she hands it over. "I shall not need two," she says, "and I am not sure I shall need one." Then she takes the coin from your hand without counting it.

options.label: "Just passing through."
options.outcome: "To be sure you are," she says, as one who has heard those words from many that did not come back. She takes up the oiling of her sword again, and you go on your way still believing as you did.

name: Exposed Child
stance_note: Steel-man: Hrolf's relativism is given its strongest form (your people burn witches; every people judges by its own law; exposure as mercy in a famine). The pass text keys the reformer's dilemma (§3.10). No option rewards "whatever a hall approves is right".

authority.why: Sets a lame newborn out on the stone to die.

text: Before a longhouse built into the rock a newborn lies wrapped in a fleece upon a cold stone, crying thinly, and one of her feet is twisted. The chief stands over her with folded arms, and he meets your eye. "I am Hrolf Ketilsson," he says. "It is a hard winter and a lame mouth to feed, and in our hall this is right. Your people burn witches and call that right. Mine leave a weak child to the gods, which is kinder than a winter of starving. Every people judges by its own law, so who are you to judge mine?"

options.label: Argue with him

pass.outcome: You ask him of the first chief of his people who ever made the law kinder: was that man wrong, because the hall had not yet approved? And what of him who first refused to set a child upon the stone? If the hall is always right, then no hall can ever become better than it was, but only different. Hrolf is a long while without an answer, and then his wife comes out and takes up the baby, and he does not hinder her.
pass.chronicle: Out-argued Hrolf on leaving babies out. His wife took up the child.

delayed.text: A Brother in a patched brown habit, from the house upon the side stair, overtakes you on your road. "Hrolf's wife brought the little one to us for the winter, where the hall cannot change its mind," he says. "She feeds like a wolf cub, and we have named her Astrid."
delayed.chronicle: A Brother says Hrolf's girl winters with them. She is feeding, named Astrid.

fail.outcome: He has an answer for all that you can say. Therefore you lift the baby yourself, fleece and all, and carry her to the Brothers' house upon the side stair, and he suffers you to do it, for by his law she belongs to nobody now.
fail.chronicle: Lost to the hall-chief in argument. Took the baby off the stone myself.

delayed.text: You are overtaken by a Brother in a patched brown habit from the house upon the side stair. "The girl that you carried in is feeding," he says, "and her mother comes by night, when the hall is asleep. We have named her Astrid."
delayed.chronicle: A Brother says the girl I carried in is feeding. Mother visits at night. Named Astrid.

road.hint: The chief might have been answered, for his own custom was new once.

options.label: Buy the child for the price of her winter's keep
options.outcome: He takes the money and argues no further. Then his wife comes out of the longhouse and lifts the baby from the stone, for the coin is now her winter's bread, and she goes in again without a word to either of you. The custom stands. The next one will be on the stone too.
options.chronicle: Bought a baby off the hall-chief's stone. The next will be left there.

road.hint: Gold could have saved that one child, though it would leave the custom standing.

delayed.text: Behind you on the road comes a Brother in a patched brown habit from the house upon the side stair. "Hrolf's wife brought us her girl to be blessed, the one that your gold bought back," he says. "She is feeding, and we have named her Astrid."
delayed.chronicle: A Brother says the girl my gold saved is feeding. Named Astrid.

options.label: Walk on. His hall, his law
options.outcome: The crying follows you a long way down the corridor, growing fainter, until there comes a time when you hear it no more.
options.chronicle: Walked past a baby left on a stone by custom. The crying stopped.

road.hint: Had you passed the stone by, the child would have been lost.

name: Scholar Evaine
text: In the midst of the corridor a woman in ink-stained robes sits cross-legged among open tomes and hasty notes, and she does not look up at your coming. "Fascinating," she murmurs. "The marble here was cut at least four centuries before the outer chambers, and the plinth in the next hall is of a size with the one in the Parthenon. Oh, you are a person! Good day to you."

options.label: Ask what a plinth that size once held

pass.outcome: "The Athena Parthenos," you say, and at last she looks up. That was the goddess whom Phidias made, with wood within, ivory for the skin and gold for the robes, nearly twelve metres tall, bearing a winged Victory in her hand and the head of Medusa on her breast. "And the gold was made to come off," says Evaine in delight, "so that when they accused Phidias of stealing it, they could weigh it." Then she reads you the writing upon the plinth, by which you learn which way the goddess faced, and so which way the halls run.
pass.chronicle: Solved Evaine's plinth: an Athena whose gold came off to be weighed.

fail.outcome: "A king?" you guess. "A goddess," says she, already writing again. "She was like the Athena that Phidias made for the Parthenon, of ivory and gold and twelve metres high, with Medusa's head on her breast. The gold came off, so that it could be weighed when they accused him of theft."
fail.chronicle: Evaine says Phidias's Athena wore gold that came off to be weighed.

road.hint: The gold of the great goddess was made to be taken off.

options.label: Buy a scroll from her notes
options.outcome: She tears a page from a lesser notebook with scarcely a pause. "I copied that one twice in any case," she says, and you see that the writing is most careful and that the ink is still faintly warm from her pen.

options.label: "I'll leave you to your research."
options.outcome: "Mm. A wise choice, for I am very near to finding it out," she says. She has forgotten you already, and her quill races furiously over a new page.

name: Gyges
text: A shepherd sits at the lip of a chasm turning a gold ring on his finger, and each time that he turns it he flickers out of sight and back again. Far below him a horse of bronze lies on its side with its belly open. "It was on a dead giant's hand, down there," he says. "Since I put it on I have taken a purse, a goat and a girl's silver comb, and nobody saw." He draws it off and holds it out to you. "Take it, or put it back on him, for I can do neither." Yet even as he speaks, his hand goes again and again to the empty finger.

options.label: Take the ring and keep it
options.outcome: He lets it go with a sound that is half a sob and half a laugh. "Better you should have it than I," he says, and then, beginning already to doubt, he asks you, "Is it better?"
options.chronicle: Took the Ring of Gyges from a shepherd who could not stop using it.

road.hint: The shepherd's ring might hide you from others, and in time from yourself as well.

options.label: Climb down and put it back on the dead giant's hand
options.outcome: The climb is long and the bronze is cold, and the giant's hand is as great as a cart. When you have pushed the ring back upon it you are sorely tempted for a moment to turn it once, only to see, but you forbear. And when you come again to the top you find the shepherd weeping for relief.
options.chronicle: Put the Ring of Gyges back on the dead giant's finger, unused.

road.hint: The ring of unseeing might have been returned to the hand of its dead owner.

options.label: Promise to hold it for him until he's ready
options.warning: His hand goes again and again to the empty finger.
options.outcome: He thanks you and sits beside you while you look to your pack, and what he does then no eye can see. When you look up again the ring is gone and a share of your purse with it, and the shepherd has gone also.
options.chronicle: Offered to mind a shepherd's ring. He vanished with some of my gold.

road.hint: The shepherd could not truly lend what he could not let go.

options.label: Walk on

name: Boundary Stone
text: On a moor of grey moss stands a boundary stone bored with six holes that are filled with vinegar, and coins lie in the vinegar. Beyond it a village has shut itself in against the plague, at the word of its rector. From the door of the nearest cottage a man calls out to you. "I am well. I swear before God that I am well, and my children are at Low Middleton, a few stairs down, so lift the bar for me." He keeps his collar buttoned to the chin, though the cave is close and warm, and his face shines with sweat even while he shivers.

options.label: Lift the bar and let him go
options.warning: He keeps his collar buttoned to the chin, though the cave is close and warm
options.outcome: He takes your hand between both of his own and shakes it hard, and then he goes running for the stair.

delayed.text: At the foot of the stair you hear a bell tolling in Low Middleton, and for as long as you are on this floor it tolls again every hour.

options.chronicle: Let a man out of the plague village on his word. A bell tolls since.

road.hint: A collar buttoned close in a warm cave may be hiding a sickness.

options.label: Look at him properly before you lift anything

pass.outcome: You ask him to open his collar, and although he knows the reason he does it. Beneath his jaw is a swelling as big as a pigeon's egg and hot to the touch, and his skin burns with fever for all his shivering. He sits down weeping on his side of the stone and you sit down on yours, and you stay with him until his lamp burns low and promise to leave word at the stone for his children. Then he writes a letter for Low Middleton and drops it in the vinegar, and you fish it out and lay it beneath the stone, where the carriers look.
pass.chronicle: Saw plague on the man, kept the bar down. Left his letter for carriers.

fail.outcome: You look, and see no more than a frightened man with his collar done up, and so you lift the bar.
fail.chronicle: Missed the signs on a man from the plague village and lifted the bar.

road.hint: Before a sealed village is opened, one should ask why it was sealed.

options.label: Leave coins in the vinegar for their supplies
options.outcome: The coins sink into the vinegar. When the watch changes, the village will find them and buy bread with them, and the baker will wash them twice over. From his doorway the man, whose name is Hawksworth, watches what you do, and he does not ask you again to lift the bar.
options.chronicle: Left coins in the plague village's vinegar to buy them bread.

road.hint: Help may be passed across the plague stone while the bar stays down.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "Please," he says once as you go, and after that he does not call to you again.

name: Brother Osias
text: A monk with shaven head sits wholly still in the corridor, his eyes closed in meditation and his hands folded in his lap, and he does not open his eyes to speak. "You carry your weariness like a second pack," he says. "I can ease it, but the mind must have an anchor if it is to be still, some one thing on which the breath may rest."

options.label: Ask him whose way he follows

pass.outcome: "Antony's," he says, and he opens one eye, pleased that you guessed it. Antony walked out alone into the desert of Egypt and shut himself in an old tomb, and when the demons came upon him by night in the shapes of lions and serpents and wolves he did not run, and he lived to a hundred and five. Osias teaches you his manner of breathing, until your mind is clear and whatever comes at you in the dark seems smaller than it was.
pass.chronicle: Brother Osias taught me Antony's way: don't run from demons in beast shape.

fail.outcome: "A good guess, but no," he says. He follows the Desert Fathers, and Antony before all the rest, who was alone in a tomb in Egypt with demons in the shapes of beasts and did not run. But he is willing even so to guide you through a little of the breathing.
fail.chronicle: Brother Osias told me of Antony, who never ran from his demons.

road.hint: A mind made quiet may ease the weariness of a long road.

options.label: Offer food to support his vigil
options.outcome: For the first time he opens his eyes, and he receives the food with a little bow. "To sustain the body is to sustain the spirit," he says. Then he speaks over you a brief blessing that warms your limbs from within, like sunshine that was long forgotten and is now remembered.

options.label: Pass quietly without disturbing him
options.outcome: He takes no notice of your passing, and yet as you round the bend you could swear that there is a little more peace in the silence behind you than in the silence that lies ahead.

name: Courteous Giant
text: A giant sits at a table far too long for the room it stands in, though the room makes no complaint of it. "None may stay in my hall who cannot do some one thing well," says he in the pleasantest manner, "but we ask only modest things. You may empty my drinking horn, or lift my cat from the floor, or wrestle with Elli, my old nurse, if you can wake her." The horn is long and the cat is grey and very large, and the old nurse lies asleep by the fire.

options.label: Take the horn and drink

pass.outcome: You drink until your eyes water and the level has fallen by the breadth of a finger, and the giant grows somewhat pale. "The far end of that horn lies in the sea," he says, "and you have lowered it. Men will call what you have done the tide."
pass.chronicle: Drank from the horn in Utgard. Lowered the sea a little.

fail.outcome: You drink and drink, and still the horn is full. "Thor did no better," says the giant kindly, "and he was a god."
fail.chronicle: Failed to empty the giant's horn. Its far end was in the sea.

road.hint: In a giant's hall the contests are seldom quite what they appear to be.

options.label: Get both arms under the cat and lift

pass.outcome: One grey paw rises from the ground. "That cat is the serpent that circles the world," says the giant, "and none was ever meant to move it at all."
pass.chronicle: Lifted one paw of the giant's cat. It is no cat.

fail.outcome: The cat arches its back and yawns at you, and all four of its feet remain upon the floor.
fail.chronicle: Failed to lift the giant's cat. Learned later it is a world serpent.

road.hint: In a giant's hall the contests are seldom quite what they appear to be.

options.label: Wake the old nurse and wrestle her

pass.outcome: She puts you down upon one knee, as gently as one sets down a parcel. "Elli is Old Age," says the giant, "and none overcomes her, but most do not last so long as you did."
pass.chronicle: Wrestled old Elli and lost, but lasted longer than most.

fail.outcome: She puts you down at once. "Elli is Old Age," says the giant, "and you will meet with her again."
fail.chronicle: Wrestled Old Age and lost at once.

road.hint: In a giant's hall the contests are seldom quite what they appear to be.

options.label: Decline his contests
options.outcome: "Then you cannot stay," says the giant with great courtesy, "but you may certainly go." It is a long way to the door, and the grey cat watches you until you reach it.
options.chronicle: Declined the giant's three contests. He let me go.

road.hint: The giant could not fool one who declined his games.

name: Hymir's Boat

tells: ate two of my oxen at supper

text: On a black lake under the ice a frost giant with icicles in his beard sits in a rowing boat, and beside him a broad young man with a red beard is baiting a hook as great as an anchor with the head of an ox. "I am Hymir," says the giant sourly. "This lad ate two of my oxen at supper, and now he would row out beyond the place where I fish, and beyond it is where the Serpent lies." The young man, who has a short-handled hammer in his belt, grins at you. "There is room for one more," he says. "Will you hold the line with me?"

options.label: Hold the line with him

pass.outcome: The line grows taut and the lake heaves, and up out of the black water comes a head as great as a hall with the ox's head in its jaws, for it is the Serpent that circles the world. You hold fast, and the young man braces himself so mightily that his feet go through the bottom of the boat and stand upon the bed of the lake. Then Hymir, white with terror, saws through the line, and the Serpent sinks. "It is so every time," says the red-bearded man, and flings Hymir over the side. You know him now for Thor, who fished for Jormungandr with the head of an ox and was robbed of his catch by a frightened giant, and he claps you so heartily on the shoulder that it hurts.
pass.chronicle: Held Thor's line on the World Serpent. Hymir cut it.

fail.outcome: The line grows taut and the lake heaves, and the rope tears through your hands until you must let it go. Something enormous rolls beneath the boat. Hymir saws through the line before the young man can prevent him, and the red-bearded lad looks upon you in sore disappointment. Long after, you call to mind the old tale of Thor, who fished for the World Serpent with the head of an ox, and of the giant who cut the line.
fail.chronicle: Lost my grip on a huge catch. The giant cut the line. I think that was Thor.

road.hint: A red-bearded lad who baits his hook with an ox's head seeks no common fish.

options.label: Help Hymir cut the line
options.outcome: You and Hymir saw at the rope together until it parts, and something vast sinks away beneath the boat. The giant is so grateful that he gives you a flask from his stores, but the red-bearded young man says nothing at all, and his silence is harder to bear than any shouting would have been.
options.chronicle: Helped a frightened giant cut his line. His young companion said nothing.

options.label: Stay on the shore
options.outcome: You remain upon the ice, and far out on the lake you see the boat rock while something enormous breaks the surface and goes down again. A little afterward a very wet frost giant comes swimming to the shore, swearing with every stroke.

name: The Hermit
text: Crouched against the wall of a chamber that smells of old smoke and dried herbs is a man wrapped in many ill-matched cloths, and his eyes are sharp and knowing as they follow you. A row of small sealed vials hangs at his belt, each with a scrap of red thread. "Twelve years I have lived down here," he says softly.
