"I have followed the gorgon-kind a long way and gathered what they leave, and you have the look of one who could make use of a secret."

options.label: Ask what a gorgon's blood is good for

pass.outcome: "Ah, you have read Apollodorus," he says, and he tells how Athena gave the gorgon's blood to Asclepius the healer, death from the veins of the left side, and from the right side life enough to raise the dead, until Zeus struck him down for it. Then the hermit unhooks a vial with a red thread. "It is from the right side," he says, "for I am careful about sides."
pass.chronicle: Have gorgon's blood from a hermit, right side. Right heals, left kills.

fail.outcome: "Poison?" you guess. "That is half right," he says. "The left side gives death and the right side healing, enough to raise the dead. Asclepius had both from Athena, and Zeus killed him for using the good half too well." And he leaves his vials hanging where they are.
fail.chronicle: Hermit says gorgon's blood kills from one side, heals from the other.

road.hint: The virtue of a gorgon's blood depends on the side it was drawn from.

options.label: Share a meal together
options.outcome: You sit and share the food in easy silence, like two people who long ago came to the end of small talk. When you rise to go you are more at peace than you have been for many days, and you find that you have gathered some strength from the stillness.
options.chronicle: Shared a meal with a hermit settled here. He knows the floor's moods.

road.hint: One who has lived twelve years in the dark may know its moods.

options.label: Buy one of his vials
options.outcome: He unhooks a vial with a scrap of red thread and holds it to the light before he gives it into your hand. "It is from the right side," he says, "for I am careful about sides."

options.label: "I prefer my own counsel."
options.outcome: He nods slowly and takes no offence. "That is how I began also," he says, and you go on your way not wholly sure of his meaning.

name: The Head of Mimir
text: Under a root as thick as a tower, in a cave white with rime, black water fills a basin of stone, and just below its surface floats a man's head with open eyes, its beard spread like weed and knotted with sprigs of dried herbs. At the very bottom some small white thing catches the light, round as a coin, and it is looking up. The head speaks, and no bubble rises from its lips. "I am Mimir. The Vanir cut off my head, and the All-Father preserved it with herbs and spells, that he might talk with me. I keep the well. Wisdom has its price, and everyone who comes here asks me how much."

text_variants.text: Under a root as thick as a tower, in a cave white with rime, black water fills a basin of stone, and just below its surface floats a man's head with open eyes, its beard spread like weed and knotted with sprigs of dried herbs. At the very bottom some small white thing catches the light, round as a coin, and it is looking up. The head speaks, and no bubble rises from its lips. "I am Mimir. The Vanir cut off my head, and the All-Father preserved it with herbs and spells, that he might talk with me. I keep the well. Wisdom has its price, and everyone who comes here asks me how much." Then the head smiles. "It was he who sent you, for he always sends the clever ones. Tell him that the eye is keeping well."

options.label: Drink, and pay what it costs

pass.outcome: The water is so cold that it hurts your teeth and then your head, until the pain is gone and for a moment you understand some very great thing. The understanding passes from you, and yet a part of it remains.
pass.chronicle: Drank from Mimir's well and paid. Some of what I understood stays.

fail.outcome: The water runs through your mind as through a sieve, and Mimir keeps the price. "Everyone asks me how much it costs," he says, "and no one asks me how much he can hold."
fail.chronicle: Drank from Mimir's well and paid. Kept none of it.

road.hint: At Mimir's well the price must be paid before the wisdom is drunk.

options.label: "What's that at the bottom?"

pass.outcome: "You know whose it is," says Mimir, and his eyes narrow with respect. It is the eye of Odin, the All-Father, who paid it for one draught from this well, and who hung nine nights upon the windy tree for the runes besides. "He thought it cheap, and he is usually right about prices," says the head. "He walks abroad in a grey cloak, with a broad hat pulled over the empty socket, if ever you should wish to thank him."
pass.chronicle: Odin's eye is in Mimir's well. He wears a grey cloak and a broad hat.

fail.outcome: "A pearl?" you guess. "It is an eye," says Mimir. "A god paid it for one draught, and he thought it cheap."

road.hint: At the bottom of Mimir's well there was something that looked upward.

options.label: Leave the well
options.outcome: "Come back when you can afford me," says the head, and it closes its eyes beneath the water.

name: Sword in the Anvil
text: You come to a churchyard beneath the rock, where a great stone bears an anvil and these words in gold: WHOSO PULLETH OUT THIS SWORD OF THIS STONE AND ANVIL IS RIGHTWISE KING BORN. The anvil is empty, for a big young knight holds the sword aloft. "I am Sir Kay, and I drew it," he says. But behind him a skinny squire stares at his own hands, which are red from the hilt, while Kay's are clean. Kay bends close to you. "Say that you saw me draw it. Tell my father so, and you shall eat at my table all your days."

options.label: Back Kay's claim
options.outcome: Sir Ector looks at Kay, and at you, and at the skinny boy. "Is it so?" he asks, and you say that it is. The boy speaks no word, for in all his life nobody has ever asked him anything.
options.chronicle: Swore Kay drew the sword, though his squire did. May eat at his table.

road.hint: A seat at Kay's table could be had for false witness, but would be dearly bought.

options.label: Tell Sir Ector what you saw
options.outcome: Ector grows very quiet, and then the old man kneels in the churchyard before the boy whom he reared. Kay turns red and afterward white, and then, to give him his due, he kneels also.
options.chronicle: Refused Kay's table. Told Sir Ector the squire drew it. Ector knelt to the boy.

road.hint: The truth of who drew the sword was worth more than a seat at Kay's table.

options.label: Put it back in the anvil and let them both try

pass.outcome: You call to mind the manner of the old test. Kay strains until his face is purple, and when he gives over he avenges himself upon your ribs. But the squire draws the sword as lightly as a knife from butter, twice over and each time more afraid, and Sir Ector kneels before the boy.
pass.chronicle: Made Kay try the anvil again. He failed. The squire drew it twice.

fail.outcome: Kay snatches back the sword before you can make the test clear. "We are done here," he says, and with that your part in the matter is ended.
fail.chronicle: Proposed the anvil's test and Kay refused it. Did not lie for him.

road.hint: The sword might have been set back, to see who could draw it a second time.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "Good," says Kay. "You are a friend." And as you go you hear an old man asking behind you, "Kay, who was it that drew the sword?"

name: Damocles
text: Beneath a ceiling of crystal a long table is laid for a king, with a couch of gold at its head, and on the couch lies a courtier in a crown, very pale and eating nothing. "I said that kings were lucky," he tells you, without moving his head, "and I would dearly like to take it back now." Above him a sword hangs point downward by a single horsehair. The horsehair runs up to a hook, and from the hook a thin cord runs to a bell above the guards' door. At the foot of the table a tired man with a clever face beckons to you. "I am Dionysius," he says. "My friend Damocles envied kings. Take his place, if you like, and eat like one."

options.label: Cut the horsehair down and pull him clear
options.warning: From the hook a thin cord runs to a bell above the guards' door.
options.outcome: The hair parts and the sword falls into the soup, and the bell above the door clamours as though the world were ending. Damocles is clear of it, but the guards come running through the door, and without waiting to hear what has passed they fall upon you.
options.chronicle: Cut Damocles's sword down, pulled him clear. Bell brought the guards.

road.hint: The horsehair that holds a sword may be tied to a bell as well.

options.label: Tell Dionysius the lesson has been learned, and show him you know it too

pass.outcome: You tell him that the sword is there to make his guest feel what a king feels at every meal, that this is the whole of the lesson, and that Damocles has felt it for three courses. A tyrant who goes on teaching it after it is learned shows only how much he enjoys the sword. Dionysius looks at you for a long moment, and then he laughs and nods to Damocles. "Get up, then," he says, and Damocles rises very carefully, and sits down upon the floor, and weeps.
pass.chronicle: Talked the tyrant into freeing Damocles. The lesson was learned already.

fail.outcome: You expound the lesson to him and mistake the point of it, and Dionysius smiles in a fashion that you do not like. "Then perhaps you should sit there and learn it," he says.
fail.chronicle: Failed to argue for Damocles. The tyrant sat me under the sword.

road.hint: The lesson of the sword was soon learned, and the tyrant might have been told so.

options.label: Take his place for an hour, and eat like a king

pass.outcome: Damocles rises and nearly falls over in thanking you. You eat like a king with your eyes always upon the hair, and you get up from that seat before you can forget to watch it.
pass.chronicle: Took Damocles's place under the sword, watched the hair, left unhurt.

fail.outcome: You take your ease and forget the hair. When the sword falls you fling yourself aside, so that it opens your shoulder in place of your skull, and Damocles at least is free.
fail.chronicle: Took Damocles's place, forgot the sword a moment. It cut my shoulder.

road.hint: An hour in the place of Damocles would have shown you what a crown may cost.

options.label: Leave him there
options.outcome: Dionysius shrugs. "He will be there at breakfast," he says, and Damocles never takes his eyes from the hair.
options.chronicle: Left Damocles under the sword. He'll be there at breakfast, says the king.

name: The Witch-Finder

authority.why: A rigged test, and twenty shillings a witch.

text: Beside a mill pond a great crowd has gathered with pitchforks, and on the bank a woman named Alys lies tied thumb to toe. A man in a tall black hat is reading from a paper. "I am Matthew Hopkins," he says. "At Manningtree a witch killed a child with a look and nobody did anything, and so it was I who did something." He nods toward the woman. "If she sinks she is innocent, and if she floats, then God's water has refused her." He mentions besides, as a man might speak of the weather, that the town pays him twenty shillings a witch. Alys turns her eyes to you. "I set their bones," she says, "and that is all I ever did."

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Hopkins does not lift his eyes from his paper. Behind you the crowd begins slowly to count, and somewhere past twelve it falls silent, and you know that it is over.
options.chronicle: Walked away from a witch ducking. The crowd counted, then went quiet.

road.hint: Had you turned from the mill pond, the crowd would still have had its way.

options.label: Cut her loose and run with her
options.outcome: You cut her free and are three steps up the bank before the crowd closes upon you. You come out of it bloody, with Alys over your shoulder, and now the whole village is sure of two witches in place of one. At the stair she slides down and runs. "I know the back ways," she calls to you, "and you would only slow me."
options.chronicle: Cut the herbalist loose from a ducking. The village thinks us both witches.

road.hint: A sword might free the herbalist, but it could never undeceive the crowd.

options.label: Take his test apart in front of the crowd, staking your own name

pass.outcome: You ask the miller what floats, and he says wood, and a boy says ducks. So does a woman tied in a ball with air in her lungs, you tell them, any woman whatever, and you offer to tie Hopkins in the same fashion and see. Somebody laughs, and soon many are laughing, and Hopkins departs in haste with his paper and his hat, while Alys with shaking hands gives you a kit of her cures.
pass.chronicle: Proved anyone bound floats. Witch-finder fled. Got the herbalist's cures.

fail.outcome: Your reasons grow tangled, and Hopkins is quicker than you. "Mark how the witch's friend speaks for her," he says, and the crowd turns upon you.
fail.chronicle: Lost the crowd to the witch-finder. They swam her, then came for me.

road.hint: The witch-finder's test was one that no innocent could pass.

options.label: Pay Hopkins his fee to let her go
options.warning: the town pays him twenty shillings a witch.
options.outcome: He takes your gold with a little bow and cuts her bonds himself. "The Lord is merciful, and so am I, for a consideration," says he, while Alys runs for her life.

delayed.text: A broadsheet has been nailed to a stair-post, and it reads "WITCH-FINDER GENERAL SWIMS TWO AT HOLLOWAY MILL. FEES AS USUAL."

options.chronicle: Paid the witch-finder to free a herbalist. Read later he swam two more.

road.hint: Had you paid the witch-finder, he would soon have sought another such fee.

name: The Moth Woman
text: In the middle of the chamber a woman stands wholly still, her arms a little outstretched and her skin dusted with a shimmering powder that takes the torchlight as wings do, and her eyes are silver from lid to lid. "You are drawn here as all things are drawn to light," she says. "Let me look at you, and I will tell you what I see."

options.label: Let her read you (costs mana)
options.outcome: She walks slowly round you, drawing a finger through the air beside your face as if she were reading some unseen writing. When she halts she presses one dusty fingertip to your temple. "There," she says. "I have opened a window." At once the world grows sharper, its colours brighter and its distances more clear, and you perceive more than you did before.
options.chronicle: Let a woman with silver eyes read me. She knew things.

road.hint: The silver-eyed woman might have read what is written on you.

options.label: Ask why her kind circles a lamp

pass.outcome: "Because the sky is up," you say, and the silver eyes grow wide. A moth flies with its back to the brightest thing that it sees, and for as long as there have been moths the brightest thing was the sky. A lamp below the sky tilts its whole world, and therefore it circles and circles, forever seeking to right itself. "Yes," she says softly. "We are not drawn to it, but lost." She touches your temple with a dusty fingertip, and the world grows sharp and clear.
pass.chronicle: Told the Moth Woman why moths circle a lamp: it tilts their sky.

fail.outcome: "Because they love the light?" you ask. She laughs, dry and dusty, and unfolds herself, and the light from her wings is too bright to look upon. When you can see again she says, "We keep our backs to the sky, and a lamp tilts the sky for us. We are not drawn to it, but lost."
fail.chronicle: Guessed wrong, was dazzled. The Moth Woman says moths keep backs to the sky.

road.hint: The moth that circles a lamp has lost its way.

options.label: Back away from her
options.outcome: She does not follow, but watches you retreat with those silver eyes, and never once does she blink. When you have rounded the corner you look at your reflection in your blade, and for a moment your own eyes are silver, though that cannot be, and then they are as they were before.

name: The Shade
text: Something that might be a shadow, and yet is none, peels itself away from the wall. It has the rough shape of a person, and very nearly the manners of one. "I collect the things that people do not know they are carrying," it says, in a voice that seems to come from a little behind the place where it stands. "Have you any mind to make a bargain?"

options.label: Offer stamina for invisibility
options.outcome: It reaches out and takes from you a thing that you cannot name, a weight that you never felt until it was gone. In exchange it lays another thing over your shoulders, a quality of being unseen, as though less than nothing stood where you stand, and for a time the dungeon will look through you.
options.chronicle: Traded some of my wind to a shade to go unseen a while.

road.hint: A shade may bargain for what you did not know you carried.

options.label: Ask what it needs to speak plainly

pass.outcome: "Blood," you say, and it grows very still. So it was in the Odyssey, when the dead flocked to the trench that Odysseus filled with blood and only those who drank could speak truly, and he held them back with his sword until the prophet Tiresias had drunk. You let it drink a few drops from a nick in your arm, and then it speaks plainly and tells you where every living thing upon this floor is lying in wait.
pass.chronicle: Gave a shade blood to speak. It told where everything here lies in wait.

fail.outcome: "Gold?" you ask, and it murmurs like a voice beyond a wall, so that you cannot make out the words. It is blood alone that gives a voice to the dead, as Odysseus knew when he filled a trench for them.
fail.chronicle: Could not understand a shade. The dead only murmur without blood.

road.hint: The dead cannot speak plainly until they have drunk.

options.label: Refuse and walk away
options.outcome: "As you wish," it says. It makes no move to hinder you, but returns to the wall, and the wall receives it without dispute. You do not look back, and yet you are certain beyond all doubting that nothing follows you.

name: Watch Sergeant
text: A long way below any city, four soldiers of the City Watch hold a barricade of overturned tables, and the sergeant has the look of a woman who was told to wait for orders and has waited ever since. "We were promised a courier with an iron scroll case and the seal of the Watch," she says. "Without it we do not know which gate to fall back on, and no more do the companies above."

options.label: Hand over Edric's dispatch
options.outcome: She breaks the seal and reads, and she is giving orders before she has come to the end. Two runners go up the stairs at their utmost speed. "He didn't make it, then," she says, and when you tell her that he made it almost all the way, she writes that down. Somewhere far overhead a city will pass a better night than it would have had.
options.chronicle: Gave Edric's dispatch to Sergeant Holt. She noted he nearly made it.

road.hint: Edric's dispatch was still awaited by those who hold the lower stair.

options.label: Ask how the siege stands
options.outcome: "It stood badly when last we heard, and that was a long time ago," she says, and looks toward the stair. "If you have seen a courier, or a scroll case with our seal, it is worth more to us than to you."

options.label: Leave food for the post
options.outcome: The soldiers share it out to the last crumb, first by rank and then by hunger, and the sergeant gives you a true salute, such as you have had from no one in a long while.
options.chronicle: Left food at a Watch post awaiting orders. The sergeant saluted.

road.hint: Even soldiers waiting for orders have need of a meal.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "The courier will come," says one of the soldiers as you go by, but none of the others answers him.
options.chronicle: Passed a Watch post awaiting its courier, his case still in my pack.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "The courier will come," says one of the soldiers as you go by, but none of the others answers him.
options.chronicle: Passed a Watch post still waiting for its courier.

name: The Brass Warden
text: A huge engine of tarnished brass bars the corridor, its breast aglow with a banked furnace, and on its body are graven the words NONE SHALL PASS WITHOUT PROVING WORTH. In a slot of its palm it holds a counting board. "CHALLENGER," it says, in a voice like a bell in a cellar. "THE EXCHANGE REQUIRES PROOF OF ARITHMETIC. STAKE A QUARTER OF YOUR PURSE. LOSE, AND IT IS FORFEIT TO THE GUILD. WIN, AND THE GUILD IS GENEROUS." It does not know that its Guild came to an end four hundred years ago.

options.label: Answer the Warden's sums, staking a quarter of your purse

pass.outcome: The furnace in its breast flares white. "WORTH PROVEN. THE GUILD IS GENEROUS." A drawer slides out of its belly with a cog in it, warm and heavy and perfectly cut, and afterward it speaks again very softly, in what is almost another voice: "IS THE GUILD STILL THERE?"
pass.chronicle: Out-counted the Brass Warden for a cog. Didn't admit its guild is gone.

fail.outcome: Without remark it counts your coins one by one into its breast, and then it steps aside none the less. "THE GUILD THANKS YOU FOR YOUR CUSTOM," it says.
fail.chronicle: Lost a quarter of my purse to a brass warden of a long-dead guild.

road.hint: The brass Warden had a sum to set you, and a prize for it.

options.label: Tell it the Guild is gone
options.outcome: It is still for a long time. "THEN WHO DO I GUARD FOR?" it asks, and you have no answer to give it. So it steps aside, and as you pass, the furnace in its breast burns a little dimmer.
options.chronicle: Told the Brass Warden its guild is long dead. It let me pass.

road.hint: It might be kinder to let the Warden keep its Guild.

options.label: Walk past by another way

name: Brothers of the Deep Watch
text: At the head of a black stair three brothers with mail beneath their habits keep a chapel, their spears leaning by the door, and over the altar is an empty niche the size of a hand. The eldest looks at your neck before he looks at your face. "Brother Cormac?" he asks, but he reads the answer there and asks instead, "Did Saint Columba come down?" And all the while you feel the reliquary warm against your breast.

options.label: Lay the reliquary in the niche
options.outcome: The brothers kneel, and the niche receives the reliquary as if it had been cut for it, as indeed it was. "From Iona to this place," says the eldest, "by a brother and a sister, and then one stranger." He gives you his blessing slowly and thoroughly, as a man pays out a debt to the last coin.
options.chronicle: Laid Saint Columba's relic in the Deep Watch chapel, as it was meant.

road.hint: A saint carried to his chapel weighs nothing once he is laid to rest there.

options.label: "I lost him on the way."
options.outcome: The eldest closes his eyes. "Then he is somewhere on the stair," he says, "and the stair is ours to search." He gives you neither blessing nor reproach, and returns to his watch.
options.chronicle: Lost Saint Columba before the Deep Watch chapel. Niche still empty.

road.hint: The brothers should still be told, if what was carried for them is lost.

options.label: Keep the reliquary
options.outcome: The brothers say nothing. The eldest looks at the empty niche and then at you, and he turns his face to the wall to pray. The reliquary remains warm upon you, but it does not seem to you the same warmth as before.
options.chronicle: Kept Saint Columba from the Deep Watch chapel. No argument from them.

road.hint: It would cost dearly to break your word at the very door of the chapel.

options.label: Ask for a blessing and say nothing
options.outcome: He gives it and asks you nothing, and if he guesses that a saint is in your keeping, he is too courteous to speak of it.
options.chronicle: Had the Deep Watch's blessing. Said nothing of what I carry.

road.hint: A blessing could be had in silence, though you must afterward live up to it.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: The brothers watch you as far as the stair, and when you look back the eldest is gazing still upon the empty niche.

text_variants.text: At the head of a black stair three brothers with mail beneath their habits keep a chapel, their spears leaning by the door, and over the altar is an empty niche the size of a hand. The eldest looks at your empty hands before he looks at your face. "Brother Cormac?" he asks, but he reads the answer there and asks instead, "Did Saint Columba come down?" And you have nothing at all to lay in the niche.

At the head of a black stair three brothers with mail beneath their habits keep a chapel, their spears leaning by the door, and over the altar is an empty niche the size of a hand. The eldest looks at your pack before he looks at your face. "Brother Cormac?" he asks, but he reads the answer there and asks instead, "Did Saint Columba come down?" And all the while you feel the reliquary warm through your pack.

name: Last Bearer
text: Against a long box of oak sits a monk with his feet bound in rags. "Seven of us carried him out of Lindisfarne when the longships came," he says, "and seven years we were upon the road. Now I alone am left, and I cannot manage the stairs." He takes a small red book from his habit. "This lay in the coffin with him. There is a chapel below where the brothers wait. The saint may rest here, but the book should not."

options.label: Take the book and give your word

oath.what: Lay Saint Cuthbert's Gospel on the reading desk of the chapel below.

options.outcome: He lays it in your hands as though it weighed more than the coffin. "It is John's Gospel, and small enough for a pocket," he says. "On the way down people will offer you money for it, as they always do." Then he closes his eyes, eased of the last thing that he was carrying.

thread.hint: A reading desk below still waits for the Gospel.

options.chronicle: Gave a Lindisfarne monk my word to carry Saint Cuthbert's Gospel down.

road.hint: The last bearer sought one who would carry his little book and never sell it.

options.label: Share a meal with him, but refuse the errand
options.outcome: He blesses the food, and after it he blesses you. "There is no shame in knowing your load," he says. "Somebody will come." But he does not sound altogether sure of it.
options.chronicle: Ate with Saint Cuthbert's last bearer but would not carry his book.

options.label: Wish him well and go on
options.outcome: He nods and puts the book away again within his habit, beside his heart, where it has been these seven years.

name: "Legitimate" Merchant
text: A goblin in a merchant's coat far too large for him has set up a stall with two skeletons to serve as racks, and he has labelled his wares in a large, confident hand: "DEFINITELY NOT CURSED RING," "POTION (PROBABLY GOOD)," and "HAT (BELONGED TO SOMEONE ELSE, NOW YOURS)." As you draw near he spreads his arms wide. "Welcome to Grix's Emporium of Totally Fine Items!" he cries. "Everything one hundred percent legal!"

options.label: Buy the ring at the honest price
options.outcome: Grix sells it to you for what it is truly worth, though it plainly grieves him to the heart. "Customer reads too well," he mutters. "Bad for business, good for customer."
options.chronicle: Read a goblin's ring before paying. Grix sold it at its true worth.

options.label: Buy the "Definitely Not Cursed" item
options.outcome: Grix takes your gold with a haste that troubles you, yet when you search your purchase carefully for a curse you can find none, and it proves to be as sound as he promised. He has watched your bewilderment with delight that he can scarcely hide. "Is being honest about dishonesty," he asks, as gravely as any philosopher, "still dishonest?"
options.chronicle: Bought a ring labelled DEFINITELY NOT CURSED, on trust.

road.hint: The goblin's boastful label was no proof either way.

options.label: Buy the Probably Good Potion
options.outcome: "Excellent choice," says Grix. "I tasted it myself three times, and the last two times were only to make sure." The potion heaves in its bottle as though it were eager to be drunk, and you put it away, reckoning that "probably good" is a better promise than most that are made in this dungeon.

options.label: Inspect the ring before you pay

pass.outcome: You turn the ring in the light, read the maker's mark and feel for the chill that a curse leaves in metal, and you find none, for it is a common ring priced as though it were a treasure. "Caveat emptor," you tell him: let the buyer beware, which is the oldest rule of every market. Grix sighs deeply, and then he names you an honest price.

fail.outcome: You peer at the ring and learn nothing from it, while Grix looks on in great contentment. The Romans of old said Caveat emptor, let the buyer beware, and a buyer whose eye has failed him must pay what the seller asks or go without.

road.hint: Let the buyer look before he pays.

options.label: "I don't trust you."
options.outcome: Grix lays a hand upon his breast as one sorely wounded. "Nobody trusts Grix," he says in sorrow, "and yet Grix is here every day with his mostly fine items, all for the ungrateful." As you go he takes up a skull and falls once more to polishing it with his sleeve.

text_variants.text: A goblin in a merchant's coat far too large for him has set up a stall with two skeletons to serve as racks, and he has labelled his wares in a large, confident hand: "DEFINITELY NOT CURSED RING," "POTION (PROBABLY GOOD)," and "HAT (BELONGED TO SOMEONE ELSE, NOW YOURS)." As you draw near he spreads his arms wide. "Welcome to Grix's Emporium of Totally Fine Items!" he cries. "Everything one hundred percent legal!" Then he looks at you very narrowly. "Cousin Brix wrote about you," he says. "Hard customer. Grix is warned."

name: Grieving Cyclops
text: The passage opens into a great hollow, and there a giant sits with his knees drawn up to his chest, weeping from his one great eye into his huge hands. His tears lie pooled upon the floor, and little silver fish of the sea swim in them, though no such fish should live in this place. "She said she would come back," says the giant, and he does not lift his head. "The sea-girl, Galatea. I sang to her, and I would have given her my sheep."

options.label: Sit with it in silence (spend SP)
options.outcome: You sit down beside him in the shallows of his grief and say nothing. He weeps a while longer, and by degrees he grows quiet. "You're still here," he says in wonder. "Most things run from me." When he has looked long upon you with his great wet eye he breathes out a breath that has peace in it, and some part of that peace settles into you like a cool wind.
options.chronicle: Sat with a weeping giant in the pool of his tears.

road.hint: A grieving giant might be glad of someone to sit beside him.

options.label: Give it something from your pack (food)
options.outcome: You lift the food up to him, and it seems a very small gift for so great a creature. The giant looks long at it and at you, and then he takes it in the hollow of one hand and eats it with the greatest care. "Thank you," he says. "She would have done that." Very gently he puts one of the shining fish into your pocket, where it melts into a light that will guard you.

options.label: Tell him why she will not come back

pass.outcome: You tell him the tale as Ovid tells it: how Galatea loved a shepherd boy named Acis, how Polyphemus found the two together and crushed Acis beneath a piece of the mountain, and how Galatea changed her lover's blood into a river that ran down to the sea. The giant sits very still until you have done. "I did that," he says at last. "I had forgotten that I did that." Then slowly he rises and rolls aside a boulder that has closed a side cave for longer than the dungeon has stood. "Take what is in there," he says, "for I want to sit by the water."
pass.chronicle: Told Cyclops he lost Galatea by killing Acis. He opened a cave for me.

fail.outcome: You tell him that she may yet return, and he nods and weeps the harder, for he knows better. It is told by Ovid that the Cyclops crushed her lover Acis beneath a rock and that Galatea made Acis a river, and such a wrong no nymph of the sea would ever forgive.
fail.chronicle: Told the Cyclops Galatea might return. She won't. He killed her love.

road.hint: The one-eyed giant had once crushed the lad whom the sea-nymph loved.

options.label: Carefully wade past
options.outcome: You pick your way through the shallows of his tears, and the little shining fish part about your boots. The giant does not see you, or does not care. For as long as you walk upon this floor you will carry with you the sight of so great a grief, alone in the dark with no one left to witness it.

name: Echo
text: At the end of the passage stands a girl as thin as mist, so faint at the edges that the stone shows through her. When you call "Hello?" she answers "Hello?" and when you ask her who she is she answers "Who she is," for she has no words of her own and can only give back the last of yours. She holds out something to you in one hand, and she looks at you as though all things hung upon what you will say next.

options.label: Say something she can answer with

pass.outcome: You know her now for Echo, whom Hera cursed for too much talking so that she could only repeat, and who faded for love of Narcissus until nothing was left of her but a voice. Therefore you ask as Narcissus asked in Ovid, "Is anyone here?" and her face shines as she answers, "Here!" You say, "Come to me," and with a glad cry of "Come to me!" she runs to you. She lays what she was holding in your hand, and then she vanishes in great happiness.
pass.chronicle: Asked Echo as Narcissus did, so she could answer. She gave me a gift.

fail.outcome: You ask her name, and she answers sadly, "Her name." You ask her what she wants. "She wants," says the girl, and she fades into the wall. Only afterward do you remember Echo, whom Hera cursed to repeat the last words of others, and how in Ovid a boy's question, "Is anyone here?" gave her leave to answer, "Here!"
fail.chronicle: Met a girl who only repeats. Never found a question she could answer.

road.hint: A girl who can only repeat must be asked a question that ends in her answer.

options.label: Echo her back
options.outcome: Softly you give back to her the words that she has given back to you. She tilts her head, and for a moment the two of you are nothing but voices in the stone. When it has passed you find that you are a little harder to see, as though some part of you had gone into the wall with her.

options.label: Back away slowly
options.outcome: "Slowly," she says behind you as you go, and again, more faintly, "Slowly."

name: The Thinking Mushroom
text: You have almost set your foot upon it before you perceive that it is thinking. It is a mushroom of great size that brightens and dims with a soft green light, and it speaks within your mind in a calm and measured voice. "I have been considering the nature of courage for forty-three years," it tells you, "and you appear to be practising it, which I find most interesting. Shall we discuss the matter?"

options.label: Engage in philosophical debate (spend SP)

pass.outcome: You sit down to dispute with it, setting forth the case of Aristotle: that courage is a mean between two vices, the cowardice that fears too much and the rashness that fears too little. The brave man, you say, fears the right things, at the right time, for the right reason. For three hours the mushroom contests this with a patient exactness, until at last it yields you one point. When you rise your mind is keener and more exact, and somewhat more dangerous to itself than it was.
pass.chronicle: Argued courage with a thinking mushroom. It conceded one point.

fail.outcome: You maintain that courage is to fear nothing at all. "Then he who leaps into a fire for no reason is the bravest of men," the mushroom says gently. "Aristotle would call that rashness, the vice that lies upon the far side of courage from cowardice, for the brave man fears what is worth fearing." You search long for an answer, and you have none to give it.
fail.chronicle: Lost to a mushroom on courage. No fear at all is rashness, says Aristotle.

road.hint: After forty-three years of thought, the mushroom might still yield to good reason.

options.label: Ask it about the dungeon
options.outcome: "The dungeon is a question," it tells you gravely, "and whoever survives it is the answer."

options.label: Nod politely and keep moving
options.outcome: "That is understandable," says the voice within your mind, and there is no reproach in it. "Courage without reflection is courage still, and I wish you well." The green glow fades behind you as you walk on, and you find that you are a little sorry for the talk that you did not have.

name: Two Mothers
text: In the mud of a mining camp two women stand, and each has a hand upon the same baby. "He's mine," says one of them, weeping, and "He's mine," says the other, and weeps the louder. The men of the camp hang back with folded arms and look to you, for you bear a weapon and they want no part in such a judgement. You notice that one of the women never once looks at the baby, but only at you.

options.label: Give him to the one who weeps loudest
options.warning: You notice that one of the women never once looks at the baby, but only at you.
options.outcome: The louder woman takes him and leaves off weeping at once, and you have marked it too late. The other sits down in the mud, and she makes no move to rise.
options.chronicle: Gave the baby to the louder mother. Her tears stopped at once. Wrong one, I think.

road.hint: One of the women had no eyes for the baby.

options.label: Call for a sword and offer to divide him

pass.outcome: "Cut him in two, then," you say, "and let each have half." The one woman answers, "It's fair. Divide him," but the other screams, "No, give him to her, only let him live!" You lay the baby in the arms of her who screamed. Men say that somewhere above a tribunal of the old king still sits in stone, awaiting the next such case as this.
pass.chronicle: Offered to divide a baby. Gave him to the woman who screamed to save him.

fail.outcome: You draw the sword, and the whole camp cries out, so that in the uproar you cannot tell which woman's cry was which. Then the men bear the baby away from you, to "decide among themselves".
fail.chronicle: Botched the sword test of two mothers. The camp took the baby away.

road.hint: A drawn sword might have shown which woman loved the child.

options.label: Leave it to the camp
options.outcome: The men dispute for an hour, and at the end of it they give him to the woman who has the louder friends.
options.chronicle: Left two mothers to the camp. The one with louder friends got the baby.

road.hint: Without a judge, the crowd in the camp would rule.

name: Weeping Mason
text: A figure that you can see through kneels beside a crumbling wall with his ghostly hands pressed to the stones, as though he would mend them, and at first he does not mark you. "Forty years," he murmurs, "forty years, and still the mortar won't hold." In life he built this part of the dungeon, and he may not depart from it until the work is perfect.

options.label: Help him find peace (offer mana)
options.outcome: You pour a little of your magic into the ancient stones, until they glow warm and golden. The mason gazes upon his mended wall with trembling hands, and then slowly he melts into the air, weeping for relief. As he goes he wraps about you all the pride of his craft, which has become a ward for your protection.
options.chronicle: Helped a mason's ghost find peace after forty years at a failing wall.

road.hint: A little magic might have ended the mason's long toil.

options.label: Tell him what his mortar is missing

pass.outcome: "Ash," you say, "volcanic ash," and he grows still. The Romans mixed their lime with ash from the hills at Pozzuoli, so that their harbour walls have stood two thousand years in the sea, and the cinders here are of the same kind. He mixes them in and sets the last stone, and when he steps back the wall holds. He smiles and says, "Forty years," and is gone. Where his wall meets the old one, a sealed door has come unstuck.
pass.chronicle: Told a mason's ghost to put volcanic ash in his lime. His wall held. He rests.

fail.outcome: "More water?" you ask, and he shakes his head. "Forty years," he says. Long afterward you remember the Roman harbours, whose lime was mixed with volcanic ash from Pozzuoli and has stood two thousand years in the sea, and you know that the cinders here would have served him.
fail.chronicle: Failed a mason's ghost. Thought too late of ash for his mortar.

road.hint: The Romans put ash in the mortar of their harbours.

options.label: Leave him to his grief
options.outcome: You pass by him quietly, and his murmuring of "forty years, forty years" grows fainter behind you, until it is swallowed up by the dungeon.

name: Relic Broker
text: A neat little man has set out a folding table of bones, each of them labelled in a confident hand. He looks you over once, and his eyes come to rest upon your pack. "If you should chance to be carrying something old and small and red," he says, "the brothers below would give you a blessing for it, but I will give you a heavy purse, and one cannot buy bread with blessings."

options.label: Sell him the red book
options.outcome: He wraps it in silk with a true tenderness. "A wise choice," he says as he puts it by, "for saints have no need to eat."
options.chronicle: Sold Saint Cuthbert's Gospel to a relic broker, against my word.

road.hint: There will be those upon the road who would pay to have the saint's book from you.

options.label: Tell him the book is promised
options.outcome: "Everything is promised to somebody," he answers pleasantly, and he lets you go upon your way.
options.chronicle: Told a relic broker the red book was promised. Did not sell.

road.hint: The book was promised, and the broker's purse might be refused.

options.label: Buy one of his vials instead

name: The Bone Diviner
text: Behind a low table strewn with many small bones, every one carved with signs, sits a woman through whom the cinders show as though she were smoke. She does not look up at your coming. "These are oracle bones of Shang," she says. "I read them for a king three thousand years ago, and I have never ceased. I ask a question and touch the bone with hot metal, and the crack gives the answer. Is there something that you would know? The bones set their own price."

options.label: Ask where this floor keeps its secrets

pass.outcome: You know how it is done, and she hears as much in your question. The diviners of Shang pressed hot metal into pits bored in the shoulder-blades of oxen or in turtles' shells, and when they had read the cracks they carved both question and answer upon the bone, in the oldest Chinese writing that anyone has found. She cracks a bone for you, and the crack runs like a map, so that she reads you the whole floor from it, room by room.
pass.chronicle: A diviner's ghost read me the whole floor from a cracked oracle bone.

fail.outcome: She cracks a bone and reads it, but your question was ill shaped, and therefore the answer is ill shaped also. "Turtle shell and ox bone," she says, "hot metal, and the question carved upon the bone beside its answer. That is how my king would ask. When next you ask, ask as a king does."
fail.chronicle: Asked oracle bones wrongly. They answer only a question asked properly.

road.hint: The oldest writing of China was carved on bones as questions and their answers.

options.label: Pay the bones' price for a long reading (130 gold)
options.outcome: She takes your coin, warms an old dark bone, and reads its cracks aloud for a long while, telling where each peril of this floor lies in wait and which of them is waiting for you. For as long as you remain upon the floor, it seems to you that someone is reading over your shoulder.

options.label: Ask about danger ahead (pay MP)
options.outcome: She heats another bone, older and darker than the rest, and twice the crack branches. "There are two dangers," she says, "one that you can see and one beneath it, and you must not fight the visible one first." The smoke of the bone curls into your eyes, and for a time you see the dungeon as clearly as one who has been truly warned.

options.label: Leave the bones unasked
options.outcome: She looks up at last as you turn to go. "The bones do not mind," she says. "They have been patient for three thousand years."

name: The Lost Soldier
text: In the midst of the passage a soldier in armour two centuries out of fashion stands at attention, facing neither toward anything nor away from it. Your breath smokes in the cold, but his does not fog, and the frost upon his shoulders has not melted for a great while. "Halt," he says, though there is no anger in him. "These halls are under the protection of King Edric the Fourth." Then he searches your face, and his voice sinks. "You do not know that name. How long have I been standing here?"

options.label: Tell him the truth gently
options.outcome: As gently as you may, you tell him that King Edric the Fourth has been two hundred years dead, that his kingdom goes now by another name, and that the war against which he stood guard was over long before his grandchildren were born. He is silent for a great while. "Then I have kept my post well," he says at last, and with a most noble dignity he salutes you and walks away into the dark.
options.chronicle: Told a soldier long out of date the war is over. He thanked me, still on guard.

road.hint: A soldier who was never told to stand down may not know that his war is over.

options.label: Pay him the soldier's tribute
options.outcome: You press the coins into his gauntleted hand, as an officer does who pays a soldier his due, and he stands straighter yet. "The King's blessing be upon you, traveller," he says. He draws a sign in the air, and you feel it settle about you like armour of plate that weighs nothing.

options.label: Relieve him of his post, properly

pass.outcome: You know that such a soldier will not stand down at a stranger's word. A Japanese officer named Onoda held his post in a jungle of the Philippines for twenty-nine years after his war was over, and came out only when his old commander flew there to relieve him in person. Therefore you do it in the old fashion, naming his post, his king and his orders, and then you give the command to stand down. He salutes you and says, "At last." Then he lays his shield at your feet, and he is gone out of the world.
pass.chronicle: Relieved a dead soldier of his post by due order. He left his shield.

fail.outcome: You tell him that the war is over, and he nods courteously and does not stir, for orders come from officers and never from strangers. Even so did Onoda hold his post in the jungle for twenty-nine years after his war, until his own old commander came in person to relieve him.
fail.chronicle: Told a dead soldier his war was over. He takes no stranger's word.

road.hint: A soldier will stand down for a lawful order, but not for a rumour.

options.label: Walk around him quietly
options.outcome: He does not hinder you, and it may be that he has returned already to whatever world he dwells in between one visitor and the next. When you look back from the corner he stands yet at his post, very straight, with his face set toward nothing.

name: Cartographer Issek
text: A small and most intent woman is pinning hand-drawn maps to the wall with a knife, from which she does not lift her eyes. "Don't talk to me for thirty seconds," she says, and when twenty-nine of them have passed she lets out her breath and turns about. "Right, I'm Issek. I map the deep floors, so I know a thing or two, and you look as if you have things that I could use."

options.label: Trade food for her maps
options.outcome: She takes the food without ceremony and eats it standing, and is already rolling up a map for you. "That's the next few floors, near enough, with the chief places marked," she says, "and the monsters too, wherever I lived long enough to mark them." The shape of those halls settles into your memory as though it had been given you for a gift.

options.label: Buy her composite survey (250 gold)
options.outcome: "The finest edition," she says in all earnest, and brings out a map written over by six surveyors, who held six opinions as to which rooms were perilous. The learning of all six together comes flooding into your mind.

options.label: Help her reconcile her six surveys

pass.outcome: Six surveyors have made six maps and hold six opinions. You sort them by their bearings and find that two were drawn with a compass which the iron in these rocks had turned from true north. These bearings you correct by the one surveyor who measured from stair to stair between fixed points, and straightway the rooms fit together. Issek stares, and then she pins up the finished survey and gives you the first fair copy of it.
pass.chronicle: Reconciled Issek's maps. Iron skewed two compasses. Got the fair copy.

fail.outcome: You labour over them, and the rooms will not close. In the end Issek finds the fault herself, that the compasses of two surveyors were drawn aside by the iron in these rocks, so that every bearing taken with them is some few degrees astray. "A compass lies near iron," she says. "Write that down."
fail.chronicle: Failed to reconcile Issek's surveys. A compass lies near iron.

road.hint: A compass may be led astray by iron.

options.label: "I prefer to discover things myself."
options.outcome: She shrugs, for she has heard this many times before. "Most of those who must 'discover things themselves' don't make it back to correct my maps," she says, and she turns to her wall again and draws out another pin. "Good luck, though. I mean that."

name: Ormond's Granary
text: You come upon a granary of stone, whose barred door is deeply scored on the inner side. No one answers when you knock, and it seems that none has answered for some while. The bar within has rotted through, so that the door would yield to your shoulder.

text_variants.text: You come upon a granary of stone, and on the step before it sits Corporal Pell, his tabard filthy now and his sword notched, grinning like a very fool. The barred door stands open behind him, where a grey sergeant is numbering his men, and they are eleven, and Pell besides. "He came back," says Sergeant Ormond, as one who scarcely believes it yet. "He stood in the door and told us he'd run, first thing, before any man could ask, and then he showed us the way out."

options.label: Shake Pell's hand
options.outcome: "Trembler, that's what they called him, that Spartan, wasn't it?" says Pell, and he is grinning still as he takes your hand. "Well, that's not me, not any more."
options.chronicle: Found Pell at the granary with eleven alive. He went back, no Trembler now.

road.hint: A man who has come back to his comrades deserves to have his hand shaken.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Pell waves you on your way with his notched sword, and he is grinning still.

options.label: Open the door
options.outcome: The door yields to your shoulder, and the rotten bar with it. On a sack of grain within lies a journal in a sergeant's square hand, and its last line reads: "Day nine. No runner. I hope Pell got out." You find the pencil lying beside it, and beneath those words you write, "He did."
options.chronicle: Opened the granary: nine days, no runner. Wrote in its book that Pell got out.

road.hint: The runner you sent away may have been the help for which others waited.

options.label: Leave it barred
options.outcome: You leave the door as you found it, rotten bar and all, and go your way.
options.chronicle: Left the granary door barred. Did not look inside.

name: Star Merchant
text: At a folding table laden with bottles of glass sits a small and delicate figure, and in each bottle wheels a cluster of lights, a constellation that has been caught and made small. "Genuine Ursae Majoris, never used," says the figure, in a voice like wind chimes. "Here are the Pleiades, slightly incomplete. As for this last, I do not know what it is, but it followed me home."

options.label: Buy the unknown constellation
options.outcome: No sooner has the bottle left the merchant's hands than it draws its own cork. Light pours from it and gathers into a solid thing, a wand of starlight that throbs to a measure known in no school of magic, while the merchant watches it go with what may be relief.
options.chronicle: Bought an unknown constellation in a bottle. Still unopened.

road.hint: Even the unknown stars might have served you.

options.label: Ask for the true Pleiades

pass.outcome: You pass over the bottle of seven bright points and take up one of six, a little hazy and blue-white, and the merchant chimes with pleasure. These are the Seven Sisters, a young cluster of hot blue stars some four hundred and forty light-years away, and most eyes can count but six of them, wherefore the Greeks said that one sister had hidden herself. "An honest eye gets an honest price," says the merchant, and the bottle uncorks itself into a wand of starlight.
pass.chronicle: Picked the true Pleiades, six stars. Bought a starlight wand at a fair price.

fail.outcome: You take up the bottle of seven bright stars. "Ah, that one is a forgery," says the merchant gently. "The Seven Sisters show but six to most eyes, and the Greeks said that one of them hides herself." And it puts the false bottle away beneath the table.
fail.chronicle: Picked forged Pleiades with seven stars. Most eyes see only six.

road.hint: Most eyes can count only six of the Seven Sisters.

options.label: Just browse. Move on.
options.outcome: "There is no haste," the merchant says warmly, "for the stars have waited this long." As you walk away one of the bottles glows a little brighter, as though it wished you good fortune.

name: Charon
text: A black river runs where no river has any right to be, and at a stone step waits a flat ferry, in which an old man with an oar looks you up and down. "The girl you paid for, Melitta, has asked me to carry you over once for nothing, when you came to deep water," he says, and he spits into the river. "I carry no one for nothing, and yet I am going to do it."

options.label: Step aboard
options.outcome: The crossing is very quiet. From the farther shore he pushes off again without a word, but when he has reached the middle of the river he calls back to you, "She says thank you. She is well, and better than well."
options.chronicle: Charon took me over free at a drowned girl's asking. He says she is well.

road.hint: The coin you paid for a stranger's crossing might have bought one for you.

options.label: Decline
options.outcome: "As you please," he says, "but she will be disappointed, for the dead do hate to be refused."

name: The Cataloguing Spirit
text: All along this passage a spirit is fixing tiny labels upon the walls, upon sconces and cracks in the stone, and upon a bewildered rat that sits very still beneath such attention. The labels bear such legends as "WALL (LOAD-BEARING)", "TORCH SCONCE, EMPTY, CIRCA UNKNOWN", and "RAT (ALIVE, CURRENTLY)." At the sight of you the spirit snatches up a quill and cries, "Oh! An adventurer, encountered! Are you available to be catalogued?"

options.label: Help it label things properly

pass.outcome: You set three of its labels to rights, and it all but weeps for joy. "RAT (ALIVE, CURRENTLY)" becomes Rattus rattus, both words in italics, with a capital for the genus and none for the species, after the manner of Linnaeus, who named each living thing with two words, the kind and then the sort, and himself Homo sapiens, the wise man. The spirit lends you its eye for names, so that for a while everything you pick up tells you what it is.
pass.chronicle: Named a rat Rattus rattus for the Cataloguing Spirit. It lent its eye for names.

fail.outcome: You write RAT (BLACK), and it shudders. "Rattus rattus," it corrects you, "with a capital for the genus and none for the species. Linnaeus gave all things two names, the kind and then the sort, and even himself: Homo sapiens." Then, as kindly as may be, it labels you UNHELPFUL.
fail.chronicle: The Cataloguing Spirit taught me Linnaeus's two words: kind, then sort.

road.hint: Every living thing has two names, first the kind and then the sort.

options.label: Bribe it for information
options.outcome: It takes your gold and labels it at once ("COIN, GOLD, PROVENANCE: ADVENTURER, WARM"). Then it shares with you all that it has catalogued of the floors about you, and the whole map of them is spread out in your mind, so that for a little while you have useful foreknowledge of what lies ahead.

options.label: "I don't want to be catalogued."
options.outcome: "Noted!" cries the spirit, writing furiously. As you depart you hear the small sounds of its labelling go on behind you, and somewhere upon these walls there is now a little card that reads: "ADVENTURER, UNCATALOGUED, UNCOOPERATIVE."

name: Antigone

authority.why: Creon forbids the burial of Antigone's brother on pain of death. An edict against the unwritten law of the dead binds no one: informing on her is betrayal, and burying him or walking on is never penalised.

text: Beside a broken gate a young woman is scraping earth over a dead man with her bare hands, and her nails are torn with the work. "He is my brother, and Creon says that the dogs may have him," she says, and she does not pause. "Creon's edict is not older than the unwritten laws, and nothing that he writes can make it right to leave my brother to the dogs." From down the road there comes a captain's voice: "A city where every sister chooses which laws to keep is no city at all. He burned our houses. Leave him."

options.label: Help her finish the burial
options.outcome: You dig together until the body is covered, and she says the words over him. Soon the captain's men are at the gate, and she does not hide. "Let him do it in daylight, before the whole city," she says, "for if I hide I am agreeing with him. Now go."
options.chronicle: Helped Antigone bury her brother. She would not hide from Creon's men.

road.hint: By refusing to hide, she would make the law do its work in daylight.

options.label: Go and speak for her to Creon

pass.outcome: You meet Creon upon the road and set it before him that a law against burying the dead must strive with a law older than his city, and that the ruler who wins in such a strife loses a thing of greater worth. He hears you to the end. Then he himself turns back to the gate and comes there in time, and he commands that the burial be finished with honours, while Antigone looks upon him as though he were a stranger.
pass.chronicle: Talked King Creon round. He reached the gate in time to allow burial.

fail.outcome: Creon hears you out with every courtesy and is unmoved. "The law is the city," he says, and he walks on toward the gate.
fail.chronicle: Argued law of the dead with Creon. Unmoved, he went on to the gate.

road.hint: Creon might be shown that the law of the dead is older than his city.

options.label: Tell Creon's men where she is
options.outcome: The soldiers thank you, but they do not look at you as they do it. They find her waiting beside the grave with her work finished.
options.chronicle: Reported Antigone to Creon's men for pay, as the law said.

road.hint: Gold was to be had for betraying her, but even the soldiers would not meet your eye.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: You walk on, and behind you she continues to scrape at the earth with her bare hands.

name: Lantern of Regret
text: A lantern hangs as high as your breast in an empty passage, though there is nothing from which it might hang. In the place of flame there burns within it a small golden person no bigger than your thumb, walking in narrow circles and sometimes sitting down with its head in its hands, and whatever it touches inside the glass has turned to gold. "Are you going to free me," it asks in a voice muffled by the glass, "or only stare like all the others?"

options.label: Free it (pay HP, unknown consequence)
options.outcome: You break the glass with your open hand, and it cuts you sharply. The little figure pours out like warm light and grows greater as it goes, until it has melted wholly into the air of the dungeon. "Thank you," says the air softly, from every side at once. Something like gratitude settles about you, and for a little while it seems that the dungeon itself wishes you well.
options.chronicle: Freed a small regret from a lantern. It thanked me and left lighter.

road.hint: The small regret would have been glad to be set free.

options.label: Tell it how the first wish like it was undone

pass.outcome: You know it for such a wish as Dionysus granted to King Midas, that all he touched should turn to gold, until his bread and his wine were gold in his mouth. Midas was bidden to wash in the river Pactolus, and the gold went out of him into the stream, whose sands have glittered ever since. You tip the lantern's water over the little figure, and the gold runs from it in a shining flood, so that it rises up like warm light and goes laughing away. In the bottom of the glass a few flakes of gold remain behind.
pass.chronicle: Washed a lantern's wish free of gold, as Midas was. A few flakes stayed.

fail.outcome: You bid it wish harder, and it sighs. "I am a wish," it says, "and that is the trouble." Afterward you remember Midas, who wished that all he touched should turn to gold and nearly starved, and who was freed by washing in the river Pactolus.
fail.chronicle: Failed to free a golden wish in a lantern. Water freed Midas.

road.hint: A golden wish was once washed away in a river.

options.label: Leave the lantern where it hangs
options.outcome: "It is understandable," it says without bitterness. "This is how it commonly goes." It takes up its small sad circles again, and the lantern grows fainter as you walk away, until you can no longer tell whether the darkness behind you is a shadow or only the want of any light.

name: Neferkaptah
text: There stands before you a door of black stone that was never meant to open, and yet it opens. The air within smells of river mud and myrrh. An open book lies upon a bier, and wherever its light falls things declare their names: your own pack murmurs the true names of all that it holds, and the bones of something that you slew on the way down tell you very clearly what they were. Beside it two ghosts sit at a senet board, a prince in a collar of gold and a woman whose hair is still wet, and a small wet footprint leads from the bier toward the wall and stops. "You have come for the Book of Thoth," says the prince, as he sets out the pieces. "Setne came for it also, and he was a prince." But the woman pays no heed to the board, for her eyes are upon you.

options.label: Listen to Ahwere
options.outcome: "I am Ahwere. That is Merib's footprint; he was six." She says it softly, as one says what she has told over to herself every night for three thousand years. "My husband read one page upon the boat, and he understood the birds and the fishes, and he laughed. Then Merib leaned out to see the fishes that his father understood, and the river took him, and when I went in after my son I did not come up again." She looks toward the book. "Neferkaptah bound it to his breast and walked in after us, and so he had it all the way to the bottom." Then she turns to you once more. "It is a true book, and every word in it is true, but the price of it is everyone you love. I beg you, do not take it."
options.chronicle: Ahwere says the Book of Thoth cost her life and her small son's.

road.hint: A true book may be bought too dearly, as the drowned woman knows.

options.label: Play Neferkaptah at senet for the book, staking yourself

per_miss.text: Your feet go into the stone as if it were mud. The cold that takes hold of them is the cold of the Nile.
You are in to the waist now, and your legs seem very far away in the cold water.
The stone closes round your throat.

pass.outcome: The last piece falls, and Neferkaptah stares at the board as though it had cheated him. "So be it," he says. He lifts the book from the bier and holds it out, yet when you take it he does not let it go. "Swear to me, as Setne swore to me once, that you will read it and then bring it back, for the gods will not leave you long alone with it." And Ahwere has turned her face to the wall, toward the little footprint.

oath.what: Read the Book of Thoth once, then lay it on an altar so it can go home.

thread.hint: Somewhere above, a drowned woman is counting floors.

pass.chronicle: Won the Book of Thoth at senet. Sworn to bring it back once read.

fail.outcome: Neferkaptah sweeps the pieces into his hand and says, "Not you, then." You are waist-deep in the floor, and it lets you go as slowly as a river gives up a boot that it has swallowed, while the book remains upon its bier.
fail.chronicle: Lost at senet for the Book of Thoth. Sank to the waist. The book stayed.

road.hint: At senet with the dead you may lose far more than you meant to stake.

0.outcome: The stone closes over your mouth. Then a wet hand takes hold of yours and pulls you upward, and you come gasping to the floor above, far away from the tomb, whose black door you shall never find again.
0.chronicle: Lost every round for the Book of Thoth. Ahwere pulled me out. Woke higher up.

thread.closed_line: Never found Neferkaptah's tomb again. Ahwere's doing, I think.

options.label: Leave the book, because she asked
options.outcome: You put your hands behind your back. Neferkaptah laughs in disbelief, until the laughter dies in him. For the first time in three thousand years Ahwere rises from the board, and she crosses to you and lays her wet hand upon your breast above the heart, as one does who would learn whether another is still alive. "Thank you," she says. "No one has ever left it." When you look back from the door she is sitting by the small footprint at the wall, and for this once her eyes are turned away from the book.

person_status.last_line: No one has ever left it.

options.chronicle: Left the Book of Thoth because a drowned mother asked me to.

road.hint: The greatest of books was guarded by a mother, and might be left at her asking.

options.label: Leave the tomb
options.outcome: "Setne left also, the first time," says Neferkaptah, as he sets out the pieces once again, and Ahwere speaks no word. The door closes behind you, and is a wall.
options.chronicle: Found the tomb of a prince who drowned for a book. Left, nothing decided.

road.hint: One might go from the tomb with nothing taken and nothing decided.

name: Snerk Ledgerscale
text: At a desk made from a dragon's toenail sits a kobold in tiny spectacles, writing in two ledgers at once, while beyond the arch some vast creature breathes in its sleep and gold shifts beneath it. "Snerk Ledgerscale, accountant to the Great Glaurveth. Shh!" he whispers. He taps the first book. "Her hoard," he says, and then he taps the smaller. "And the villages she took it from. It goes back where it came from, a coin at a time. Will you help me carry?" You see that the second ledger has a third column, which is headed in tiny letters with the word ME.

options.label: Pick up a sack and help him carry
options.warning: You see that the second ledger has a third column, which is headed in tiny letters with the word ME.
options.outcome: When you are halfway to the arch the dragon's tail twitches and lays you flat. By the time that you rise Snerk has gone out the other way with the sack marked ME, leaving you the sack marked VILLAGES, and an enormous eye is opening upon you, so that you drop it and run.
options.chronicle: Helped a kobold rob a hoard, books unread. Left me the sack. The dragon woke.

road.hint: The kobold's books were worth reading before his sacks were carried.

options.label: Audit his books first

pass.outcome: Two of the columns add up truly and the third does not, for a third of every coin "returned" has gone to ME. You lay your finger upon it, and Snerk turns a deeper green. "Handling fees," he says, but you gaze at him until he strikes out the column, coin by coin, and the whole of it goes to the villages.
pass.chronicle: Audited the dragon's kobold. All he takes now goes back to the villages.

fail.outcome: The columns swim before your eyes. "All in order," says Snerk, closing the books a little hastily, and you help him to carry. When you are halfway to the arch the dragon's tail twitches and lays you flat. By the time that you rise Snerk has gone out the other way with the sack marked ME, leaving you the sack marked VILLAGES, and an enormous eye is opening upon you, so that you drop it and run.
fail.chronicle: Missed the trick in a kobold's books. The dragon's tail laid me flat.

road.hint: A kobold's good cause may hide a dishonest column in his books.

options.label: Take a cut to keep quiet
options.outcome: Snerk rules a fourth column and heads it YOU. "A pleasure doing business with you," he whispers.
options.chronicle: Took a cut from the dragon's skimming kobold. I'm in his books now.

road.hint: The kobold would gladly rule one more column for you.

options.label: Leave him to his sums
options.outcome: "Shh," he says, and he does not look up from his figures.

name: The Merry Wanderer
text: A man in grape-leaf garlands sits upon a barrel of something that was assuredly not here before, laughing at nothing at all, with eyes bright as wine held up to the sun. About him the dungeon seems a little more joyful, and the very torches burn warmer. "Excellent timing!" he cries. "I have been waiting for someone cheerless enough to need cheering. Sit down and drink, for all is well, I promise you, it is all very well indeed!"

options.label: Share food and drink with him
options.outcome: The drink has the taste of three seasons all happening at once, and he watches you drink it with the deepest satisfaction. "There, you see?" he says. "The dungeon is as dreadful as ever, but now you are full of warmth, and I do not think that the two are unrelated." Thereupon your body begins to knit itself together with all the eagerness of a growing vine.
options.chronicle: Drank with a merry man in grape leaves. I think I know who he was.

road.hint: The stranger's barrel was not there before, and he may be more than he seems.

options.label: Accept his toast (free, but risky)
options.outcome: He lifts his cup to you and says, "To surviving," and he means it with his whole heart. You drink nothing, and yet you feel the better for it, at which he shows no surprise. "There are blessings," he says, "that have no need of your help."

options.label: Ask him about the pirates who kidnapped him

pass.outcome: His laughter stops. "Who told you about that?" The old hymn tells how Tyrrhenian pirates seized a youth in a purple cloak to sell him; how the ropes fell from him, wine ran over the deck and a vine climbed the mast; how he became a lion, so that they leapt overboard and came up as dolphins, all but the helmsman, who had said from the first, "That is a god." Then Dionysus lifts his cup to you as to that helmsman's heir. "You are a clever one," he says.
pass.chronicle: Knew Dionysus's pirate tale. He toasted me as the helmsman who knew him.

fail.outcome: You ask him about pirates, and for a moment his face is empty, and then it fills with delight. "Pirates! I love pirates. They make such good dolphins," he says, and will explain no further.
fail.chronicle: Asked a merry wanderer about pirates. He says they make good dolphins.

road.hint: Pirates once laid hands upon a youth in purple, and came up out of the sea as dolphins.

options.label: "I don't drink with strangers."
options.outcome: He sighs, as one who has heard this since the world was young. "Every stranger was a friend whom you had not yet met," he says, "and every friend was once a stranger whom you chose to trust. But no matter." He waves you onward most graciously. "Go, and be careful, and at the very least drink water."

name: Ysra Deepsong
text: You hear the music before you see her, a deep humming that makes the walls tremble. In a carven niche sits a dwarf with skin as grey as stone and eyes like polished obsidian, who sings into the rock and taps it with a little bar of iron, listening between the notes, and the stones seem to lean nearer to hear. When she sees you she pauses. "I am Ysra," she says. "A living one! It has been so long. My people sing to the stone, and the stone sings back. Would you hear what it says?"

options.label: Ask for a song of strength
options.outcome: She sings so low that you feel the song in your bones rather than hear it with your ears, and it mends what lies deeper than wounds: your weariness, your old hurts, and all that the weight of the dungeon has slowly worn away. When you go on you walk a little straighter, and quietly your body continues to heal itself.

options.label: Ask her what the stone sings back

pass.outcome: "I think you know already," she says. For sound runs through granite more than ten times as swiftly as through air, and it rings true in sound rock and dull in rock that is cracked or hollow, so that miners have always sounded a roof with a bar before they would trust it: a ring is safe, and a drummy thud is loose. She taps and listens until you have learned to hear the difference, and for a while every hollow wall and hidden gap near you speaks aloud.
pass.chronicle: Ysra taught me to sound rock for secrets: a ring is solid, a thud hollow.

fail.outcome: "Echoes?" you guess, and she shakes her head. "It rings or it thuds," she tells you. "Solid rock rings and hollow or cracked rock thuds, and that is how a miner sounds a roof before he walks under it." She sings you a short song none the less, and you feel less weary afterward.
fail.chronicle: Dwarf singer Ysra says solid rock rings, hollow rock thuds.

road.hint: Solid rock will ring, and hollow rock will thud.

options.label: Keep moving
options.outcome: She does not call after you, but her song follows you down three passages and fades so slowly that you cannot be sure when it ceases.

name: Dream Weaver
text: A woman sits weaving ahead of you, and her threads are of a silver light that seems to come out of the empty air. "They are dreams," she tells you, before you can ask. "They drift down here when folk sleep in the world above, and I gather them and make things. Will you trade me one of yours? You will not miss it, or at least I do not think you will."

options.label: Trade a dream (pay MP)
options.outcome: With two fingers that feel cold but not unpleasant she reaches into your mind, and she draws out a thing that shimmers. She holds it up before her eyes. "Oh, this is a good one," she says. "You dreamed of flying." She adds it to her loom and hands you a scroll woven of finished dream-thread. You do not feel the loss, but afterward you find that you cannot well remember what it was like to fly.
options.chronicle: Traded a dream to a dream weaver. Cannot recall which dream.

road.hint: A dream that is traded away may leave an empty place behind it.

options.label: Commission a dream of strength
options.outcome: She weaves so swiftly that her fingers are a blur, and she presses the finished cloth to your brow. For the space of three seconds you dream that you stand whole and healed in the sunlight, and when you open your eyes some of that wholeness has remained within your body. She smiles at you and says, "I do good work."

options.label: Ask her which gate your dream came through

pass.outcome: "You know of the gates?" she says in delight. Penelope tells in the Odyssey that dreams come to us by two gates, and that those which pass through the gate of ivory deceive us, but those which pass through the gate of polished horn come true. She holds your dream up to the light. "Horn," she says. "This one is true." And for a while it shows you all that waits near you in the dark.
pass.chronicle: My dream is of horn, a true one. The weaver showed what waits near me.

fail.outcome: "The front door, you say?" She laughs. "There are two gates, as Penelope said, ivory for the dreams that lie and horn for those that come true. Yours came by the ivory, I'm afraid. It is pretty, and of no use at all."
fail.chronicle: Dream weaver says my dream came by the ivory gate, so it was false.

road.hint: True dreams come to us through the gate of horn.

options.label: Keep your dreams to yourself
options.outcome: "That is wise," she says, and she means it. "Dreams are worth more than most folk know, so hold fast to yours." Then she turns again to her loom, where the threads of light go on with their slow and shining dance.

name: Brother Sacristan
text: You enter a side chapel that has been swept clean, where a lamp burns beside an empty reading desk. A monk starts up from his knees so hastily that he overturns the stool. "Is he coming? Is the saint coming down?" he cries. Then he sees your face and masters himself. "No, of course he cannot, with all those stairs. Did the bearers send anything at all?"

options.label: Lay the red book on the reading desk
options.outcome: At first he does not touch it. Then he opens it at the first line, "In the beginning was the Word," and the lamp burns the steadier. "You were offered money for this," he says, as one who has no need to ask.
options.chronicle: Laid Saint Cuthbert's Gospel on the desk it was meant for, unsold.

road.hint: A book that is brought safely to its desk may be read for a thousand years.

options.label: Read the first lines aloud with him

pass.outcome: You read it together, he in his Latin and you stumbling after him, and somewhere in the third line you cease to stumble.
pass.chronicle: Read the start of Cuthbert's Gospel aloud with Brother Sacristan.

fail.outcome: You lose your place, and he finds it for you and quietly goes on reading.

options.label: Tell him a bearer still lives, on the floors above
options.outcome: He is out at the door before you have finished, with the lamp in one hand and a blanket in the other, so that the chapel is left in darkness and its desk is empty still.
options.chronicle: Told Brother Sacristan of the living bearer. He ran. I still have the book.

options.label: Ask for a blessing and say nothing about any book
options.outcome: He gives it gladly and asks you nothing, though if there is a small red book in your pack it grows no lighter for his blessing.

name: The Pardoner
text: Outside a camp of pilgrims a man with long yellow hair and a voice like a goat's sits upon his pack of relics, and he has a glass of pig's bones, a pillowcase which he swears is Our Lady's veil, and a sheaf of pardons sealed hot from Rome. He winks at you. "My text is always the same, friend: The love of money is the root of all evil. It never fails." Then he nods toward the pilgrims. "Only tell them that you saw a miracle by my bones, and I'll split the takings with you."

options.label: Tell the pilgrims you saw a miracle
options.outcome: The pilgrims empty their purses into his cap, weeping for joy. Afterward he divides the money with you very fairly, though it is the only honest dealing that he does all that day.
options.chronicle: Swore a pig's bones worked miracles. Split the take with the Pardoner.

road.hint: The Pardoner needed a witness, and would pay with the pilgrims' own money.

options.label: Refuse him
