options.outcome: "A pity," he says. "You have an honest face, and it would have been worth a fortune." He goes off to preach none the less, and he does well enough without you.
options.chronicle: Would not vouch for the Pardoner. He did well enough without me.

road.hint: The Pardoner might have been refused, however much he would pay for an honest face.

options.label: Show the pilgrims his pardons are forged

pass.outcome: Every pardon declares itself "given at Rome" and is dated in the reign of a Pope who had lain a hundred years dead when the seal was cut. You read aloud the date and the name, and the years of that Pope's reign, until an old pilgrim who once walked to Rome begins to laugh, and soon they are all laughing. The Pardoner packs up his pig's bones with great dignity and takes his departure.
pass.chronicle: Got the Pardoner run out for false pardons, but his minders hit me.

fail.outcome: You mistake the Pope, and he corrects you beautifully before them all, so that the pilgrims buy twice as much as before.
fail.chronicle: Got the Pope wrong. Pardoner's minders hit me, pilgrims bought double.

road.hint: A pardon dated in a dead man's reign can be proved a forgery.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: Behind you the Pardoner begins his sermon upon the text that has never failed him: The love of money is the root of all evil.

name: Weeping Mother
text: She comes slowly into sight, first the outline of her and then the tears, which fall like silver and vanish before they reach the stone, and a glowing locket circles about her like a small moon. "My boy Pip was nine," she says. "He went in after the dog, and the dog came back without him." Her voice breaks. "Will you pray with me? I don't ask it for him, but for me, because I'm so tired, and I only want to stop looking."

options.label: Kneel and pray with her until she can rest

pass.outcome: You find the right prayer, which is Simeon's, that the old man said in the Temple when he held the child whom he had waited all his life to see: now let your servant go in peace. The prayer is long in the saying, and her weariness lies upon you like a stone, for it is the weariness of twelve years of walking. When you have finished, her tears fall more slowly. "I can feel it," she breathes. "It's peace, after so long." And she passes smiling into a warm light, and the locket goes with her.
pass.chronicle: Prayed Maud's ghost to rest. Her boy followed a dog twelve years ago.

schedule.lost_line: Never did find Maud Ferrers's boy.

fail.outcome: You pray, but the words will not come right, and her weariness is heavier than your prayer. "Thank you," she says. "Most walk right through." And with that she takes up her long search again.
fail.chronicle: Could not pray Maud's ghost to rest. She is still searching.

road.hint: One who has searched very long may ask no more than to be allowed to stop.

options.label: Tell her that her love has outlasted death
options.outcome: Her shape wavers like a flame. "Thank you for seeing me," she says. "Most walk right through." Then she goes on with her search, and she will be searching always.

options.label: Walk on

name: Pip Ferrers
text: On a step sits a boy of about nine with a frayed dog's lead in his hand, and you can see through him as through breath upon glass. "Have you seen my mum?" he asks. "I went in after Bracken and I couldn't find the way back, and then I couldn't find her. Bracken went home, and I heard him barking up there. I've been waiting for someone to come and get me."

options.label: Tell him where his mother went
options.outcome: You tell him that she looked for him for twelve years, until she was allowed to stop, and that she went smiling into the light with her locket. He stands up. "Then that's where I'll look," he says very sensibly. He winds the dog's lead about his hand and walks up into a light that is hidden from your eyes, and never once does he look back.
options.chronicle: Told Pip Ferrers where his mother went. He followed her to the light.

options.label: Leave him on his step
options.outcome: "That's all right," the boy says patiently. "Someone will come."

name: Andvari
text: Beneath a waterfall lies a pool, and in it a great pike that watches you with the eyes of an old man. A net of grey silk lies on the rock beside the water, such as Ran uses for the drowning of sailors, and someone has cut a notice in the stone in neat runes: ANDVARI'S POOL. THE GOLD IS UNDER HIM. THE NET IS HOW. The pike makes no move to swim away, and he has the look of one grown very weary of all this.

options.label: Net him and take all his gold, ring and all
options.outcome: He comes up as a dwarf, dripping and wrathful, and yields you everything, as once he yielded everything to Loki. Then he says very low, "The ring will be the death of whoever holds it, and never yet has it failed."
options.chronicle: Netted Andvari for gold and ring. The ring is death to its holder.

road.hint: The curse on that ring was strong enough to kill a dragon.

options.label: Take the net and leave him be
options.outcome: You roll up the grey silk, which is lighter than it looks and colder than water. The pike watches it go into your pack and sinks a little lower in the pool, as a man sits down heavily when he knows that the next visitor will come carrying it.
options.chronicle: Took Ran's net and left Andvari be. Must mind whom I give it to.

road.hint: The net may still do harm in another's hands.

options.label: Throw the net into the waterfall, so nobody can use it again
options.outcome: The grey silk goes down the falls and is lost. Slowly the pike rises as a dwarf, and he sits upon the rock and considers you for a long while. "Loki didn't do that," he says. Then he tells you a thing concerning Fafnir, that a dragon wears all his armour on top, and that this one crawls to the water each evening along the same groove in the rock.
options.chronicle: Sank Ran's net for Andvari. He says Fafnir is soft underneath.

road.hint: Without that net, no one could take Andvari's gold from him.

outcome_variants.outcome: The grey silk goes down the falls and is lost. Slowly the pike rises as a dwarf, and he sits upon the rock and considers you for a long while. "Loki didn't do that," he says. Then he sniffs, and he smells the dragon upon you. "And Fafnir's dead, isn't he? Then there is nobody left on my gold but me." And he laughs a little, for the first time in a great while.
outcome_variants.chronicle: Sank Ran's net for Andvari. He smelled Fafnir's blood on me and laughed.

options.label: Walk on

name: Swift Stranger

tells: two small pinions tucked in the band
a staff with two snakes carved round it

text: A young man leans against the wall with folded arms, smiling like one who knows a jest that is yet to be told. His traveller's hat has two small pinions tucked in the band, and he carries a staff with two snakes carved round it, of which one blinks. On his back hangs a tortoise shell with strings. "I left something for you at a crossroads," he says, "probably, or else I will have done. Do you care to make a trade?"

text_variants.text: A young man leans against the wall with folded arms, smiling like one who knows a jest that is yet to be told. His traveller's hat has two small pinions tucked in the band, and he carries a staff with two snakes carved round it, of which one blinks. On his back hangs a tortoise shell with strings. "I left something for you at a crossroads," he says, "probably, or else I will have done. Do you care to make a trade?" Then he looks at you again. "We have met before. You watched my father's pitcher, and he is still talking about it."

options.label: Trade food for his gift
options.outcome: He sniffs at it with approval and flicks a feather from his hat at your boots. It melts into the leather, and thereafter each step carries you farther than it should.
options.chronicle: Traded lunch to a grinning stranger for a feather. Walk faster now.

options.label: Ask whether Apollo ever got his cattle back

pass.outcome: He laughs until he must hold to the wall. "I was one day old!" he says. "I walked them backward so that the tracks pointed the wrong way, and then I paid him off with the lyre of my making." He taps the tortoise shell and says, "Clever mortal."

delayed.text: At the meeting of two passages a wand lies upon the flagstones, tied with a ribbon that is knotted in the shape of a winged sandal.

pass.chronicle: Asked a stranger about stolen cattle. He left a gift at a crossroads.

fail.outcome: "Cattle?" says he, and looks innocent, which in him is a warning. When he is gone you count your purse twice over, and it is all there, and you are none the easier for that.

road.hint: The thief who invented music would gladly tell you how he stole.

options.label: "You're a long way from Olympus, Messenger."
options.outcome: He tips his hat to you in true respect and says, "Most of them look only at the sandals." Before the hat has come down again he is gone from your sight.
options.chronicle: Hailed a grinning stranger by his proper title. He vanished.

options.label: Decline the trade
options.outcome: "Fair enough. You are the careful kind, and I respect that, mostly." With that he saunters away, whistling a tune that sounds as though it has not yet been written.

name: Azarias
text: As you go upon your way, a young man with a traveller's staff and a dog at his heels falls into step beside you as though it had been agreed between you. "I am Azarias, son of the great Ananias, one of your own kin," he says, while the dog wags at you as at an old friend. Beneath his arm is a fish wrapped in leaves, and he talks of it a great deal. He breaks a loaf of his own and offers you the half. The other half he holds as he speaks, and later it is gone, though you never see him eat.

on_arrive.outcome: At the foot of the second stair he halts. "I was sent thus far and no farther," he says, and he gives you a pouch that holds the fish's gall, wrapped in a leaf. "It is for eyes that have ceased to see, and you will know when it is needed."
on_arrive.chronicle: Walked with Azarias and his dog. Have his fish gall, for blind eyes.

on_fail.outcome: Azarias goes down beneath the blows, but when you come to him he is simply not there any more, and neither is the dog.
on_fail.chronicle: Lost Azarias and his dog on the stairs.

on_fail_variants.outcome: You look about for Azarias, and he is not there any more, nor is the dog.

options.label: Walk with him a while
options.outcome: "Good," he says, "for the road is better with company, and the dog is of the same mind."

road.hint: A guide who is never seen to eat may be more than he appears.

options.label: Ask him what the fish is for

pass.outcome: "The heart and liver, when they are burned, drive off a demon, and the gall heals eyes," he says, and he glances at you sidelong. "You know the story."
pass.chronicle: Azarias, a traveller with a dog, says a fish's gall heals eyes.

fail.outcome: "It is for supper," he says, and at that the dog sneezes.

road.hint: The traveller's fish may have been meant for more than his supper.

options.label: "You haven't eaten all day, Azarias."
options.outcome: He laughs, and for a moment there is more light in the passage than all the torches could give. "I am Raphael, one of the seven who stand before the Lord," he says. "All this way you only thought that you saw me eat." With two fingers he blesses you as a priest does, and the dog wags its tail.
options.chronicle: Saw that Azarias had not eaten. He owned that he is Raphael.

options.label: "I travel alone."
options.outcome: "Then go with God," he says, "and mind the third step." And when you come to the third step, there is a trap upon it.

name: The Mast
text: In a flooded hall of the goddess's temple a ship has driven its bow upon the marble steps at your feet, with black water all about the stern, so that you could climb aboard. A man is lashed to the mast hand and foot, and his crew sit at the oars with wax in their ears. Somewhere across the lake voices are singing, and it is the most beautiful sound that ever you heard. The man strains at the ropes and weeps. "Cut me loose!" he cries. "I am the captain, and I order it. I shall die if I do not hear the end!" But scratched upon the mast in his own hand are the words: WHATEVER I SAY, DON'T.

options.label: Cut him loose

pass.outcome: The ropes part and he springs for the water, but you get an arm about him and hold fast, and you give him back his own words: "Whatever I say, don't." You ask him which captain gives the orders, he who wrote that or he who is shouting now. At this he ceases to strain, and he remains trembling upon the deck until the song is ended.
pass.chronicle: Cut a captain free and held him to his own orders. He stayed aboard.

fail.outcome: He is over the side before you can speak a word, and a moment later the singing stops, as though it were satisfied.
fail.chronicle: Cut a captain from his mast when he begged. He went into the water.

road.hint: The captain gave two orders, and he might be asked which of them was truly his.

options.label: Keep him bound
options.outcome: He curses you, and then begs, and then curses you again until the song is ended, when he hangs limp in the ropes. "Thank you," he says. "That was the worst hour of my life, and I would not give it back."
options.chronicle: Kept a captain bound while the Sirens sang. He was glad of it after.

road.hint: It may be kinder to obey what the captain ordered an hour ago than what he begs now.

options.label: Listen to the end of the song yourself
options.outcome: The song promises you every answer and all things that have ever happened. When you come to yourself you are waist-deep in black water with the captain screaming your name from the mast, and you remember almost none of what you heard, though some little of it remains.
options.chronicle: Heard out the Sirens and woke in the lake. Recall one line of it.

road.hint: A song that promises every answer may exact a price from the listener.

options.label: Stop your ears and walk on
options.outcome: You walk on with your fingers in your ears, and the song follows you a long way before it passes at last out of hearing.

name: Neferkaptah
text: The torches upon this floor burn blue, and through the cracks in its stones water is rising that smells of river mud and myrrh. Neferkaptah walks out of the wall in his collar of gold, and after him come the dead of the tomb, wrapped and silent, more than you care to number. "You swore to me," he says, "and you have read it, for I can smell it upon you." Far behind them all a woman with wet hair stands very still, and she comes no nearer.

text_variants.text: The torches upon this floor burn blue, and through the cracks in its stones water is rising that smells of river mud and myrrh. Neferkaptah walks out of the wall in his collar of gold, and after him come the dead of the tomb, wrapped and silent, more than you care to number. "You swore to me," he says, "and you never even opened it. All this way you carried my book, and never once did you look inside." For a moment he sounds more hurt than angry. Far behind them all a woman with wet hair stands very still, and she comes no nearer.

options.label: Give the book back
options.outcome: He takes it and holds it to his breast, where once the linen band bound it, and one by one the dead return into the walls. Ahwere is the last to go, and she speaks no word, for there is no need of any.
options.chronicle: Gave the overdue Book of Thoth back to the dead as Ahwere watched.

road.hint: The book might still be given back late, though the lender would remember the delay.

options.label: "I don't have it any more."
options.outcome: "Then you shall bring me to where it is," he says, "or you shall come with me to where I am," and as he speaks the water rises over your boots.
options.chronicle: Lost Neferkaptah's book, against my oath. He raised his dead on me.

road.hint: The promise was yours to answer for, even if the book had left your pack.

options.label: Refuse. The book is yours now
options.outcome: "Then you shall keep it as I kept it," he says, and the water rises over your boots.
options.chronicle: Kept the Book of Thoth, forsworn. Neferkaptah raised his dead on me.

road.hint: The dead will come themselves to collect what was promised them.

name: Socrates

authority.who: the Athenian jury, on Meletus's charge
authority.why: Condemned an innocent man on a charge his accuser could not prove.

text: You come to a cell with the door open and the jailer asleep, and within it a snub-nosed old man sits in a worn cloak, cheerfully barefoot, while on the sill a cup waits for the changing of the watch and a friend stands wringing his hands. "Crito has a boat waiting," says Socrates, "and he thinks that I should run. I think that I should not, but show me that I am wrong and I will go." He pats the bench beside him. "Only you will have to show me, and I am very annoying about such things."

options.label: Argue with him, staking your strength

pass.outcome: You put it to him squarely. "Meletus could not name one young man whom you had corrupted, and still the jury voted against you. When a verdict is built on a lie, it is your accusers who speak in the borrowed voice of the laws of Athens, and if you drink the cup you let them keep it." Twice he must stop to think, and once he laughs aloud and says, "Oh, that is good!" Yet when the watch changes he drinks the cup. "You nearly had me," he tells you, "and nearly is the most that anyone has ever got. I thank you for the best argument that I have had in a month."
pass.chronicle: Argued well that a lying verdict is no law. Socrates drank anyway.

fail.outcome: He takes your argument apart so gently that you scarcely notice until you have nothing left to stand on. "Don't be sad," he says kindly, "for that is the useful part," and you are left wholly spent.
fail.chronicle: Lost every point to Socrates. Learned much, and am worn out.

road.hint: Even to lose an argument with Socrates might leave you the richer.

options.label: Carry him out by force
options.outcome: He makes no struggle, but all the way to Crito's boat upon the black water he continues to discuss whether a man who is carried away against his will has escaped at all. "They condemned you on a lie," Crito tells him, weeping for relief, "and to liars you owe nothing." You watch the boat draw away, and Socrates looks back toward his cell until it is lost to him in the darkness.
options.chronicle: Carried Socrates from his cell to Crito's boat against his will.

road.hint: The old man could be carried from his cell, though his reasons would go with him.

options.label: Stay for the last conversation
options.outcome: You stay with him. He talks of the soul, and he puts questions to you that you will be answering for years. When the watch changes he drinks, and walks about until his legs grow heavy, and then he lies down. At the very last he says, "Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius. Don't forget."
options.chronicle: Stayed with Socrates to the end. Must not forget his debt of a chicken.

road.hint: At the very end Socrates would be mindful of one small debt.

name: Thorleif Grimsson
text: Against a wall that is white with frost in the shape of a hand sits a man with a harp upon his knees, and the frost has taken him also from the breast downward, yet he is wholly calm. "I am Thorleif the skald," he says. "A draugr shook my hand, and I'll not see the morning." He smiles at you. "My brother Eyvind went over the edge of the Long Dark, and there's a stone there with room on it. I made him a verse. Will you carve it for me? I will teach it to you, and it is short, for he was not a patient man."

options.label: Learn the verse and swear to carve it
options.outcome: Three times he teaches it to you, beating the measure upon the harp: Eyvind went where the dark goes down; no mead, no fire, no brother's hand. Stone, say his name to the wind that stays. "Good," he says, when you have it by heart. "Now you are a skald, though a bad one, and it will serve."

oath.what: Carve his verse for his brother Eyvind on the rune-stone at the Long Dark.

thread.hint: I carry Thorleif's verse until I find the stone for it.

options.chronicle: Must carve Thorleif's verse for his brother at the Long Dark stone.

road.hint: The verse weighs nothing, but whoever learned it would bear a duty with it.

options.label: Give him a healing potion for the cold
options.outcome: It warms his face and his hands, though against the frost it avails nothing at all. "That is good," he says none the less, "for now I can feel my fingers to play."

options.label: Ask him to play while there's time
options.outcome: He plays the verse for his brother, and after it a long, bad, merry song about a goat, until in the middle of a line his hands fall still upon the strings, and you see that he is dead.
options.chronicle: A dying skald played his brother's verse, then died mid goat song.

options.label: Walk on

name: Pellok the Slightly Lost
text: A man in a wine merchant's apron sits upon a crate marked FINE VINTAGES, studying a map upside down with the greatest care, and he does not hear you until you are very near. "Gah! Oh, I beg your pardon, I do beg your pardon. Is this the 40th floor? I was told there was a marketplace on the 40th floor, and I have come down a great many stairs, and I begin very strongly to feel that I have not yet come down enough of them."

options.label: Buy a bottle from him
options.outcome: He is so glad to make a sale that he all but embraces you. Beyond all expectation the wine is excellent, a deep red that tastes of some summer many decades gone, and it warms you to the marrow and is kind to your wounds. Upon the map of his route he writes you down as a 'reliable customer'.

options.label: Give him food for the last stretch
options.outcome: He takes the food with the deepest gratitude. "You are a saint, a genuine saint! Here, take this, for I've been using it as a paperweight. The last owner said that it was powerful, and was very sure of it, too." He presses a potion into your hands and sets out muttering upon the long walk upward.

options.label: Tell him why half his bottles have gone sour

pass.outcome: You draw a cork that has shrunk and grown dry. "The air got in," you tell him. "Lay the bottles upon their sides, so that the cork stays wet and swollen, for once the air gets in a little bacterium turns the wine to vinegar." He gazes upon the crate that he has carried upright for two hundred miles, and then he gives you the best bottle that is left to him, which is very good indeed.
pass.chronicle: Told a merchant his dry corks soured the wine. Got his best bottle.

fail.outcome: "Too much shaking?" you offer, and he considers it very earnestly. Only afterward do you think of the corks, shrunken and dry because he carries his bottles upright, so that the air came in and the wine was turned to vinegar.
fail.chronicle: Could not tell a wine merchant why his wine soured. It was the corks.

road.hint: A dry cork will let the air into the wine.

options.label: Tell him what is really on the fortieth floor
options.outcome: "A gorgon in a temple," you say, "and no market at all." Slowly he grows white above his apron. "Up," he says. "Up is good. Up has customers." He hoists his crate, takes two steps in the wrong direction, corrects himself, and sets out for the stair a great deal faster than he came down it.
options.chronicle: Pointed a lost wine merchant upward. He is far from daylight.

road.hint: The merchant's map was leading him to a market that was not there.

name: Mourne, Dwarf Alchemist
text: In what was once a guardroom a dwarf has set up her laboratory, amid glass that has no right to have stayed whole so far beneath the earth. Her goggles glow faintly green, and her beard is singed at the ends. "Oh, a live one. Excellent! My people have brewed in the cinders since before your kings were born, and I have a work in hand that needs a subject to test it. Before you refuse, know that I offer fair payment, for I am an alchemist and no monster."

options.label: Volunteer, but check her working first

pass.outcome: Before you drink you read her notes, and you find that she has doubled one reagent and halved another. You show her that a compound strong enough to knit flesh has need of a measured dose and no hopeful one, for the dose makes the poison, as Paracelsus said. She swears in dwarvish as she amends it. This time the compound has a taste of copper and plums, and your wounds begin at once to knit.
pass.chronicle: Fixed a dwarf alchemist's dose first. Her compound knit my wounds.

fail.outcome: You drink it without reading the notes. An alarming heat kindles within you, and after it comes a long sour sickness, while Mourne frowns at her page. "Ah, I doubled that one," she says. "The dose makes the poison, as the old Swiss said." And she writes down all that has befallen you with the keenest interest.
fail.chronicle: Drank a dwarf alchemist's compound unchecked. The dose was poison.

road.hint: The dose makes the poison.

options.label: Buy her regeneration salve
options.outcome: "Tested and approved," she says, by which she means that she tested it upon herself, as you learn when she draws up her sleeve to show old burns in every stage of alchemical healing. The salve is thick and has a dreadful smell, and it begins its work upon you at once.

options.label: Buy a sealed bottle for the road
options.outcome: She wraps a bottle in a scrap of hide and seals the cork with wax. "It's properly dosed," she says, "which is more than I can say for the last batch."

options.label: "Hard pass."
options.outcome: "Noted," she says, and takes no offence. "A healthy mistrust of unbidden chemistry is a good instinct, as it happens. Come back if you change your mind, for I shall be here until I run out of subjects or the dungeon runs out of patience with me." With that she returns to her bubbling vessels.

name: Sir Lorvaine the Certain
text: A knight in spotless armour of a long-forgotten fashion stands squarely in your path, and though the cold makes your breath smoke, his does not fog at all. "I am Sir Lorvaine the Certain," he says, "and I have a riddle out of the old book at Exeter, which I have asked for forty-seven years. Answer it and you shall have the gift of my failed quest. A moth ate words. A thief in the dark swallowed a man's song, and was not one whit the wiser for it. What am I?"

options.label: Answer his riddle

pass.outcome: "A bookworm," you say, "a moth that eats the page and learns nothing." Sir Lorvaine stares at you, and then he sits down upon the floor in all his armour with a great clang. "Forty-seven years!" he says. "The monks at Exeter wrote it down a thousand years ago, and nobody has ever got it." He presses the gift of his quest into your hands, and as he does so he fades a little, like a man who may rest at last.
pass.chronicle: Solved Sir Lorvaine's riddle: a bookworm. Got his gift, and he faded.

fail.outcome: Your guess is wrong, and very slowly he nods. "It is a bookworm," he says, "a moth that eats the words and is none the wiser. The monks at Exeter wrote it down a thousand years ago." He keeps his gift, and with a sigh he says, "It shall be forty-eight years, then," and begins again.
fail.chronicle: Failed Sir Lorvaine's riddle. It was a bookworm. He waits on.

road.hint: The knight would gladly be done with his riddle, were it answered.

options.label: Wish him well and continue
options.outcome: "Of course," he says, a very little too loudly, and as you walk away you hear him begin to compose a new riddle.

name: Ulf Haraldsson, of the Einherjar
text: Upon the ice sits a mighty warrior, polishing a coat of mail that was hewn to pieces this morning and is whole again tonight. "I am Ulf Haraldsson, one of the einherjar, Odin's chosen dead," he says. "We fight all the day, and at evening the fallen stand up whole. We eat the boar that is cooked each night and is whole again by morning, and we wait for the wolf." Then he lifts his eyes to you, and something wakes in them. "Are they still coming down? That is good, for the deep floors have need of witnesses."

options.label: Ask him to train you the old way

pass.outcome: He trains you for the holmgang, the duel of the island, in which a cloak is pegged out upon the ground with ropes about it and each man has his shield-bearer and three spare shields. Whoever steps off the cloak with both feet has fled and is named nithing for life, and the first blood upon the cloak ends the fight. "Small ground teaches small, sure steps," he says, and he corrects your grip until your blade bites truer.
pass.chronicle: Ulf's holmgang lesson: pegged cloak, three shields, no stepping off.

fail.outcome: He drills you hard, and still you give ground. "Off the cloak," he says each time. "In a holmgang that is flight, and they will call you nithing for life." When you leave him you are bruised and have no more skill than before.
fail.chronicle: Failed holmgang drill with the einherjar. Stepping back is running.

road.hint: The whole ground of the old duel was no wider than a cloak.

options.label: Share a meal with him
options.outcome: He receives the food with the dignity of one who has forgotten what it is to be given anything, and he eats it slowly. "It is the first meal that I have shared in..." He begins to count, and gives it up. "I thank you," he says, and he fills some empty place in your pack with rations that you did not know you lacked. "You will need them more than I."

options.label: "What are you waiting for?"
options.outcome: He looks down upon the mail in his hands, and it is long before he has an answer for you. "For this," he says at last, "that someone should still be here when the next one comes through, so that the next may know that the road has been walked before." Then he gravely waves you onward, to go down that road as others have gone.

name: Squire Tobyn
text: A squire of some sixteen years sits on a broken step with a wooden practice sword across his knees, watching the stair by which you came. At the sight of you he stands up too quickly. "Is Ser Brennan behind you? He said he'd catch up. He always catches up."

options.label: Give him the sword, and Ser Brennan's message
options.outcome: He takes the sword as Brennan held it out, hilt foremost, before he has understood, and then he understands. "He said I was ready?" he asks, and you nod. He weeps as boys do who are striving not to weep, and when he has done he buckles on the sword.
options.chronicle: Gave Squire Tobyn his knight's sword, and said he was not left behind.

road.hint: A message that the dead have entrusted to you should not be kept waiting.

options.label: Give him Ser Brennan's message, without the sword
options.outcome: You give him Brennan's message, and then you must tell him the rest, that the sword was lost upon the way down. He hears all of it. "Ready," he says. "He said I was ready." And when he takes up the wooden sword he does not hold it as he held it before.
options.chronicle: Gave Squire Tobyn his knight's last words. Had lost the sword.

road.hint: A dead knight's words may be carried to his squire though his sword be lost.

options.label: Keep the sword. Tell him Brennan fell, nothing more
options.outcome: "Fell," he says, and nods slowly. "Then I'll wait for his body." When you look back he is still sitting on the step.
options.chronicle: Broke my word to Brennan and kept his sword. His squire still waits.

road.hint: A promise to the fallen knight would be broken in his squire's sight.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: "He'll catch up," Tobyn says as you pass, speaking for the most part to himself.

name: The Lingering Echo
text: In the centre of the passage flickers a figure made wholly of letters that are slowly drifting apart, and it is the echo of a wizard who died in the middle of a word. Again and again it lifts its hand and shapes the word letter by letter, a-b-r-a-c-a-d-a-b-r, and begins anew. When it sees you it breaks from that round with a great effort. "I require... the last letter," it says. "I have forgotten the last letter, and I have knowledge yet to spend."

options.label: Let the echo channel through you
options.outcome: It is like grasping a bolt of lightning by the wrong end. The study of decades pours through your body in a few seconds, and though you understand little of it, the naked power of the magic fills you to the brim. The echo completes its word at last in a single syllable of great contentment and is scattered, and what it leaves behind swells your store of mana.
options.chronicle: Let a dead wizard's echo finish his spell through me.

road.hint: The half-spoken word had need of a living mouth.

options.label: Offer a scroll as a vessel instead
options.outcome: The echo considers the scroll with something like hope, and then it pours itself into the parchment in a cascade of shining script. The scroll blackens and crumbles, all used up, but in its place a wand builds itself out of signs and will, as solid as steel and humming with the last purpose of the dead wizard.

options.label: Give him the last letter, and tell him what it was for

pass.outcome: "A," you say. "Abracadabra." The echo trembles with relief. The oldest record of that word is a Roman physician's, Serenus Sammonicus, who bade it be written on parchment in a triangle, losing a letter in each line down to a single A, and worn about the neck, that the fever might dwindle as the word did. And so the echo finishes its spell at last, which was made neither for fire nor for lightning but to lessen a sickness, and it spends upon you all that is left of itself.
pass.chronicle: Gave a wizard's echo the last A of abracadabra, the Roman fever charm.

fail.outcome: Your guess is wrong, and with lifted hand the echo begins anew, letter by letter. Afterward it comes to you that the word was abracadabra, ending in A, the Roman charm against fever, which was written in a triangle one letter shorter in each line, so that the fever would dwindle with it.
fail.chronicle: Failed a wizard's echo. The word was abracadabra, its last letter A.

road.hint: An old charm against fever dwindles by one letter at a time.

options.label: Leave the echo in peace
options.outcome: You step with care around the figure. Behind you the hand is lifted and the mouth shapes the word, and all begins again, for the spell has outlasted the caster and is not yet finished.

name: Rune-Stone
text: At the edge of a great dark gulf stands a stone carved with runes in a ribbon that ends in a serpent's head. The greater part of the ribbon is filled with names, telling who raised the stone and for whom, but the last loop is empty, and a chisel has been left in a crack, as if it were known that someone would have need of it.

options.label: Carve Thorleif's verse for his brother
options.outcome: You carve it as he spoke it, line by line, and the serpent's head last of all. When you step back the stone is complete, as a sentence is when its full stop is set. Far below in the darkness you hear someone laughing, as a brother laughs.
options.chronicle: Carved Thorleif's verse for his brother on the rune-stone, as sworn.

road.hint: The empty loop upon the stone was waiting for Thorleif's verse.

options.label: Carve your own name in the empty loop instead
options.outcome: It looks very well there. All who come this way will read it and wonder who you were, but no one will ever read Thorleif's verse.
options.chronicle: Broke my oath to Thorleif. Carved my name in place of his verse.

road.hint: If your name filled the loop, there would be no room left for the verse.

options.label: Walk on

name: Lady Bertilak
text: In a warm hall hewn from the rock a lady in green sits by the fire, winding a sash of green silk about her fingers. "My lord said that whatever you win in his house you shall give to him before you depart, and those are the terms," she says. Then she holds out the sash. "This is a girdle that no blade can cut through. You go soon to meet the Green Knight, and he will swing at your neck." She smiles upon you. "My lord need never know of it."

options.label: Take it and keep it secret
options.outcome: She ties it about your waist with her own hands. At the door her husband asks what you won in his house, and you answer him that you won nothing.

thread.hint: Somewhere below, the Green Knight is sharpening an axe for my neck.

schedule.lost_line: Still have the girdle. I never did find the Green Chapel.

options.chronicle: Took the girdle against the Green Knight's axe. Hid it from my host.

road.hint: A secret kept from your host would go with you to the chapel.

options.label: Take it, and give it to your host at the door, as agreed
options.outcome: Her husband turns the sash over in his hands, laughing, and does not give it back. "Honest," he says. "We shall see how honest the Knight finds your neck." That night you sleep but little, and as Gawain did on the eve of the chapel you hear every cock crow and know the hour.
options.chronicle: Won a girdle to save my neck. Gave it to my host, as the terms were.

road.hint: To keep a bargain that might be broken unseen would be the whole test.

options.label: Refuse it
options.outcome: She winds the sash about her fingers again. "Gawain took it," she says, "and he was very nearly perfect." It seems that you have at once disappointed and impressed her.
options.chronicle: Refused the lady's girdle, proof against the Green Knight's axe.

road.hint: The gift that would save your life might cost you something you meant to keep.

name: The Green Knight

authority.who: the Green Knight, keeper of the Green Chapel
authority.why: He keeps his bargains exactly, and his judgement of the girdle is honest: a nick for a small lie, and forgiveness for the truth.

chronicle_meet: Found the Green Chapel, a holly mound. An axe is ground for my neck.
text: In a hollow of the rock rises a green mound, grown over with turf and with holly in full berry, like an old barrow that was never closed, and from within it comes the shriek of an axe upon a grindstone. Presently the Green Knight stoops out of it, his head set upon his shoulders and a great axe laid across one of them. "So you have come," he says, "as few men do." He considers you at leisure, as a host considers the guest at his door. "You owe me one blow. Kneel, and bare your neck."

text_variants.text: In a hollow of the rock rises a green mound, grown over with turf and with holly in full berry, like an old barrow that was never closed, and from within it comes the shriek of an axe upon a grindstone. Presently the Green Knight stoops out of it, his head set upon his shoulders and a great axe laid across one of them. "So you have come," he says, "as few men do." He considers you at leisure, as a host considers the guest at his door, until his eyes stop at your waist. "You owe me one blow. Kneel, and bare your neck."

options.label: Kneel, and bare your neck
options.outcome: You kneel on the cold turf, but when the axe goes up you flinch, and he stays it in the air. "Gawain never flinched," he says, almost kindly. At the second stroke you hold still, and the blade halts a hair's breadth from your skin. The third falls in earnest and bites the side of your neck, so that you feel a nick, hot and running. Then he leans upon the haft, and for a moment he is the lord of the warm hall, Bertilak, laughing beside his own fire. "One stroke was for our bargain," he says, "and one to try your nerve, but the nick was for what you won in my house and called nothing." And with that he waits to hear what you will say.
options.chronicle: Knelt at the Green Chapel. Third stroke nicked me. He knows of my lie.

road.hint: You may still honour your bargain, though it is paid under the axe.

options.label: Tell him about the girdle before he swings
options.outcome: Before you kneel, you untie the green sash and hold it up between you. "Your lady gave me this," you say. "When you asked at your door what I had won in your house I told you nothing, and I lied because I wished to live." The Green Knight gazes long upon the girdle, and then he laughs aloud, so that the snow is shaken from the holly, and takes it out of your hand. He must still swing three times, for such was the bargain, but each stroke stops a hair's breadth from your skin. "Gawain had to feel the axe before he could confess as much," says Bertilak. "You said it first, and therefore I hold you as clean as the day you were born."
options.chronicle: Owned to the girdle before the axe and gave it back. Unhurt, called clean.

road.hint: If you confess before the axe falls, it may spare your neck.

options.label: Refuse his game, and draw on him
options.outcome: You tell him no and draw your weapon. The Green Knight sighs, as a master sighs over a slow pupil, and lifts the axe from his shoulder. "Then we shall play the game in the old fashion," he says. "Strike first if you will, and I shall take my turn after."
options.chronicle: Would not kneel at the Green Chapel. Drew on the Green Knight.

road.hint: The Green Knight has lost his head before, and does not fear the sword.

options.label: Walk away from the chapel
options.outcome: You turn your back upon the mound, and behind you the grindstone begins to sing once more. "The girdle goes with you," he calls after you, not unkindly, "and you must bear along with it the reason for which you carry it."
options.chronicle: Left the Green Chapel with the girdle, and the reason I carry it.

road.hint: You may leave the Green Chapel, but the debt will go along with you.

options.label: Tell him the truth about the girdle, and give it back
options.outcome: Though your neck is bleeding into your collar, you untie the green sash and hold it out to him. "Your lady gave me this," you say. "You asked what I had won in your house and I told you nothing, and I lied because I wished to live." Bertilak turns it over in his huge hands and laughs until the holly shakes. "You lacked a little loyalty," he says, "and only for love of your life. That is the whole of your fault, and you have owned it." Then he lays a handful of snow upon the wound with great gentleness. "I hold you as clean as the day you were born."
options.chronicle: Nicked, told of the girdle, gave it back. The Knight called me clean.

road.hint: The truth about the girdle may yet be told after the blow is taken.

options.label: Call it a fair blow, and say you're quits
options.outcome: "It was a fair blow," you say, "and now we are quits." Bertilak regards you for as long as the snow takes to settle upon the turf, and though he agrees that you are quits, he does not laugh. "Keep it, then," he says, "and as often as you buckle it on you will know it for what it is." With that he shoulders his axe and goes back into his hill, where the grindstone begins again.

outcome_variants.outcome: "It was a fair blow," you say, "and now we are quits." Bertilak regards you and your empty belt for as long as the snow takes to settle upon the turf, and though he agrees that you are quits, he does not laugh. "Wherever it may be now," he says, "you will know what it was." With that he shoulders his axe and goes back into his hill, where the grindstone begins again.
outcome_variants.chronicle: Called it a fair blow and quits. The Green Knight agreed, unsmiling.

options.chronicle: Called it quits. The Green Knight agreed, and let me keep the girdle.

road.hint: To call it quits is to hide the girdle from your host a second time.

options.label: Say nothing, and go
options.outcome: You lay a hand upon your neck and say nothing at all, and Bertilak nods slowly, as though that were an answer of its kind. "Go your way, then," he says. "The girdle is yours, and so is the knowledge of what it is." When you look back from the end of the hollow he is still watching you go.

outcome_variants.outcome: You lay a hand upon your neck and say nothing at all, and Bertilak nods slowly, as though that were an answer of its kind. "Go your way, then," he says. "Wherever the girdle may be now, the knowledge of it is yours." When you look back from the end of the hollow he is still watching you go.

options.chronicle: Said nothing of the girdle, though the Green Knight knew. He let me go.

road.hint: The Green Knight will accept your silence, though he hoped for the truth.

name: Vafthrudnir
text: You come into a hall of stone as black as winter ice, where a giant sits upon a high seat with his beard hanging like frozen rope, and on the shelf behind him stands a row of skulls, each labelled in runes. "I am Vafthrudnir," he says, "and I know more than any who has ever sat upon that bench. Sit there, and we will trade questions. If you lose, your head goes upon my shelf, and if you win you shall carry home more than you brought."

options.label: Wager your head

pass.outcome: He sits back, for his questions are spent and yours are not. "Take your head home," he says slowly, "and take with it some part of the wisdom in mine."
pass.chronicle: Won Vafthrudnir's contest for my head. Got some of his wits besides.

fail.outcome: "That was close," he says, and takes less than your whole head for his fee, yet some part of you stays upon his shelf.
fail.chronicle: Lost at questions to Vafthrudnir. Part of me stays on his shelf.

road.hint: Look well upon the giant's shelf before you stake your own head.

options.label: Play a short contest for coin instead

pass.outcome: You answer his one question and he answers yours, but to your second he can find no answer. The giant laughs and pays what he owes, as a giant of honour must. "It is a small contest," he says, "for one who has played against Odin with his own head for the stake."
pass.chronicle: Won coin at questions from Vafthrudnir, whom Odin played for his head.

fail.outcome: He asks, and you have no answer to give, so he keeps your stake with a courteous nod. "In my hall a guest must always wager either head or coin," he says, "and you may be glad that you wagered coin."
fail.chronicle: Lost my coin to the giant Vafthrudnir at questions. Kept my head.

options.label: "What did Odin whisper in Baldr's ear on the pyre?"

pass.outcome: The giant's face turns grey, for no man has ever asked him that and none living knows the answer, and he perceives now who it was that taught you to ask. "You have been talking with a one-eyed man," he says, and he rises from the high seat and yields it to you, as to one who has overcome him.
pass.chronicle: Stumped Vafthrudnir with the one-eyed man's question. Have his seat.

outcome_variants.outcome: The giant's face turns grey, for no man has ever asked him that and none living knows the answer, and he perceives now where it was that you learned to ask. "You have been drinking at Mimir's well," he says, and he rises from the high seat and yields it to you, as to one who has overcome him.
outcome_variants.chronicle: Stumped Vafthrudnir with a question from Mimir's well. Have his seat.

fail.outcome: You stumble in the very question that you came to ask. He lets you go for all that, but his laughter follows you out of the hall.

road.hint: Some contests may be won by recalling whom you met beside a well.

options.label: Decline

name: The Chooser of the Slain
text: Frozen into the wall of ice is a young warrior in old mail, with open eyes and a spear-wound beneath his ribs, and beside the body his shade sits shivering. "I am Eyvind," he says. "I fell here against the frost-giants. When our line broke I ran, but afterward I came back and held the gap alone until they killed me." Over him stands a woman in mail, whose spear and helmet are bright as frost, and ravens wait upon the beams. "I am Skogul, a chooser of the slain," she says, "and of those we choose, half go to Odin's hall and half to Freyja's field. He has told you how he died, living one. Tell it now to me, and I will make my choice." But Eyvind catches at your sleeve and begs you, "Tell her I never ran."

options.label: Tell her he never ran
options.warning: Tell her I never ran.
options.outcome: "No one may lie to a chooser of the slain about the slain," she says, and she turns her spear about and smites you hard across the ribs with the butt of it. Then she is gone and all her ravens with her, while Eyvind's shade gives you one look and fades unchosen into the ice.
options.chronicle: Lied to a valkyrie for a dead man. She struck me and left him unchosen.

road.hint: The valkyrie will know any lie that is told her about the slain.

options.label: Tell her all of it: he ran, and he came back

pass.outcome: You tell it as a skald would, holding nothing back: how the line broke and he ran, and how he turned again and came back alone into the gap and held it until they killed him. "It is for the coming back that I take him," says the valkyrie, "for most men are never asked to choose twice, and he chose twice." The name of her order, valkyrja, means a chooser of the slain, and half of those she chooses ride to Odin's Valhalla and half to the field of Freyja. She lifts Eyvind up behind her, and as she departs she touches your shield with the point of her spear.
pass.chronicle: Told a valkyrie a dead man ran and returned. She chose him for it.

fail.outcome: You stumble in the telling, so that the running is told and the coming back is not, and her face grows stern. "Then I cannot choose him," she says. With that she is gone among her ravens, and Eyvind fades into the ice.
fail.chronicle: Told a valkyrie of a warrior's death, badly. She did not choose him.

road.hint: If his tale is told entire, the valkyrie may yet receive him.

options.label: Tell her only that he ran
options.outcome: "That is true," she says, "but it is not all the truth, and a chooser cannot choose upon half a tale." She looks long at you before she departs, and behind her Eyvind fades without a word into the ice.
options.chronicle: Told a valkyrie a dead warrior ran, and left out the rest.

options.label: Leave the choosing to her
options.outcome: You step back, and the valkyrie watches you go before she turns again to the ice, and what choice she made there you never learn.

name: Crossroads Fiddler

tells: one of his boots is the wrong shape

text: Where four corridors meet, a gentleman in a black coat sits upon a milestone tuning a fiddle, and about him is the scent of good cologne and, beneath it, of struck matches. "Are you not weary of being questioned?" he asks. "Everyone down here is forever putting you to the test. Only sign, and the answers will come to you sooner from here to the bottom." He holds out a pen and a paper covered in very small writing, and you notice that one of his boots is the wrong shape, as though there were no toes within it. "The payment comes later," he says, "and very much later."

options.label: Sign
options.outcome: The ink is warm beneath the pen. He plays you a little tune in celebration, and it is the fairest that you have ever heard, though you know that you will never hear the end of it. Answers begin to arrive in your mind a moment ahead of the questions, and there is little comfort in the feeling.
options.chronicle: Signed a crossroads gentleman's paper for early answers. Beware the bill.

road.hint: The fiddler's easy answers are themselves a trial of you.

options.label: Read the small print before you decide

pass.outcome: It is slow work, for the print grows smaller as it goes, but in the last line, in a hand like a scratch, you find it: that the signatory's name shall be set down in the book that is not kept by the Other Fellow. You understand that this is the wrong book to have your name in, and when you look up he is already smiling, a little ruefully. You tear the paper in half and then in quarters. "Some other crossroads, then," he says, and afterward there is only a scorched place on the milestone where he sat.
pass.chronicle: Crossroads paper would put my name in the wrong book. Tore it up.

fail.outcome: The small print swims before your eyes, and he leans over kindly and reads it out to you in a beautiful voice, so that every clause sounds most reasonable. Then he holds out the pen again.

road.hint: Read to the last line, for the price is written smallest of all.

options.label: Refuse to sign
options.outcome: When you refuse, he folds the paper into his coat without dispute. "There is always another crossroads," he says mildly, and returns to his tuning.
options.chronicle: Refused the crossroads paper. Never did find out what was in it.

road.hint: You may refuse the paper, though you will never learn what was written there.

options.label: Walk past without a word
options.outcome: He plays a few bars after you, and for some way down the passage you find that you are walking in time to them.

name: Something in a Copper Jar
text: In the midst of the corridor stands a great copper jar, and its lead stopper is stamped with a six-pointed seal and with a warning in three dead languages. The jar is rattling, and out of it speaks a voice of great dignity. "I am aware how this must appear to you, but I have been shut in here for eighteen hundred years. Open it, and I will reward you as you deserve."

options.label: Open the jar
options.warning: Open it, and I will reward you as you deserve.
options.outcome: The seal cuts your hands as it yields, and the jinni pours out in a pillar of furious wind and towers over you. "For the first hundred years I swore that I would make my deliverer rich," it says, "and for the next that I would open to him the treasures of the earth, and for the next that I would grant him three wishes. But after that I swore that I would slay whoever set me free."
options.chronicle: Opened a copper jar for reward. Its prisoner had sworn off rewards.

road.hint: A long captivity may sour a prisoner's promise.

options.label: Slide coins under the stopper and bargain (150 gold)
options.outcome: You slide your coins beneath the stopper, and the jinni sighs in elaborate exasperation. "I have no means of spending gold in here," it says, "but I do thank you for the thought." Then it breathes something old and bright through the leaden seal, and your mind is filled as a cup is filled.

options.label: Let it out, but first doubt that it was ever in

pass.outcome: You know the tale of the fisherman from the Thousand and One Nights, so you raise the stopper an inch and declare that you do not believe so great a being was ever in so small a jar. The jinni is affronted and pours itself back within to prove it, whereupon you drive the seal home. Then you make your bargain with the jinni on the inside, and it ends as the tale does with a promise kept, for it tells you where a thing of value lies and who must never hear of it.
pass.chronicle: Tricked a jinni back into its jar by doubt. Bargained with it inside.

fail.outcome: You try to bargain through the stopper, and it laughs at you. "In the old tale a fisherman got the better of one of my kind by doubting him," it says, "and you are not that fisherman."
fail.chronicle: Failed to bargain with a jinni in a jar. It says I am no fisherman.

road.hint: A fisherman of old mastered a jinni by doubting him.

options.label: Leave the jar sealed
options.outcome: "That is sensible, and I mean it sincerely," says the jar. "I have been in here a very long while and my temper is not at its best, and you have judged rightly." As you walk away from it the rattling begins once more.

name: Grey-Eyed Woman

tells: eyes the grey of storm clouds
an owl that is not quite an owl
a spear propped like a broom

text: A woman stands among the fallen columns as though the temple had been raised about her. Her eyes are the grey of storm clouds before the lightning, and upon her shoulder perches an owl that is not quite an owl. Beside her a spear is propped against the wall like a broom, and the air smells faintly of olives. "You have come a long way into my house," she says, "and I am curious to learn whether your mind has grown as keen as your ambition."

options.label: Ask whether Arachne's tapestry had a single flaw

pass.outcome: Her eyes turn the grey of a storm about to break. "There was no flaw," she says at last, "not a single one, and it was that which I could not endure." The owl hoots softly, as at a jest. "Most mortals ask me what lies at the bottom, but you have asked the one question upon which I still brood." With that she touches your eyelids.
pass.chronicle: Grey-eyed woman says the weaver had no flaw. I see more clearly now.

fail.outcome: "That is a foolish question," she says, and even the owl turns its head away from you.
fail.chronicle: Asked a grey-eyed woman of a weaver, foolishly. Her owl looked away.

road.hint: Ask the grey-eyed woman of her rival at the loom, and watch her face.

options.label: "Grey-eyed Pallas. This was your house."
options.outcome: "It is my house still," she answers, almost smiling. "Go on, for I wish to see how your tale will end."
options.chronicle: Named the grey-eyed woman. She means to see how my story ends.

options.label: "What lies at the bottom?"
options.outcome: She tilts her head and allows that it is a fair question, while the owl blinks slowly. "At the bottom lies that which has long asked itself what lies above it," she says, "for all things look upward, child, and even the Abyss has its ambitions."

options.label: Bow and pass
options.outcome: She inclines her head, and that small courtesy weighs more than any blessing you could name. The owl watches you until you are out of sight.

name: The Unseen Archivist
text: You can see no one, and yet you hear a quill at work upon parchment and the polite clearing of a throat, and you feel that a chair is occupied. "I set down the deeds of those who descend," says a voice at the height of a desk, though no desk is there. "I have questions, if you have answers to give me, and I pay for my interviews."

options.label: Agree to be interviewed
options.outcome: The questioning is long and thorough. It would know your earliest memory and your greatest fear, what you believe to lie at the bottom of the dungeon, and whether you are fond of mornings, and it writes down each answer with the same eager care, as one to whom all answers matter alike. When at last it has finished, a purse of gold appears upon the floor before you. "You have given me most excellent matter for the book," it says warmly, "and I thank you."
options.chronicle: Was questioned by an unseen archivist. My answers are in its book.

road.hint: An unseen scribe will pay to hear of you.

options.label: Ask it to read you a page about the people you met
options.outcome: The quill is stilled, and near the back of a book that you cannot see a page is turned. Then, very softly, the voice begins to read:

people_lines.none: "I find nobody," it says in puzzlement, "for as yet you have met nobody, or saved nobody, or lost nobody. Come back to me when you have."
people_lines.after: "That will be enough," it says, "for the rest must wait until the end."

options.chronicle: The Unseen Archivist read me a page on the people I met coming down.

road.hint: The unseen scribe can tell you what became of those you met.

options.label: Decline the interview
options.outcome: "So noted," says the voice, and you hear your refusal being written down. "That also is worth the recording. May you walk in safety." The scratching of the quill follows you along the corridor for longer than seems possible, and then all at once it ceases.

name: The Mirror Shade
text: The figure before you has your very likeness, as you were before the descent, cleaner and with fewer scars, and it smiles at you with your own face. "You have come a long way," it says in your voice. "I am all that you left behind, and I have kept it warm for you. There may be some part of it that you would wish to have again."

options.label: Reach for what was lost
options.outcome: You lay your hand upon its breast and feel pain, though it is the pain of no wound, but of remembering who you were before you knew all that you know now. When you draw back the shade is gone, and yet something has returned to you, a vigour and a readiness such as come only of knowing full well what you are fighting for.
options.chronicle: Met myself as I was before the descent, and cleaner.

road.hint: Some strength may be drawn from the one you used to be.

options.label: Ask it whether you are still the one it remembers

pass.outcome: "Then you know what the wise have said," it answers with your mouth. Heraclitus said that no one steps twice into the same river, for the water is ever new, and Locke that a man is the same person as far back as his memory reaches. Others have held that it is the soul that makes him so, or the body, or that there is no single self at all. "I do not know which of them is right," says the shade, "and you must carry the question now, though it is lighter than the burden I have borne." It gives something warm back into your keeping and departs.
pass.chronicle: Am I still myself? My reflection cites Heraclitus and Locke. Unsolved.

fail.outcome: "Surely I am," you say, and the shade smiles as one unconvinced. "Heraclitus would say that the river is new water every time," it tells you. "Ask yourself again when you are not in haste." With that it melts away like mist before a beam of light.
fail.chronicle: Told my reflection I am the same. It cited Heraclitus and went.

road.hint: No one steps into the same river twice.

options.label: Walk through it
options.outcome: It does not hinder you, and you pass through cold air and a brief stream of scents half remembered, of one kitchen and one rain that you knew long ago. You do not look back, and if the shade watches you it says nothing.

text_variants.text: The figure before you has your very likeness, as you were before the descent, cleaner and with fewer scars, and it smiles at you with your own face. "You have come a long way," it says in your voice. "I am all that you left behind, and I have kept it warm for you. There may be some part of it that you would wish to have again." In its hands it holds a thing of yours from a day that you would gladly forget.

name: Death
text: A chessboard is set upon a rock, and at it sits a pale man in a black hood who is no man at all. Behind you a juggler, his wife and their baby are hiding very still behind a painted cart. The locust cult took them upon the road above and dragged them down the long stair for an offering, cart and all, but they fled. "I am Death," says the pale man, as one who begs your pardon. "They are mine tonight, and so shall you be in your time. Will you play? It is my custom to offer, and a knight once played me upon a beach to win a little time." He sets out the pieces. "Your years are the stake, and you may name what you play for."

options.label: Play for the family, staking your own years

pass.outcome: For a long while he studies the board, and then with his own hand he lays down his king, very carefully, as though it mattered that this be rightly done, and says, "They may go." Behind you the cart creaks away along the road, and you hear the baby laughing.
pass.chronicle: Beat Death at chess. The juggler's family went free.

fail.outcome: He takes your pieces one after another, and some few of your years along with them. Then he rises and goes very gently round the cart, and the painted masks upon it turn to watch him pass.
fail.chronicle: Lost chess for a juggler's family. Death took them, and years of mine.

road.hint: A game played for another's sake is not all lost, though you lose it.

options.label: Play for yourself, staking the same years

pass.outcome: "That was well played," he says, and makes a small mark in a small book. "When you go homeward with your Stone I will give you back, once only, a breath that I would otherwise have taken."
pass.chronicle: Death owes me a breath, won at chess. Nothing for the juggler's family.

fail.outcome: Death takes your years from you, and afterward he takes the family as well.
fail.chronicle: Played Death for myself, lost years. He took the juggler's family too.

road.hint: What you win for yourself alone will not save the family.

options.label: Offer him the family if he lets you pass
options.outcome: He looks long upon you before he nods and goes round the cart. You do not look back, but you hear the little bells upon the cart fall silent one by one behind you.
options.chronicle: Gave Death a juggler's family for my passage. He took them.

road.hint: Should you bargain so with Death, the family would pay for it.

options.label: Walk away
options.outcome: "Another time," he says courteously. "There is always another time, until the last of them is spent."

name: The Old Titan
text: A slow golden light beats within a crack in the wall, too regular for fire and too living for stone, and through it you see an eye as great as a cartwheel, very old and very weary. When you stoop close you feel the heat of some enormous being that is pent behind a door of bronze, in a space far too small for it. Then a voice speaks from the crack, as slow as a clock. "I am less than I was, traveler, but I am not gone, and I was king of the world before my son. Open the door a crack, and I will give you time."

options.label: Name the old king behind the bronze

pass.outcome: "Kronos," you say, for this is the Titan who cast down his own father with a sickle. He was warned that a child of his would cast him down in turn, and so he swallowed his children one by one, until Rhea gave him a stone in swaddling clothes in place of the infant Zeus. When Zeus was grown he made him yield them all up, and shut the Titans behind bronze doors in Tartarus, so deep, says Hesiod, that an anvil dropped from the earth would fall nine days and nights and land upon the tenth. The great eye closes. "You are clever," says the voice, "and so was my son." About you the air grows steady, as if time had grudgingly consented to wait for you.
pass.chronicle: Named the Titan behind bronze: Kronos, child-eater, shut in Tartarus.

fail.outcome: You cannot put a name to him, and the eye watches you fail with boundless patience. Only afterward do you remember what Hesiod told of the Titans shut behind bronze doors in Tartarus, and of Kronos their old king, who swallowed his own children and was given a stone in place of Zeus.
fail.chronicle: Could not name the old Titan. It was Kronos, who ate his children.

road.hint: Remember the old king who swallowed a stone in place of his son.

options.label: Open the bronze door a crack
options.warning: Open the door a crack, and I will give you time.
options.outcome: The door moves by a finger's breadth, and at once you feel your years being drawn out of you. Little by little they pass into the crack, and the eye grows brighter as they go, until you throw all your weight upon the bronze and it booms shut. "I thank you," says the voice, "for I had great need of them," and you are left with limbs that are heavy and slow.
options.chronicle: Opened a Titan's bronze door for promised time. He took mine instead.

road.hint: The old god who offers you time has little enough of his own.

options.label: Offer your mana to the old Titan
options.outcome: The magic goes out of you in a slow warm sigh and is drawn into the crack like breath upon a cold day. "Ah, the old power," says the voice. "I am too much diminished to repay you as once I could, but take this, which is the least that I have." Out of the stone a warmth returns into your wounds.

options.label: Press on without engaging it
options.outcome: The light dims as you pass, like an eye that closes. "Another time," says the voice. "I have nothing left to me but time, and one day I shall not have even that."

name: Kneeling Herald
text: In the middle of the corridor kneels a man in the black and yellow of the Locust's heralds, his banner cast down and his hands held high. "Give me sanctuary," he begs, "for I have done with them. I know where the Destroyer is weak, and I will tell you all of it if only you will hide me." As he speaks he glances often back along the way. You see also that his shadow lies the wrong way, toward the torch.

options.label: Hide him in the side passage and hear him out
options.warning: You see also that his shadow lies the wrong way, toward the torch.
options.outcome: He thanks you with tears, but while you are watching the corridor for his pursuers he drives a knife into your back, and then he runs to bring them to you.
options.chronicle: Sheltered a false Locust herald. Should have checked his shadow.

road.hint: Look to the man's shadow, for an honest man's does not fall toward the torch.

options.label: Ask him how he got past the pickets, and keep asking

pass.outcome: He says first that he came past the eastern pickets at dusk, and next that they were the western ones, at the changing of the watch, and at last that there were no pickets at all, since he is a herald and they let heralds pass. You lay the three tales side by side before him, and he hears the flaw as clearly as you. At once he takes to his heels, and from his sleeve falls a folded paper. It holds his true orders, and it names the place to which he was to lead you, so that you may now go round it.
pass.chronicle: Caught a herald in three stories. Have the orders he dropped.

fail.outcome: His tale holds together as far as you can follow it, so that you do not see the knife until he has struck.
fail.chronicle: Found no flaw in a herald's tale of escape. He knifed me.

road.hint: Have him tell his tale again, for a true one will not change.

options.label: Turn him away
options.outcome: He gets to his feet, brushes the dust from his knees and takes up his banner, and then he walks back by the way he came, in no haste at all.
options.chronicle: Refused sanctuary to a herald of the Locust. He left in no hurry.

road.hint: A man who flees for his life will seldom walk at ease.

options.label: Strike him down where he kneels
options.outcome: Before your stroke can land he is on his feet and fighting, more swiftly than any penitent could move.
options.chronicle: Struck down a kneeling herald mid-tale. Too quick to be a penitent.

road.hint: A blow would find the traitor out only by luck.

name: The Twin Flame
text: Along the floor of a burning ditch moves a tall flame with two tips, and from the greater tip comes a man's voice, slow and grand. "Two of us burn in this fire, he and I. You are going downward, as once I went, beyond the pillars where no man was meant to sail. Listen, and I will tell you the short way to the bottom. It is the same way that my crew took." The flame bends toward you. "Consider what you were made for. You were not made to live like beasts, but to follow virtue and knowledge."

options.label: Take his short way to the bottom
options.warning: It is the same way that my crew took.
options.outcome: His short way is magnificent, and it is false. It leads you along a ledge and down a chimney in the rock and round about for some hours, until you climb wearily out of a ditch beside a tall flame with two tips, and hear it laughing at you.
options.chronicle: Took a burning man's short way down. It led back to him, hours on.

road.hint: A grand voice in a flame once persuaded a whole crew to their drowning.

options.label: Name the flame before you take its counsel

pass.outcome: You know this flame from the poem of Dante, for here Ulysses and Diomedes burn in one fire among the false counsellors, because of the guile of the wooden horse. Ulysses told that poet how with this very speech he drew his old crew beyond the Pillars of Hercules into the forbidden sea, and how they sailed five months, until they beheld a mountain and a whirlwind struck the ship and the sea closed over them all. You thank him for the speech, which is a fine one, and hold to your own road.
pass.chronicle: Knew the flame for Ulysses, who drowned his crew. Kept my own road.

fail.outcome: You cannot tell whose voice it is, and the speech is so fair that it is long before you can step back from the brink of the ditch. Only afterward do you remember the Ulysses of Dante, who burns in one flame with Diomedes, and who drowned his crew with such a speech as that.
fail.chronicle: Nearly took a flame's short way. Knew Dante's Ulysses too late.

road.hint: Learn who the counsellor is, for even true words from him may drown you.

options.label: Hear his story, and go your own way
options.outcome: He tells it nobly, the pillars and the open sea, the stars of the other sky, the mountain and the whirlwind. When he has ended you set out by the long way, and the flame watches you go with something like respect.
options.chronicle: Heard a burning man's tale of his last voyage, and kept my own road.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: The flame calls after you down the passage, "Remember virtue and knowledge."

name: Disreputable Imp
text: Upon a crate stencilled with the words 'DEFINITELY FINE GOODS', in a handwriting that changes from one letter to the next, sits a small red creature who is exceedingly pleased with himself. He points at you with a claw as small as a needle and cries, "YOU! You have the look of one with gold and very poor judgement, and that is perfect. PERFECT! I have things to show you."

options.label: Buy something from his definitely-fine crate
options.outcome: He hauls something out of the crate with a great show of labour, for which he needs both arms and one foot. "Finest quality, or mostly! The cursed ones are in the OTHER crate, and I DEFINITELY did not mix them up this time." Then he takes your gold, bites it to make trial of it, and pronounces it acceptable.
options.chronicle: Bought from an imp's crate marked DEFINITELY FINE GOODS.

road.hint: Mark well the changing handwriting on the crate before you buy.

options.label: Look for the catch in his bargain

pass.outcome: He offers you a ring at a tenth of its price, and you turn it over until you find within it a hair-thin line of runes, saying that whoever wears it shall pay later, with interest. It is the oldest of devils' bargains, such as Marlowe's Faustus signed for twenty-four years of all that he desired, and his reckoning fell due at midnight. "FINE!" howls the imp, and he gives you an honest potion if only you will go away and stop explaining such things in front of the merchandise.
pass.chronicle: Imp's ring has a catch: pay later, with interest. He paid me to go.

fail.outcome: It seems a fine ring at a tenth of its price, and so you put it on, and at once you learn that it is nothing of the kind. A devil's bargain always falls due, as Faustus found when his twenty-four years were spent. You work it off again, but for a while the cold of it lingers in your fingers.
fail.chronicle: Took an imp's bargain without looking. It had a catch.

road.hint: A bargain with one from below always falls due.

options.label: "No thank you, actually."
options.outcome: His face falls in the most tragic despair. "NO, no, no! Do you know how few come this deep? Do you know how long I have been waiting?" And as you go he calls after you, "I shall be here! I am always here!"

name: Medical Construct
text: In an alcove stands a golem of white stone, and the sign of serpent and staff that is graven on its breast has been worn almost smooth by the centuries. It turns toward you with great care, as one that was made for the handling of fragile things. "SUBJECT ASSESSED: ALIVE. CONDITION: SUBOPTIMAL. SERVICES AVAILABLE. INDICATE REQUIREMENT."

options.label: Request wound treatment
options.outcome: It labours upon you without passion, as it has laboured for seven hundred years, finding the work neither wearisome nor pleasant, but only right and fitting. When it has finished your wounds are closed and your breath comes evenly, and it has slipped a little receipt into your pocket, written in a tongue that may be spoken no longer.
options.chronicle: Paid a stone healing golem to patch me up.

road.hint: The stone healer will not shrink from any wound.

options.label: Read the symbol on its chest aloud

pass.outcome: "It is the rod of Asclepius," you say, "one serpent upon one staff, the healer's sign." The caduceus with its two snakes and its wings belongs to Hermes the messenger, but an army doctor confused the two in 1902, and a great many hospitals have borne the mistake upon their signs ever since. The eyes of the golem brighten. "CORRECT. RARE. PATIENT ELIGIBLE FOR COURTESY TREATMENT." And it tends you without any fee.
pass.chronicle: Read the golem's rod of Asclepius, one serpent. It healed me free.

fail.outcome: "Is it the caduceus?" you ask. "INCORRECT," says the golem, and it sounds weary. "CADUCEUS: TWO SERPENTS, WINGS. HERMES. MESSENGERS AND MERCHANTS. ROD OF ASCLEPIUS: ONE SERPENT. HEALING. A COMMON ERROR." It will still tend you, though at the usual price.
fail.chronicle: Misread golem's sign: one serpent Asclepius, two with wings Hermes.

road.hint: The healer's staff bears but a single serpent.

options.label: Request a restoration of drained strength
options.outcome: "DEFICIT DETECTED. RESTORING." The golem lays two cold palms of stone upon you and stands very still, and all that the dark had taken from you piece by piece comes flooding back at once.
options.chronicle: A stone golem restored what the drainers took from me.

road.hint: What has been drained from you may here be given back.

options.label: "I am fine. Thank you."
options.outcome: It considers this for a space. "ASSESSMENT INDICATES STATEMENT INACCURATE. HOWEVER: PATIENT AUTONOMY PROTOCOLS APPLY." Then it steps back into its alcove and says, "SAFE TRAVELS, SUBJECT," and against all likelihood it sounds as though it means what it says.

name: Berengar the Gold
text: A warrior of great stature has slumped against the wall with his golden armor broken, and from a dozen wounds he bleeds light in place of blood. "I had come almost to the bottom once," he says hoarsely, "when the thing with a thousand mouths found me. I shall go no farther, but there is breath yet in you."

options.label: Give him bread for the road, and the words that go with it

pass.outcome: You break the bread and give it to him after the old custom, as viaticum, the dying knight's last bread, whose name means provision for the journey. His face is eased. "Then I go provisioned," he says, and lays the hilt of his sword against your own. "Take the edge from Berengar's blade and let it taste whatever lies below, and say my name to it when you strike." After that he passes quietly, with the bread in his hand.
pass.chronicle: Gave Berengar the Gold his viaticum bread. My blade has his edge.

fail.outcome: You give him the bread without the words, for you do not know them, and he eats a little none the less. "Viaticum," he says in your stead. "It is food for the road, and someone ought to know it." He is gone before he can say more.
fail.chronicle: Gave a dying knight bread, not the words: viaticum, food for the road.

road.hint: A dying man may need bread for the journey before him.

options.label: Sit with him a while
options.outcome: Neither of you speaks, and your silence is the fellowship of those who know the price of this place. When at last he lies still you feel something settle softly over you, the final wish of a dying man that another should live, and you know yourself blessed.
options.chronicle: Sat with a dying hero once near the bottom. He told what found him.
