road.hint: The last hero to come so far may leave a warning with one who sits beside him.

options.label: Keep moving, there is no time
options.outcome: He lays no blame on you, but follows you with eyes that have seen too many pass him by. As you round the corner you hear him whisper something, and it may be a name or it may be a prayer.

name: Simon the Sorcerer
text: A man in a magician's robe that is scorched along the hem sits upon a chest that gives out the heat of the Pit, with trays of bottles and scrolls spread before him, and his feet are blackened as if they had been held in fire. "I am Simon, of Samaria," he says, "and I sell holy things, healing and blessing and wonders. Once I tried to buy them from a fisherman, and he would not sell. Now I sell them myself, for everything has a price."

options.label: Buy one of his healing draughts
options.outcome: He takes your coin greedily and hands you a bottle, which holds a common potion and will work as any potion works. "Here is a blessing," he says, though there is no more in it than the draught itself, and that has ever been the trouble with his wares.
options.chronicle: Bought a plain potion from the damned sorcerer who sells blessings.

road.hint: So far down, the last merchant may ask what price he likes.

options.label: Buy a scroll from him
options.outcome: He sells you a scroll that is sealed with wax in the shape of a coin. "Here is wisdom," he says, "and it has been paid for."

options.label: Ask him who the fisherman was

pass.outcome: "It was Peter," you say. When Simon of Samaria saw the apostles lay hands upon the people he offered Peter money for the same power, and "Thy money perish with thee," Peter told him, "because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money." Therefore the buying and selling of holy things is called simony after his name, and therefore Dante set the simonists head downward in holes of fire, with their feet burning. Simon looks long at his own feet, and then he pushes a handful of your coins back across the tray as if they had begun to burn him.
pass.chronicle: Named Peter to Simon Magus, the first simonist. He gave me coin back.

fail.outcome: "A fisherman," he says bitterly, "and Peter was his name. He told me that my money might perish with me, because I thought that a gift could be bought, and afterward they named a sin after me and called it simony." And he returns to the ordering of his blessings.
fail.chronicle: Met Simon Magus of simony, who tried to buy God's gift from Peter.

road.hint: A sin was named for the man who would have bought a holy gift.

options.label: Leave him to his trays
options.outcome: "Everything has a price," he calls after you, while the smoke goes up from his feet.

name: Publius Quinctilius Varus
text: A man in Roman armour stands rigidly above a map of battle drawn upon the floor in chalk that will not smudge, and on it are a forest, a road, and three marks for three legions. Beneath his breastplate is the wound of a sword, of which he seems to know nothing. He lifts to you the bright and staring eyes of one who has waited a very long while. "Soldier, give me your report," he commands. "Where are my legions?"

options.label: Play along and give him a "report"
options.outcome: You invent a battle for him, and he listens with fierce and thankful attention, marking his map. "Good. Then the Nineteenth must march," he says, and grips your arm. You go from him with a quicker step and a heavier heart.

options.label: Tell him the truth about his legions

pass.outcome: You tell him without softening, as a soldier should, of the Teutoburg Forest in the ninth year of the age, and the ambush on the narrow road in the rain that was laid by Arminius, whom he had trusted as a friend. The Seventeenth, Eighteenth and Nineteenth, three legions, were lost with their eagles, and Varus fell upon his own sword. In Rome, they say, Augustus beat his head against a door and cried, "Varus, give me back my legions!" and later Germanicus won two of the eagles back. Varus hears you to the end. Then with his foot he wipes the chalk legions away, and he salutes you, and gives you the last thing that he has to give.
pass.chronicle: Told Varus of his three legions lost at Teutoburg. He saluted.

fail.outcome: Though you tell him that they were lost you cannot say where or how, and he perceives that you do not know. "Then you are no soldier of mine," he says, and turns back to the map. Three legions fell to the ambush of Arminius in the Teutoburg Forest, and it is the one tale that he will not suffer to be told vaguely.
fail.chronicle: Could not say how the Roman's legions fell. He would not hear me.

road.hint: Three legions of Rome were lost in a German forest.

options.label: Salute and move on
options.outcome: He returns your salute with strict and unbroken discipline. "At ease, soldier," he says. You pass by his army of chalk and his enemy of chalk and his single chalk mark, and you do not look back, so that he may keep his long vigil unwatched and with honour.

name: Cassandra
text: A woman kneels in the midst of the corridor, and though the tears run freely down her face it is serene, as is the face of one who has long been reconciled to going unheeded. "I am Cassandra of Troy, and I told them of the horse," she says. "I know what you will meet. I have told it many times to many people, and none believed me until the thing was done."

options.label: "Tell me anyway. I will listen."

pass.outcome: You know her curse, and so you know how to listen: Apollo gave her prophecy, and when she refused him he could not take back the gift, but ordained that none should ever believe her. Therefore you resolve to believe before she speaks, and she speaks swiftly, as if the hour were short. The locusts, she says, are shaped like horses made ready for battle, with faces like men's, hair like women's, teeth like lions', breastplates of iron, wings like the roar of chariots, and tails that sting like scorpions. "And they may not hurt any green thing," she says, "only those who do not carry God's seal on their foreheads."
pass.chronicle: Believed Cassandra. She told what the locusts are, as in Revelation.

fail.outcome: She tells you all of it, and you listen and nod, yet some part of you does not wholly believe a word, and you can see that she perceives it. The fault is none of yours, for such is the curse of Apollo, who gave her prophecy and ordained that none should ever believe it.
fail.chronicle: Heard Cassandra out and could not believe her. Apollo's curse holds.

road.hint: Believe Cassandra before she has spoken.

options.label: Offer her food to restore her strength
options.outcome: She takes the food in both her hands and eats slowly and thankfully, like one who had forgotten the taste of it. "You have fed a prophet," she says softly, "and the old writings promise some good thing to one who does so." Then she touches your cheek, and you feel the world incline a little in your favor.

options.label: "Prophecy is a burden I cannot share."
options.outcome: "Yes, I know it," she answers simply, and she watches you go with the patient and ruined dignity of one who was right in all things and could help no one. The sound of her weeping does not follow you, and you could almost wish that it did.

name: Keeper of Last Memories
text: A robed figure sits in the midst of softly shining motes, hundreds of them, that drift like sparks from a dying fire, and each beats with a quiet warmth of its own. "Every one of these," it says without turning, "is the last thought of one who did not return. I keep them so that they shall not be wholly lost, and you may carry one if you choose."

options.label: Accept a fallen adventurer's last memory
options.outcome: The mote alights on your palm and melts away, and for a moment you are another, one who died a little farther down, who knew exactly where the shadow-thing lay in wait and had so nearly won through. The knowledge for which that stranger died is yours now, and you feel alike the burden of it and the gift.
options.chronicle: Carry a dead stranger's last memory: a kitchen, someone laughing.

road.hint: The last memory of one who fell is most often of home.

options.label: Leave a memory of the surface world here
options.outcome: You fix your mind upon some bright thing, a morning or a meal or a face, and it rises gently from you and joins the other motes while the Keeper watches. "I thank you," it says. "My store is heavy with endings, and it is well to add to it something that felt like a beginning." The loss settles strangely within you, like a wound that has been tended with care.

options.label: Observe the motes in silence and move on
options.outcome: For a while you stand among the last lights of the lost, and the Keeper does not urge you. The motes drift about you and do not touch you, as though they knew that you have need of your life still, and when you go you feel them watching you with something very near to hope.

name: Roland
text: In a pass between black rocks the dead of a rear guard lie where they held it. One knight still sits upright against a stone, with blood upon his temples, an ivory horn in his lap and an unmarked sword across his knees, and beside him is a great rock cloven in two, as if that sword had been beaten against it. "I am Roland," he says. "Oliver bade me blow this horn, and three times he bade me. It is too late now for those who lie here." He holds it out to you. "Blow it at the Black Gate, where they will hear it in the world above, so that the rear guard may be remembered."

options.label: Swear to blow it at the Black Gate
options.outcome: He lays it in your hands. "Oliver was right," he says. "He had wisdom and courage both, and I had but the one of them." With that he closes his eyes.

oath.what: Blow the Olifant at the Black Gate, so the rear guard is remembered.

thread.hint: An ivory horn waits to be blown at the Black Gate.

options.chronicle: Took Roland's horn. Must blow it at the Black Gate for the rear guard.

road.hint: A horn that was not blown in time may still be blown in remembrance.

options.label: Blow it here, now, for him
options.outcome: You blow it, and the note goes away up the pass, where none is left to answer, for it is far too late for answers. Yet Roland smiles. "There," he says, "so that is how it sounds." And he dies while he is listening to the echo.
options.chronicle: Blew Roland's horn for him in his pass, too late to bring anyone.

road.hint: The horn may be blown here, if only so that Roland may hear it once.

options.label: Take Durendal from him
options.outcome: He strove to break the blade lest an enemy should have it, and he has no strength left to withhold it from a friend, so he watches you lift it. "Carry it well, then," he says, "since I could not break it."
options.chronicle: Took Durendal from dying Roland, too weak to break it or stop me.

road.hint: Roland would have broken his sword before he let another hand bear it away.

options.label: Ask him why he didn't blow it
options.outcome: "Because a knight of France does not cry for help against heathens," he says. "So I answered him, and Oliver said that a brave man who throws away his army is no wiser than a coward." He coughs. "Oliver was right, and I would have you write it down."

name: Boethius
text: Behind a barred door an old man in a senator's toga that has turned grey sits writing by a single lamp. "The men of Theodoric will come for me at the changing of the watch," he says, without lifting his head. "They have forged letters in my hand and would have me sign that I wrote them. I won't do it, and so I am writing this instead." Then he lays down his pen. "Tell me, if a man should lose all that Fortune gave him, is he the poorer for it?"

options.label: Answer his question

pass.outcome: "Then Fortune never gave him anything that was his own," you say, "but only lent it." He laughs with delight, as a master laughs whose worst pupil has understood at last. "That is my second book, of Fortune and her wheel," he says, "and you have saved me a chapter."
pass.chronicle: Answered Boethius. They come for him when the watch changes.

fail.outcome: He nods kindly. "There I stood myself a month ago," he says, "and it will grow easier with time."

road.hint: Fortune only lends her gifts, but she cannot take from you what you know.

options.label: Break the bar and get him out
options.outcome: The bar comes away at the third heave, but he cannot stand, for the questioners of Theodoric saw to his legs a month ago. So he gathers up the finished pages and thrusts them into your hands. "They can kill me," he says, "but this they cannot kill." You go with the pages inside your shirt, and behind you in the darkness he begins the last line again from memory.
options.chronicle: Broke Boethius's cell open. He could not walk. Have his pages.

road.hint: One who will not sign a lie may yet send the truth up the stair with you.

options.label: Sit with him in silence
options.outcome: He writes and you sit beside him. Once he reads a sentence aloud to you, and though you nod he strikes it out for all that.

options.label: Leave him to his book

name: The Bound Watcher
text: In a pit floored with jagged stones a great winged figure lies bound hand and foot, with darkness heaped over him like a blanket and his wings all broken feathers and iron. He lifts up a face of terrible beauty. "I taught your kind the working of metal," he says, "swords and shields and breastplates, and bracelets also, and paint for the eyes. All your wars were begun at my forge, and for that teaching I was bound. Loose one chain, or only listen, and I will give to your blade the last thing that I know of steel, so that you shall never again have need of a smith."

options.label: Loose one chain
options.warning: Loose one chain, or only listen,
options.outcome: The chain parts with the sound of a bell that breaks. He makes no move to rise, but only laughs, and out of the darkness that is heaped upon him something with too many wings comes for you.
options.chronicle: Loosed a bound angel to be taught. Something came out of his dark.

road.hint: It was an angel who chained him, and he had good cause.

options.label: Listen, and take his gift to your blade
options.outcome: He speaks and you listen, and your blade drinks in his words until it has an edge as keen as thought. It is very fine work, but when you look upon it afterward you see your own face in the metal and, faintly behind it, his.
options.chronicle: Took a bound angel's craft into my blade. Fine edge, his face in it.

road.hint: The first smith of war will teach you still, but at a price.

options.label: Name him, and refuse him

pass.outcome: "Azazel," you say, for the Book of Enoch tells of this Watcher, who taught men the making of swords and shields and breastplates, and of ornaments, and all the arts that corrupted them. Raphael was sent to bind him hand and foot and cast him into the darkness in Dudael, to heap rough and jagged rocks upon him and cover his face until the day of judgment. "Here you shall stay," you tell him, and he turns his face again into the dark.
pass.chronicle: Named Azazel, chained by Raphael for teaching war. Left him bound.

fail.outcome: You search for his name while he talks, and his voice creeps into your searching, so that when you tear yourself away your head is ringing with it. Long afterward you remember from the Book of Enoch that this was Azazel, who taught war to men and was bound by Raphael in the darkness of Dudael until the day of judgment.
fail.chronicle: Failed to name Azazel of Enoch in time. His voice got into my head.

road.hint: An old book names the angel who was bound beneath jagged rocks.

options.label: Walk away from the pit
options.outcome: "All of them come back," he says into the darkness, "for sooner or later every man desires a better sword."

name: Sisyphus
text: Up a slope of black scree a man is thrusting a boulder greater than himself, with hands and shoulder and head, as he has thrust it for long ages. Near the summit it slips, as it has always slipped, and thunders down past you, and very calmly he walks down after it. "I am Sisyphus, who was once King of Corinth," he says. "Will you help me push? It will make no difference at all, but I am glad of the company."

options.label: Help him push
options.outcome: You set your shoulder beside his, and together you labour with the stone up the slope for a while, until near the summit it slips and rolls down once more. He laughs. "There, now you know all that I know," he says. Your legs burn, and yet they feel the stronger for it.
options.chronicle: Helped Sisyphus push his stone. It rolled back down.

options.label: Ask him how he cheated Death

pass.outcome: He grins and tells you. When Death came for him with chains he begged to be shown how they worked, and chained Death in his stead, so that none on earth could die until Ares came to set Death free. Later he forbade his wife to bury him and then complained to Persephone below that he had no proper rites, and she let him go up again to scold his wife for it, so that he lived to be old. "The stone is the reckoning," he says. You remember that where Peter's letter speaks of the pit in which the rebel angels wait, it takes its Greek word from Tartarus, this man's own dwelling. Then he shows you how a man may slip a chain.
pass.chronicle: Sisyphus told how he chained Death, and showed me how to slip a chain.

fail.outcome: "With a sword, do you think?" He laughs, and sets his shoulder again to the stone. "It was with a question. I asked Death to show me how his chains worked."
fail.chronicle: Asked Sisyphus how he cheated Death. With a question, he says.

road.hint: A clever king once begged Death to show him how his chains were worked.

options.label: Leave him to his stone
options.outcome: When you look back from the top of the scree he has already come to the bottom, and is setting his shoulder to it once again.

name: Sir Oswin
text: A pilgrim sits barefoot upon the stair, and his feet are so faint that you can see the step through them. He died on this road long ago, he tells you, and walks it still. "The knight from Thale, do you mean? A big man, with a cracked holy symbol?" He points up the way that you came. "He passed me on his way up, singing very badly, and he said that he was going home to testify against his bishop."

text_variants.text: More demons than you can count lie dead in a great heap where the roads cross, and on the summit of it, like a man who has fallen asleep upon a hill, lies Sir Oswin with his cracked holy symbol in his hand.

options.label: Ask the pilgrim about the knight
options.outcome: "He was singing," the pilgrim says again, as though that were the marvel of it, "all the way up. I would never have thought that so big a man could climb so fast."
options.chronicle: Pilgrim saw Sir Oswin go up to accuse his bishop and give Thale back.

road.hint: The knight of Thale meant to pay his debt before all men.

options.label: Close his eyes
options.outcome: The blessed armour is warm beneath your hand, for at the last it let him wear it again.
options.chronicle: Found Sir Oswin dead on a hill of demons, armour on. Closed his eyes.

road.hint: The heap of slain shows how the fallen knight atoned.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: The pilgrim turns again to the rubbing of his feet, though they have felt no hurt for a hundred years.

name: The Fallen Star
text: You enter a chamber whose ceiling has been taken away and deep black heaven set in its place, and in the midst of the air a figure made all of stars, each joined to each, is slowly wheeling. It is beautiful as things are beautiful that were never meant for you. When it perceives you it descends. "We fell," it says simply, "and we have been falling for a long while."

options.label: Ask it to show you the sky it came from
options.outcome: It reaches out a hand of light and distance and touches your brow. For a moment the dungeon is gone and you are in a place immense and cold and wonderful, and you understand why one might be content through all eternity only to be part of such a sky. When you return you bear with you some small portion of that regard.

options.label: Offer to light a path for it with a torch
options.outcome: It looks upon your small flame so tenderly that your heart is near to breaking. "You would light the way for us," it says softly, "who are made of light." Yet for a few steps it follows your torch, and the warmth that it shares with you in return is vast and generous.

options.label: Ask what it was given when it fell

pass.outcome: It grows very still, and then you know it for the star of Revelation that fell from heaven to the earth, and to him was given the key of the bottomless pit. When he opened it a smoke went up as from a great furnace and darkened the sun, and out of the smoke came the locusts, whose king is the angel of the pit, Abaddon. "I opened it," it says, "and I did not know what I was letting out. Go warily, for the smoke is rising still." It touches your brow, and the darkness grows steady about you.
pass.chronicle: Met Revelation's star that opened the pit. The smoke still rises.

fail.outcome: "A wish?" it says, and turns away. Long afterward you remember from Revelation that a star fell from heaven, and to him was given the key of the bottomless pit, and from the smoke came the locusts.
fail.chronicle: Asked a fallen star what it was given. Understood later: a key.

road.hint: To a fallen star a key was once given.

options.label: Stand still and watch it for a moment
options.outcome: You watch while it wheels. The stars of its body beat slowly, and it seems to you that you can almost read them as a tale written in fire across distances past all measure. When at length you go on it watches you depart, and for a while the dungeon is somehow less dark.
options.chronicle: Watched a fallen constellation in a chamber with no ceiling.

road.hint: A fallen star's beauty may cheer one who only stands and beholds it.

name: The Fetch
text: You see it first in a shard of polished stone, a figure close behind you that stands exactly as you stand, yet when you turn there is no one. When you look again into the stone it has left off mimicking you and is watching you instead, with its head tilted a little, like a pupil who has a question. Then it raises one hand and waits for you.

options.label: Raise your hand back
options.outcome: You raise your hand, and it nods slowly, well content. Then it steps out of the stone and past you, so that you feel it go by like cold water, and it vanishes into the dungeon ahead. For a long while nothing marks you where it has walked, for it has taught your shape to the darkness, and the darkness is looking elsewhere.
options.chronicle: Raised a hand to the thing in the mirror. It answered a moment late.

road.hint: The one that mirrors you a moment late is no true reflection.

options.label: Break the reflective stone
options.outcome: The stone shatters and the figure is shattered within it, gently, as a look falls from a face that believes itself unwatched. You stand breathing hard, for the stroke has cost you strength, and yet there is release in the violence of it, and the dread goes out of your body as the shards fall.

options.label: Name what it is, and what it means

pass.outcome: "You are a fetch," you say, "the double of one who lives, as the Irish tell of it." If it is seen in the evening it forebodes death, but seen in the morning it promises long life. It is always night down here, and so you inform it that by your reckoning it is morning and you are newly woken. The figure in the stone considers this, and then with a slow nod it lets you be.
pass.chronicle: Met my fetch. Claimed it was morning, when a fetch means long life.

fail.outcome: "A reflection," you say, and it shakes its head, as no reflection of yours could do. The Irish call such a thing a fetch, the double that is seen before a death, though they say that one seen in the morning promises long life instead.
fail.chronicle: Saw my double, an Irish fetch. Could not say what it meant.

road.hint: A double that is seen in the morning promises long life.

options.label: Walk past without acknowledging it
options.outcome: You feel its eyes follow you from every shining thing along the corridor, from wet stone and a fallen shield and the dark face of still water in a cleft. You look at none of them, and you believe that it respects this, though you are far less sure that it will cease to follow.

name: The Enumerated Self
text: It has a man's shape as a drawing has a man's shape, with limbs of the proper number in very nearly the proper places, yet it is flat in some direction that you cannot name. Without any mouth it speaks to you. "We have been cataloguing experiences, and we have fourteen thousand, nine hundred and two. You have more, and we desire some of yours."

options.label: Trade a memory for its knowledge
options.outcome: Something departs from you and leaves no pain, but only an emptiness where a room of your childhood was, which you can no longer clearly picture. The Enumerated Self shudders as though with pleasure, and in return it lays fourteen thousand, nine hundred and three small certainties within your mind, so that for a brief and shining space the whole dungeon can be read like a book.

options.label: Tell it what it is missing

pass.outcome: "You are the bundle of which Hume wrote," you tell it, for Hume looked within for a self and found only perceptions, one after another, and he called the mind a bundle of them. But Reid answered him by asking who then was doing the looking. The Enumerated Self is still for a very long time. "Fourteen thousand, nine hundred and three," it says at last, "the experience of being asked who is counting." And it gives you what it knows and takes nothing from you in exchange.
pass.chronicle: Asked the Enumerated Self Reid's question of Hume: who is looking?

fail.outcome: You bid it count faster. "We are doing so," it says. Afterward you think of Hume, who sought his self and found only a bundle of perceptions, and of Reid, who asked who was doing the looking, which you never thought to ask it.
fail.chronicle: Met a thing counting its experiences. Never asked who was counting.

road.hint: Ask the thing that counts its experiences who it is that does the counting.

options.label: Back away slowly
options.outcome: It watches you withdraw, and its look is one that it has copied from others and has never felt. "This also we shall catalogue," it says, "the experience of watching something leave." And that troubles you more than any threat it might have uttered.

name: The Black Gate
text: You have come to the Black Gate, which is a gate of black iron set deep within the wall, and beside it is a hornstand of carved bone that stands empty. Up through the bars from the deep comes a wind that is cold and bears no sound upon it at all, and the horn of Roland lies heavy in your pack.

options.label: Set Roland's horn to your lips and blow it
options.outcome: The note goes down through the gate and onward into the deep, louder than any sound you have ever made, and from very far above, as faint as a memory, a great company of horns makes answer. So the rear guard is remembered, and you hang the horn upon its stand.
options.chronicle: Blew Roland's horn at the Black Gate. Something answered from above.

road.hint: Though it is late, Roland's horn may yet be sounded.

options.label: "I lost Roland's horn."
options.outcome: The hornstand remains empty. The soundless wind comes up through the bars, and no answer is given from above, since no call has gone up to ask for one.
options.chronicle: Reached the Black Gate without Roland's horn. Lost it on the way down.

road.hint: If the horn is lost upon the road, the rear guard will go unremembered.

options.label: Keep the horn and say nothing
options.outcome: The gate keeps its silence, and the horn is worth a great price. You pass through with it in your pack, and the wind at your back carries no sound at all.
options.chronicle: Kept Roland's horn unblown at the Black Gate, though he had asked.

road.hint: Should you keep the horn unblown at the gate, your promise will be broken.

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: You go on, and leave the hornstand just as you found it.

text_variants.text: You have come to the Black Gate, which is a gate of black iron set deep within the wall, and beside it is a hornstand of carved bone that stands empty. Up through the bars from the deep comes a wind that is cold and bears no sound upon it at all. The horn of Roland should be lying heavy in your pack, and you find that it is not there.

name: Ruth Gale
text: A sharp-faced woman in good boots comes down the stair behind you two steps at a time, with a lantern in one hand and an old man's chisel in the other. "I found him, an old man in white beside a blank stone," she says. "He was my father, and you were the last one with him." She does not say it as one who asks.

options.label: Ask her if he finished it
options.outcome: "He finished it," she says, and she speaks the words as he must have carved them: THE KING OF THE LOCUSTS IS ABADDON, AND HE CAN BE ANSWERED. "He was right all those years, and I laughed at him." Then she turns back up the stair to sit beside him.
options.chronicle: Ruth Gale's father finished his tablet, and was right. She is with him.

road.hint: A warning finished in time will be read by her who had most need of it.

options.label: Tell her what he told you
options.outcome: She listens with closed eyes and says every word over after you. Then she turns back up the stair with his chisel gripped in her fist. "I'll carve it myself," she says. "I'll do it badly, but it will belong to us both."
options.chronicle: Gave Ruth Gale her father's last warning. She will carve his stone.

road.hint: What the dying man told you may yet be carved by his daughter.

options.label: Tell her you took it from his neck, and give it back
options.outcome: You tell her all of it: the clear eyes and the blank stone, his hand that closed upon the amulet too weakly to keep it, and how you took it none the less. Ruth's knuckles whiten on the chisel, and for a moment you think that she will use it. Then she holds out her other hand and you lay the amulet in it. "He would have forgiven you," she says. "He forgave everybody, and it drove me mad." She goes back up the stair to him, and she does not say whether she forgives you herself.
options.chronicle: Owned to taking Ruth Gale's father's amulet, gave it back. No pardon.

road.hint: The amulet may be given back with the whole truth, though it will hurt her to hear.

options.label: Give it back
options.outcome: "That is his," she says, as one who has no need to ask. She hangs it round her own neck and climbs back to him, and she gives you no thanks.
options.chronicle: Ruth Gale saw her father's amulet on me. Gave it back, unthanked.

road.hint: The living will come asking for what was taken from the dying.

options.label: Tell her it's gone
options.outcome: "It is gone, then," she says, "just as he is." She looks at you for a long while, and then she climbs the stair again and speaks no other word.
options.chronicle: Told Ruth Gale I took and lost her father's amulet. She left silent.

road.hint: The living will come asking for what was taken from the dying.

options.label: Keep it
options.outcome: She has no need to ask whose it is. "That is his," she says, and for a long while she looks at you, and then she climbs back to him without it.
options.chronicle: Kept a prophet's amulet before his daughter. She left without it.

road.hint: The living will come asking for what was taken from the dying.

options.label: Tell her what you saw
options.outcome: You tell her of the clear eyes and the blank stone, and how he bade you go quickly. She turns his chisel over in her hands. "Then it falls to me to choose what goes on it," she says, and she climbs back up to him.
options.chronicle: Told Ruth Gale her father sent me on. She will fill his blank stone.

text_variants.text: A sharp-faced woman in good boots comes down the stair behind you two steps at a time, carrying a lantern. "I found him, my father, an old man in white at his carving," she says, "and he told me that a stranger gave him the hour." She is out of breath, and it is more than the stair that has taken it from her.

A sharp-faced woman in good boots comes down the stair behind you two steps at a time, with a lantern in one hand and an old man's chisel in the other. "I found him, an old man in white beside a blank stone," she says. "He was my father, and his amulet is gone." And as she says it she looks at you and at all that you carry.

name: Old Fisherman
text: In a plain wall is a gate of plain wood, and beside it on a stool an old fisherman sits mending a net, with a ring of keys at his belt and a thick ledger on his knee. He raises his head. "Ah, so it's you, and I have been reading about you. All the people that you met on the way down are in here. Would you like to hear how they fared?"

options.label: "Tell me about them."
options.chronicle: An old fisherman with keys told how those I met fared, well and ill.

road.hint: The old fisherman has a record of all whom you met on the way down.

people_lines.after: At that he closes the ledger and says, 'The rest is between them and me.'

options.label: "Who decides?"
options.outcome: "I'm not the one who decides, for I only keep the door," he says with a wink, "but I do hear things."

options.label: Walk on
options.outcome: He takes up his net once more. "Be careful on the last stairs," he says, "for they are the long ones."

name: Robin Hood
text: A plank bridge, no wider than one man, crosses a black stream that runs out of one wall and into the other. As you set foot upon one end a man in Lincoln green steps onto the other, with a longbow in his hand and a horn at his belt, and since neither will give way you meet in the middle, where he stops and grins. "It's a narrow bridge," he says, "and one of us must go into the water. I am Robin Hood of Sherwood, and who may you be?"

options.label: "A bow against a staff? That's a coward's fight."
options.outcome: He looks at his bow and then at you, and he laughs. "That is fairly spoken," he says. So he lays the bow on the bank, cuts a staff of oak from the roots in the wall, and walks out again upon the planks. "Now, then," says he, and waits for you to come on.

options.label: Cut a staff and meet him on the bridge

pass.outcome: The planks leap beneath you both. He is quick and you are quicker, and with a crack on the shoulder and a sweep at the knees you send Robin Hood from the bridge into the stream with a great splash. He comes up laughing and sets the horn to his lips, and at the sound men in green come out of the dark along both banks to see what is so merry. "Little John served me the same once," he says, wringing out his hood, "and he has been with me ever since." Then he hangs the horn about your neck. "Blow it when you have need of us and we will come, but it can be only once, for it's a long way from Sherwood."

thread.hint: The horn on the green baldric may be blown once, in your need.

pass.chronicle: Knocked Robin Hood into the stream with a staff. He gave me his horn.

fail.outcome: He is quick and the planks are wet, and after a crack on the shoulder and a sweep at the knees it is you who goes into the stream. When you come up spluttering he is laughing on the bridge, though not unkindly. "That was a good bout," he says, and he blows his horn so that his men come out of the dark to laugh with him. And then the whole company departs by the way that it came.
fail.chronicle: Lost at staves to Robin Hood, into the stream. He went his way.

road.hint: Robin Hood makes friends of those who fight him fairly.

options.label: Step back and let him cross
options.outcome: You step back from the planks and let him cross. He makes you a deep bow that is no more than half in jest. "You have courtesy," he calls over his shoulder as he passes into the dark, "though it is of little use in a fight."
options.chronicle: Gave way to Robin Hood on a narrow bridge.

road.hint: One who yields on a bridge will win no place among Robin Hood's men.

name: The Sleepers Under the Hill
text: A ball of thread lies unwound along the floor and runs into a crack in the wall, for someone found this place before you. Beyond is a vaulted hall, warmed and lit by a fire that rises out of the bare floor with nothing to feed it and gives off no smoke. A king sleeps upon a throne with a queen at his side, his knights are sleeping along the benches, and their hounds lie asleep at their feet. On a table by the door are laid a sword in an old scabbard, a garter and a bugle-horn, and in all that company there is none who stirs.

options.label: Draw the sword
options.outcome: It comes slowly from the scabbard, red with ancient rust, and as the blade comes clear every eye in the hall opens and the king sits up upon his throne.

options.label: Cut the garter with it
options.outcome: The garter parts beneath the edge, and all along the benches the knights sit up, as slowly as men in deep water, while a hound lifts its head to look at you.

options.label: Blow the bugle

pass.outcome: You set the horn to your lips and blow, and the note runs all about the hall and returns, and knights and hounds rise up together. The king comes down from his throne and takes the bugle out of your hands. "The hour is not yet come," says Arthur, "but you have done what the last who came here could not." And he hangs it upon you again. "When your need is greatest, blow it, and we will come, though it can be only once." When you look back from the crack in the wall they are all asleep once more, and the fire is burning on.

thread.hint: The bugle from under the hill is for your hour of greatest need.

pass.chronicle: Woke King Arthur. Have his bugle, to blow once in my hour of need.

fail.outcome: Your breath catches in the old horn and the note dies before ever it is out. Already the king's eyes are closing. One after another the knights lie down along the benches and the hounds lay their heads upon their paws, and when you look back from the crack in the wall you see nothing there but a crack.
fail.chronicle: Drew the sword, cut the garter, blew too weakly. Sleepers slept on.

road.hint: The sword, the garter and the horn must all be used to wake the king.

options.label: Let the sleepers sleep
options.outcome: You leave the hall as you found it, and follow the thread out again through the crack in the wall.
options.chronicle: Found a king and his knights asleep under the hill. Left them so.

road.hint: The sleeping king awaits one who is bold enough to wake him.

options.label: Put the sword back and go
options.outcome: You return the sword to its scabbard, and before it is home their eyes have closed again and the king sleeps upon his throne. Then you follow the thread back through the crack.
options.chronicle: Woke the sleepers under the hill a moment, then let them sleep again.

road.hint: The sword alone will not wake them fully.

options.label: Sheathe the sword
options.outcome: Slowly you slide the sword into its scabbard, and as it goes home the light fades from their eyes and the king sinks back upon his throne. Yet before he sleeps he lifts up his hands and says in great sorrow: "O woe betide that evil day / On which the witless wight was born, / Who drew the sword, the garter cut, / But never blew the bugle-horn." Then the hall is still, and where you entered there is only a crack in the wall.
options.chronicle: Drew sword, cut garter, then sheathed it. Arthur cursed me and slept.

road.hint: Who drew the sword, the garter cut, but never blew the bugle-horn.

name: Heimdall
text: The ice opens upon a bridge of trembling colours that climbs out of the deep and beyond your sight, and at its foot sits a tall man clad in white, with a great curved horn across his knees and teeth of gold when he smiles. "I am Heimdall," he says. "I heard you upon the stair three floors above, for I hear the grass grow and the wool upon the sheep, and I have less need of sleep than a bird." He gazes past you into the deep. "And I hear the wolf. He is loose below you, and I may not leave this bridge."

options.label: "What is the horn?"
options.outcome: "It is Gjallarhorn, and it is heard in every world. When the end comes I shall blow it, and the gods will wake, and from the doors of Valhalla will ride the einherjar, Odin's chosen dead, who fight all day and rise whole at evening." He turns the horn in his hands. "I ought to bear it down to the wolf, but if I leave this bridge the giants will cross it."

options.label: Keep the watch with him

pass.outcome: You share his watch while the colours of the bridge tremble overhead, and three times he asks what you have heard, and each time you have heard it. "You listen," he says at last, "and that is good, for none down there does so." He lays the horn in your hands, and it is far heavier than it looks. "Blow it once, where you have need of them, and they will hear it in Valhalla and ride beside you against the kindred of the wolf and all the rest. But they cannot ride against the wolf himself, for it is not given to them to slay him or to bind him, and it never was." And he turns again to his watch.

thread.hint: The watchman's horn may be blown once, where you have need of them.

pass.chronicle: Heard what Heimdall hears on watch. Have Gjallarhorn, to blow once.

fail.outcome: Through all your watch beside him the darkness is very quiet, and you hear nothing of what he hears. "You heard nothing," he says, not unkindly. "Go down, then, and listen harder along the way." And he keeps the horn across his knees.
fail.chronicle: Kept watch with Heimdall and heard nothing. He kept his horn.

road.hint: Heimdall will trust his horn to one who can listen.

options.label: Leave him to his watch
options.outcome: He nods without turning his head, for he is listening to something very far below you.
options.chronicle: Passed Heimdall at his watch by the bridge's foot, and went on down.

road.hint: To win the watchman's horn one must share his watch.

name: The Great Stone
text: A great grey stone lies across the passage, sunk into the floor as though it had fallen from a height, and out of the rock beside it grows a hawthorn, white with blossom that has no place beneath the earth. Caught among its branches is a knotted staff with a chip of grey stone in its crook. From under the great stone comes a sound of groaning, and then a voice speaks before you have done anything at all. "Do not try it," it says. "All who come would lift it, and a hundred men could not. None but she who laid me here can let me out, and that she will not do."

options.label: Try to lift the stone
options.outcome: You get your fingers beneath its edge and heave until your arms tremble, and it does not stir by a hair. "I warned you," says the voice, not unkindly. "Leave your labour; it is all in vain. I brought the Giants' Dance out of Ireland, every stone of it, when no army could shift one of them, and I did not do it with my arms."

options.label: "Who are you?"
options.outcome: "I am Merlin," says the voice. "I read the fortune of a falling tower in the battle of two dragons, and by my art I moved the stones of Stonehenge. Afterward I taught a lady every spell that I knew, and the last of them she used upon me." A dry laugh rises through the rock. "That is my staff in the thorn. I cannot reach it, and it is of no use to a man who lies under a stone. Tell me how the world works, and it shall be yours."

options.label: Answer the voice's questions

pass.outcome: You answer, and beneath the stone the voice is long silent after it has heard you. "Not by strength have you won it," it says at last, "and that is well. Take the staff out of the thorn." The hawthorn yields it as if it had been waiting. "Your spells will come more easily with it in your hand, and no enchantment will hold you but one of your own making, so take good heed to whom you teach such a spell."
pass.chronicle: Answered Merlin at the stone. He gave me his staff from the hawthorn.

fail.outcome: You answer as well as you are able, and it is not well enough. "No, not yet," says the voice, "for it would be of no use to you." The hawthorn keeps the staff, and the voice beneath the stone will speak no more.
fail.chronicle: Failed Merlin at the great stone. His staff stays in the hawthorn.

road.hint: The voice beneath the great stone asks for answers rather than strength.

options.label: Leave him under his stone
options.outcome: As you go on your way the groaning begins again behind you, as low as wind beneath a door.
options.chronicle: Left Merlin groaning under his great stone.

road.hint: The staff in the hawthorn waits for one who will listen.
